when: When you want to combine a large processor with several memory stacks or chiplets and still cool them easily.
3D
When connection length, power and footprint matter most, as in stacked memory.
Together
High-end AI accelerators use both: HBM is a 3D stack of DRAM dies, placed beside the processor on a 2.5D interposer.
faq: What is a silicon interposer?
A silicon layer with very fine wiring, and often TSVs, that connects several chips placed side by side in 2.5D packaging.
Why is 3D packaging harder to cool?
Heat from the lower chips must pass through the chips stacked above them, while in 2.5D each chip can be cooled from the top.
Is HBM 2.5D or 3D?
Both. HBM is a 3D stack of DRAM dies, and it is placed beside the processor on a 2.5D interposer.
What is a TSV?
A through-silicon via is a vertical connection that passes through a thinned silicon chip, used to link stacked chips.

sem-vs-tem.title: SEM vs TEM: Electron Microscopes in Semiconductor Analysis
sem-vs-tem.description: SEM vs TEM compared in a table: principle, what each shows, resolution, sample preparation, voltage, speed, cost and typical uses in chip analysis.
sem-vs-tem.lead: Both microscopes use a beam of electrons instead of light, but they look at samples in different ways. A scanning electron microscope (SEM) scans a focused beam over the surface and builds an image from the electrons that come back, so it shows the shape of the surface. A transmission electron microscope (TEM) sends electrons through an extremely thin slice, so it can show the inside of the structure down to individual atoms. SEM is fast and easy; TEM is far more powerful but slow and demanding.
rows: Principle
A focused beam scans the surface; secondary or backscattered electrons form the image
Electrons pass through a very thin sample; transmitted and diffracted electrons form the image
What it shows
Surface shape and composition contrast
Internal structure, crystal lattice and atomic-scale interfaces
Resolution
About 1 nm at best; typically a few nanometers or more
Below 0.1 nm: individual atoms can be seen
Sample preparation
Little: bulk samples can be used (insulators need a conductive coating)
Very demanding: the sample must be thinner than about 100 nm, often cut by focused ion beam (FIB)
Beam energy
About 0.5 to 30 kV
About 80 to 300 kV
Speed
Fast: minutes per sample
Slow: hours, including sample preparation
Cost
Lower
Higher
Typical uses
Line-width measurement (CD-SEM), defect review, cross-section views of devices
Gate-oxide thickness, thin-film stacks, crystal defects and interface structure
when: SEM
For routine inspection and measurement, where speed matters, such as checking patterns and finding defects.
TEM
When you need to see inside a structure at the atomic scale, such as the thickness of a gate dielectric a few atoms thick.
Together
In failure analysis, SEM and FIB find and expose the problem spot, and a thin slice is then cut out for TEM.
faq: Which has higher resolution, SEM or TEM?
TEM. It resolves below 0.1 nm, so individual atoms can be seen, while an SEM resolves about 1 nm at best.
Why does TEM need such a thin sample?
Electrons must pass through the sample, so it must be thinner than about 100 nm. Preparing it, often with a focused ion beam, takes hours.
What does a CD-SEM measure?
A critical-dimension SEM measures the line widths and hole sizes of patterns on wafers. It is a key tool for process control in lithography and etching.
Why are insulating samples coated before SEM?
Insulators build up charge under the electron beam, which distorts the image. A thin conductive coating, or imaging at low voltage, prevents this.

soi-vs-bulk-silicon.title: SOI vs Bulk Silicon: Differences for Chip Makers
soi-vs-bulk-silicon.description: SOI vs bulk silicon wafers compared in a table: structure, isolation, parasitic capacitance, latch-up, back biasing, self-heating, cost and uses.
soi-vs-bulk-silicon.lead: Most chips are built directly in a plain silicon wafer, called bulk silicon. A silicon-on-insulator (SOI) wafer adds a thin layer of oxide buried under the thin silicon layer where the transistors sit. That insulating layer isolates the transistors from the substrate, which reduces parasitic capacitance and removes latch-up, so circuits can be faster or lower in power. The price is a more expensive wafer and poorer heat removal.
rows: Structure
Transistors are made directly in the silicon wafer
A thin silicon layer sits on a buried oxide (BOX) on a silicon substrate
Isolation
Wells and shallow trench isolation
Complete isolation from the substrate by the BOX, plus trench isolation sideways
Parasitic capacitance
Larger junction capacitance
Smaller, because the junctions sit on oxide
Latch-up
Possible, because of parasitic thyristor structures
Eliminated
Soft errors
More sensitive to charge from radiation
Less sensitive, because the charge-collection volume is small
Threshold tuning
Body bias possible but limited
Fully depleted SOI (FD-SOI) allows strong back-gate biasing through the BOX
Self-heating
Heat flows into the substrate
Worse: the oxide layer conducts heat poorly
Wafer cost
Low
Substantially higher
Typical uses
Most CMOS chips: memory, processors and general logic
RF switches in smartphones, low-power FD-SOI chips for IoT and automotive, MEMS, high-voltage and radiation-tolerant ICs
when: Bulk
The default for mainstream chips, because the wafers are cheap and the ecosystem is mature.
SOI
When low power, RF performance, radiation tolerance or body biasing is worth the extra wafer cost.
faq: What does the buried oxide do?
It insulates the thin silicon layer where the transistors sit from the substrate, which reduces parasitic capacitance and eliminates latch-up.
Why is SOI more expensive?
SOI wafers need extra manufacturing steps to create the buried oxide layer, so they cost substantially more than bulk wafers.
What is FD-SOI?
Fully depleted SOI uses a very thin silicon layer that is completely depleted of carriers. It gives good control of the channel and allows back-gate biasing through the buried oxide.
Why is self-heating worse in SOI?
The buried oxide conducts heat poorly, so heat from the transistors cannot escape into the substrate as easily as in bulk silicon.

igbt-vs-power-mosfet.title: IGBT vs Power MOSFET: Which to Use for What
igbt-vs-power-mosfet.description: IGBT vs power MOSFET compared in a table: structure, voltage range, conduction loss, switching speed, tail current, body diode and typical uses.
igbt-vs-power-mosfet.lead: Both are voltage-controlled power switches with an insulated gate, but they conduct differently. A power MOSFET carries current with one type of carrier and behaves like a resistor, so it is fast and efficient at low and medium voltage. An IGBT adds a bipolar output stage that floods the device with carriers, which keeps conduction loss low at high voltage and current, but makes turn-off slower. The usual split is MOSFETs below a few hundred volts or at high frequency, and IGBTs at high voltage and power.
rows: Structure
Unipolar: majority carriers only, controlled by a MOS gate
MOS gate driving a bipolar output stage, so both electrons and holes take part
Typical voltage range
From a few volts up to about 900 V (silicon); SiC MOSFETs reach several kV
About 600 V up to several kV
On-state loss
Resistive (RDS(on)); rises steeply as the voltage rating increases
Nearly fixed saturation voltage (about 1.5 to 3 V); lower loss at high voltage and high current
Switching speed
Fast: tens or hundreds of kHz, and higher
Slower: usually up to a few tens of kHz
Turn-off tail current
None
Yes: stored minority carriers keep current flowing briefly
Body diode
Built in
None: a separate antiparallel diode is added in the package
Parallel operation
Easy: on-resistance rises with temperature, so current spreads out
Possible, but needs more care
Gate drive
Voltage-driven, with gate charge to supply at each switching event
Voltage-driven, about 15 V typically
Typical uses
Switching power supplies, DC-DC converters, chargers, low-voltage motor drives
Electric-vehicle inverters (silicon IGBTs), industrial motor drives, trains, welding, grid equipment
when: Power MOSFET
When switching frequency is high and the voltage is not too high: power supplies, converters, battery-powered motor drives.
IGBT
When voltage and current are high and frequency is moderate: traction inverters, industrial drives, heavy equipment.
Trend
SiC MOSFETs are taking over part of the IGBT range, offering high voltage with fast switching and low loss.
faq: When should I choose an IGBT over a MOSFET?
At high voltage and high current (roughly 600 V and above) with a moderate switching frequency, where the low and nearly fixed conduction voltage of an IGBT gives lower loss.
Why is an IGBT slower at turn-off?
Stored minority carriers keep current flowing for a short time after the gate turns off. This tail current limits the switching frequency.
Does an IGBT have a body diode?
No. A separate antiparallel diode is added in the package to carry reverse current.
Are SiC MOSFETs replacing IGBTs?
Partly. SiC MOSFETs offer high voltage with fast switching and low loss, so they are taking over part of the IGBT range, such as electric-vehicle inverters.

sar-vs-delta-sigma-vs-pipeline-vs-flash-.title: SAR vs Delta-Sigma vs Pipeline vs Flash ADC: Architectures Compared
sar-vs-delta-sigma-vs-pipeline-vs-flash-.description: Flash, SAR, pipeline and delta-sigma ADCs compared in a table: how they work, resolution, speed, latency, power, area and typical uses.
sar-vs-delta-sigma-vs-pipeline-vs-flash-.lead: An analog-to-digital converter (ADC) can be built in several ways, and each architecture trades speed against resolution. Flash ADCs are the fastest but only a few bits. SAR ADCs are small, low-power and the general-purpose choice for medium speed. Pipeline ADCs reach high speed with medium-to-high resolution. Delta-sigma ADCs trade speed for the highest resolution, which is ideal for audio and precision sensors.
rows: How it works
Compares the input with all thresholds at once using 2ᴺ − 1 comparators
Binary search: one comparator and an internal DAC decide one bit per clock cycle
A cascade of stages, each resolving a few bits and passing an amplified residue to the next
Oversamples with a coarse modulator that shapes noise, then a digital filter produces the output
Typical resolution
4 to 8 bits
8 to 18 bits
8 to 16 bits
16 to 24 bits or more
Typical speed
Fastest: up to several GS/s
kS/s up to tens or hundreds of MS/s
10 MS/s up to hundreds of MS/s
Slowest: up to about 1 MS/s
Latency
One clock
N clocks for N bits
Several clocks
Long, because of the digital filter
Power and area
Grows rapidly with resolution; large and power-hungry
Very low power and small
Moderate to high
Moderate; the digital filter takes area
Anti-aliasing filter
Needs a sharp filter
Needs a sharp filter
Needs a sharp filter
Relaxed, thanks to oversampling
Typical uses
High-speed oscilloscopes, optical and wireless receivers, sub-ADC inside pipelines
Microcontroller ADCs, IoT sensors, general data acquisition
Video, communications and imaging systems
Audio codecs, weigh scales, precision measurement
when: Flash
When you need extreme speed and only a few bits, or a fast building block inside another architecture.
SAR
The default for medium speed and medium-to-high resolution, especially when power and size matter.
Pipeline
When you need both high speed and good resolution, as in video and radio receivers.
Delta-sigma
When resolution matters more than speed: audio, scales and low-frequency sensors.
faq: Which ADC architecture is the fastest?
The flash ADC. It compares the input with all thresholds at once and can reach several gigasamples per second, but only with a few bits of resolution.
Why is a delta-sigma ADC so accurate?
It oversamples with a coarse modulator and pushes quantization noise to high frequencies, where a digital filter removes it. This gives 16 to 24 bits of resolution at low speed.
What is a SAR ADC?
A successive-approximation ADC finds the input value by binary search, using one comparator and an internal DAC and deciding one bit per clock. It is small, low-power and common in microcontrollers.
Why does a flash ADC need so many comparators?
An N-bit flash ADC needs 2ᴺ − 1 comparators, for example 255 for 8 bits, so its size and power grow rapidly with resolution.

latch-vs-flip-flop.title: Latch vs Flip-Flop: Differences Explained
latch-vs-flip-flop.description: Latch vs flip-flop compared in a table: triggering, output behavior, construction, size, timing analysis, glitches and when each is used in digital design.
latch-vs-flip-flop.lead: Both store one bit, but they are triggered differently. A latch is level-sensitive: while its enable signal is active it is transparent and passes the input straight to the output, and when the enable goes inactive it holds the value. A flip-flop is edge-triggered: it captures the input only at the clock edge and ignores changes in between. A flip-flop is built from two latches working in opposite phases.
rows: Trigger
Level-sensitive: acts while the enable is active
Edge-triggered: acts only at the rising or falling clock edge
Output behavior
Follows the input while transparent, then holds
Changes only at the clock edge, stable otherwise
Construction
A single storage stage
Two latches in series, working in opposite phases (master-slave)
Size and power
Smaller, with lower power
Larger, roughly twice the transistors
Timing analysis
More complex: time borrowing across the transparent phase
Simple: setup and hold times around the clock edge
Sensitivity to glitches
Glitches and races pass through while transparent
Immune to input changes between clock edges
Typical uses
Custom high-speed designs with time borrowing, clock-gating cells
Registers, counters and state machines in synchronous design
when: Latch
When area, power or speed justify the harder timing analysis, typically in custom or high-performance circuits.
Flip-flop
The default building block in synchronous design, because timing is simple and robust.
HDL tip
In Verilog or VHDL, an incomplete if or case statement in combinational logic creates an unintended latch. Assign a value in every branch to avoid it.
faq: What is the difference between a latch and a flip-flop in one sentence?
A latch is level-sensitive and transparent while its enable is active, while a flip-flop is edge-triggered and captures its input only at the clock edge.
Is a flip-flop made of latches?
Yes. A master-slave flip-flop is two latches in series, working in opposite phases.
Why do designers prefer flip-flops?
Timing analysis is simple, with setup and hold times around one clock edge, and glitches between edges do not matter.
How does an unintended latch appear in HDL code?
When a combinational always block or process does not assign an output in every branch (an incomplete if or case), synthesis keeps the old value and infers a latch.

jfet-vs-mosfet.title: JFET vs MOSFET: Differences Explained
jfet-vs-mosfet.description: JFET vs MOSFET compared in a table: gate structure, normally-on or off behavior, gate current, noise, ESD robustness, integration and typical uses.
jfet-vs-mosfet.lead: Both are field-effect transistors in which a gate voltage controls the current between source and drain. In a MOSFET the gate is insulated by an oxide layer. In a JFET the gate is a reverse-biased PN junction that squeezes the channel. This makes a JFET normally on and gives it very low noise, while the insulated gate of the MOSFET draws almost no current and makes it far easier to integrate by the billions.
rows: Gate structure
A PN junction, which must stay reverse-biased
A metal gate separated from the channel by a thin oxide
Default state
Normally on (depletion mode): the gate voltage pinches the channel off
Usually normally off (enhancement mode); depletion types also exist
Gate current
Small reverse leakage; it rises sharply if the gate is forward-biased
Almost zero in steady state, because of the insulator
Input impedance
High
Very high
Noise
Low noise, especially at low frequency
Higher low-frequency (1/f) noise
ESD robustness
Better, because there is no thin gate oxide to break down
Sensitive: the gate oxide can be destroyed by static discharge
Integration
Rarely used for large-scale integration
The basis of CMOS: billions of transistors per chip
Typical uses
Low-noise preamplifiers, op-amp input stages, audio and RF front ends, analog switches
Digital logic, memory, power switching and most modern ICs
when: JFET
When low noise and high input impedance matter in an analog front end, such as a microphone or sensor preamplifier.
MOSFET
For nearly everything else: digital circuits, power switching and anything that must be integrated at scale.
faq: Why is a JFET normally on?
Its channel exists with no gate voltage, and a reverse-biased gate junction squeezes it shut. This is depletion-mode behavior.
Which has lower noise, a JFET or a MOSFET?
A JFET, especially at low frequency, which is why it is used in low-noise preamplifier input stages.
Why is a MOSFET more sensitive to static electricity?
Its thin gate oxide can be destroyed by an electrostatic discharge. A JFET has no gate oxide to break down.
Why are MOSFETs used in ICs instead of JFETs?
The insulated gate draws almost no current, and MOSFETs are easy to shrink and to build in complementary pairs (CMOS), so billions fit on one chip.

write-through-vs-write-back-cache.title: Write-Through vs Write-Back Cache: Differences Explained
write-through-vs-write-back-cache.description: Write-through vs write-back cache compared in a table: write policy, memory traffic, speed, consistency, complexity, eviction cost and typical use.
write-through-vs-write-back-cache.lead: A write policy decides what happens when the CPU writes to data that is in the cache. A write-through cache updates the cache and main memory at the same time, so memory is always current but every write costs memory traffic. A write-back cache updates only the cache, marks the line dirty, and writes it to memory later when the line is evicted. Write-back is faster and uses less bandwidth, but it is more complex to keep consistent.
rows: Write policy
Every write goes to both the cache and the next memory level
A write updates only the cache and sets the dirty bit; memory is updated on eviction
Memory traffic
High: every write goes out
Lower: repeated writes to one line are merged into one write-back
Write speed
Slower without help; a write buffer hides much of the delay
Faster: writes complete at cache speed
Consistency with memory
Memory is always up to date, which simplifies sharing with DMA and other cores
Memory can be stale until the line is written back, so coherence needs more care
Complexity
Simple
More complex: dirty bits, write-back on eviction, coherence protocols
Cost of eviction
Cheap: nothing needs to be written
Evicting a dirty line costs an extra write to memory
Usual write-miss policy
No-write-allocate
Write-allocate
Typical use
Some L1 caches and simple or reliability-focused systems
Most modern CPU caches, especially L2 and L3
when: Write-through
When simplicity and an always-current memory matter more than write bandwidth.
Write-back
When performance matters, especially for code that writes to the same lines many times.
faq: What is a dirty bit?
A bit on each cache line in a write-back cache that marks the line as modified. A dirty line must be written back to memory when it is evicted.
Why is write-back faster?
Repeated writes to the same line stay in the cache and are merged into a single write to memory, which reduces memory traffic.
What does a write buffer do?
In a write-through cache it queues the writes to memory, so the processor does not have to wait for them to finish.
Which is simpler for multiple cores?
Write-through, because memory is always up to date. Write-back needs more care, such as coherence protocols, because memory can be stale.

direct-mapped-vs-set-associative-vs-full.title: Direct-Mapped vs Set-Associative vs Fully Associative Cache
direct-mapped-vs-set-associative-vs-full.description: Direct-mapped, set-associative and fully associative caches compared in a table: where a block can go, tag comparisons, speed, cost, conflict misses and uses.
direct-mapped-vs-set-associative-vs-full.lead: A cache must decide where each block of memory may be stored. In a direct-mapped cache each block has exactly one possible line, which is simple and fast but suffers conflicts when two blocks share a line. In a fully associative cache a block can go anywhere, which avoids conflicts but needs a comparison against every line. A set-associative cache is the compromise: a block can go in any of a few ways within one set. Most CPU caches are set-associative.
rows: Where a block can go
Exactly one line, chosen by the index bits
Any of the ways (for example 4 or 8) in one set
Any line in the cache
Tag comparisons per access
One
One per way (for example 8)
All lines at once, in parallel
Hit time
Fastest
Slightly slower
Slowest
Hardware cost and power
Lowest
Moderate
Highest: a comparator for every line
Conflict misses
Most frequent
Reduced as the number of ways grows
None: only compulsory and capacity misses remain
Replacement policy
Not needed: only one choice
Chosen within the set (LRU or approximations)
Chosen among all lines
Typical uses
Small, simple caches and some microcontrollers
L1, L2 and L3 caches in most CPUs, usually 4 to 16 ways
Small structures such as TLBs and victim caches
when: Direct-mapped
When simplicity, low power and speed matter more than hit rate.
Set-associative
The practical choice for most caches, since a few ways remove most conflict misses at modest cost.
Fully associative
For very small structures where the hit rate is critical and the comparison cost is affordable.
faq: What is a conflict miss?
A miss that happens because two blocks map to the same place even though other cache lines are free. Direct-mapped caches suffer most, and fully associative caches have none.
How many tags does an 8-way cache compare per access?
Eight, one for each way of the selected set.
Why are most CPU caches set-associative?
A few ways remove most conflict misses at a modest cost, while a fully associative cache needs a comparator for every line.
Where is a fully associative cache used?
In small structures such as TLBs and victim caches, where the hit rate matters most and the comparison cost is affordable.

mutex-vs-semaphore.title: Mutex vs Semaphore: Differences Explained
mutex-vs-semaphore.description: Mutex vs semaphore compared in a table: purpose, value, ownership, operations, signaling, priority inversion, typical uses and common pitfalls.
mutex-vs-semaphore.lead: A mutex protects a critical section so that only one thread at a time can use a shared resource, and the thread that locked it must be the one that unlocks it. A semaphore is a counter: it controls how many threads can use a limited resource, and it can also be used to signal events from one thread to another. A mutex is about ownership and exclusion; a semaphore is about counting and signaling.
rows: Purpose
Mutual exclusion: one thread at a time in a critical section
Counting: limit access to a pool of N resources, or signal events between threads
Value
Locked or unlocked (binary)
A non-negative integer count (a binary semaphore is the special case of 0 or 1)
Ownership
Owned by the thread that locked it, and that thread should unlock it
No owner: any thread can post or signal
Operations
Lock and unlock
Wait (P, decrement) and post (V, increment)
Signaling between threads
Not intended for it
Yes: for example a producer signaling a consumer
Priority inversion
Often avoided with priority inheritance
Usually not supported
Typical uses
Protecting a shared data structure such as a list or a counter
Limiting a connection pool, bounded producer-consumer buffers, signaling from an interrupt handler to a task
Common pitfalls
Deadlock from inconsistent lock order, or forgetting to unlock
Lost signals and deadlock when counts do not match
when: Mutex
When several threads touch the same data and only one may do so at a time.
Semaphore
When you need to limit how many threads use a resource, or to wake a thread when something happens.
faq: Is a mutex the same as a binary semaphore?
Not quite. Both have two states, but a mutex has an owner that must unlock it and often supports priority inheritance, while a semaphore has no owner and can be signaled by any thread.
When do I need a counting semaphore?
When you must limit how many threads use a resource, such as a pool of N connections, or count the available items in a producer-consumer buffer.
What is a deadlock?

A situation where threads wait for each other forever, for example thread A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2 while thread B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1. Taking locks in a consistent order avoids it.
What is the difference between a spinlock and a mutex?
A spinlock busy-waits and suits very short waits on multicore systems. A mutex puts the waiting thread to sleep, which is better for longer waits.

static-vs-dynamic-linking.title: Static vs Dynamic Linking: Differences Explained
static-vs-dynamic-linking.description: Static vs dynamic linking compared in a table: when linking happens, executable size, memory use, updates, start-up, deployment, performance and typical uses.
static-vs-dynamic-linking.lead: Linking joins your compiled code with the library code it uses. With static linking, the needed library code is copied into the executable at build time, so the program is self-contained. With dynamic linking, the executable only records which shared libraries it needs, and the operating system loads them when the program starts, so many programs can share one copy. Static is simpler to deploy; dynamic saves memory and makes updates easier.
rows: When it happens
At build time: library code is copied into the executable
At load or run time: a dynamic linker finds and maps shared libraries (.so, .dll)
Executable size
Larger
Smaller
Memory use
Each program carries its own copy of the library code
One copy of a shared library can be shared by many processes
Updates and security fixes
The program must be rebuilt and redistributed
Update the library once; programs benefit without rebuilding (if the interface stays compatible)
Start-up time
Slightly faster
Slightly slower: symbols must be resolved (often lazily)
Deployment
Self-contained: runs without the libraries being installed
Needs the right library versions on the target system, or the program fails to start
Run-time cost
Allows whole-program optimization and direct calls
Small overhead from indirect calls through the GOT and PLT
Version problems
None at run time
Possible mismatches between the program and the installed library
Typical uses
Embedded firmware, single-file tools, minimal containers
Most programs on general-purpose operating systems, plug-ins, system libraries such as libc
when: Static
When you want a self-contained binary that runs anywhere, or when there is no operating system loader, as in embedded firmware.
Dynamic
When many programs share the same libraries and you want to save memory and patch libraries centrally.
faq: Why does my program fail with a missing library error?
It was dynamically linked, and the shared library it needs (a .so or .dll file) is not installed on that computer. Install the library or link the program statically.
Does dynamic linking save memory?
Yes. One copy of a shared library in RAM can be shared by many processes.
Is static linking faster?
Slightly. It avoids resolving symbols at start-up and the indirect calls through the GOT and PLT, and it allows whole-program optimization.
Why does dynamic linking help with security updates?
A shared library can be patched once, and every program that uses it benefits without being rebuilt.

interrupt-vs-polling.title: Interrupt vs Polling: Differences and When to Use Each
interrupt-vs-polling.description: Interrupt vs polling compared in a table: how each works, CPU use, latency, overhead, complexity, power and typical uses in embedded and operating systems.
interrupt-vs-polling.lead: There are two ways for a processor to learn that a device needs attention. With polling, the CPU keeps checking the device status in a loop. With interrupts, the device signals the CPU, which pauses what it is doing, runs a small handler and then resumes. Polling is simple and predictable but wastes time; interrupts are efficient and responsive but add overhead and make the program harder to reason about.
rows: How it works
The CPU repeatedly reads a status register to see whether the device is ready
The device raises a signal; the CPU suspends its work and runs an interrupt handler (ISR)
CPU use while waiting
Busy: the CPU spends cycles checking
Free: the CPU can do other work or sleep
Response time
Set by how often the loop checks; predictable
Fast (microseconds), but varies with masking, priority and context saving
Overhead
Constant, even when nothing happens
A cost per event; a very high event rate can overwhelm the CPU (interrupt storm)
Complexity
Simple to write and debug
More complex: handlers must be short, and shared data with the main code needs care (volatile, atomic access)
Power
Keeps the CPU awake
Allows low-power sleep until an event wakes the CPU
Timing behavior
Easy to reason about
Concurrency bugs are possible between handler and main code
Typical uses
Very fast or continuous events, simple programs, high-speed networking drivers
Timers, buttons, communication events, sensor alerts, waking from sleep
when: Polling
When events are frequent or the loop is simple, and you want predictable timing without handler complexity.
Interrupt
When events are rare or unpredictable, you want a quick response and low power, and the CPU has other work to do.
Hybrid
Some systems combine them: an interrupt announces the first event, and the driver then polls while traffic is heavy, as in high-speed network drivers.
faq: Which is better, interrupts or polling?
Neither always. Interrupts give a fast response and let the CPU sleep, while polling is simple and predictable. Use interrupts for rare events and polling for very frequent ones.
What should an interrupt handler do?
Be short: do the minimum, set a flag or queue the work, and return. Long work or blocking calls inside a handler hurt responsiveness.
What is an interrupt storm?
When events arrive so fast that the CPU spends all its time entering and leaving handlers. High-speed network drivers switch to polling in that case.
Why do interrupts save power?
The CPU can sleep until an event wakes it, instead of waking up constantly to check.

dma-vs-programmed-io.title: DMA vs Programmed I/O: Differences Explained
dma-vs-programmed-io.description: DMA vs programmed I/O (PIO) compared in a table: who moves the data, CPU load, throughput, setup cost, complexity, bus use and typical uses.
dma-vs-programmed-io.lead: There are two ways to move data between a device and memory. In programmed I/O (PIO), the CPU itself reads or writes every word through registers. In direct memory access (DMA), a DMA controller moves the data on its own, and the CPU only sets up the transfer and is notified when it is done. DMA frees the CPU and handles large transfers much faster, but it needs more setup and care.
rows: Who moves the data
The CPU, word by word, with load and store instructions
A DMA controller or the device itself, directly to or from memory
CPU load
High: the CPU is busy during the whole transfer
Low: the CPU sets up the transfer and does other work
Throughput for large transfers
Limited by the CPU speed
High
Setup overhead
None
Needs an address, a length or descriptors, and completion handling
Small transfers
Often faster, because there is no setup
The setup cost can outweigh the benefit
Complexity
Simple
More complex: descriptor rings, buffer alignment, cache coherency and IOMMU settings
Memory bus use
Through the CPU
The DMA engine competes with the CPU for memory bandwidth
Typical uses
Small control registers, simple sensors, legacy PIO modes
SSDs and NVMe, network cards, audio buffers, ADC sample streams, GPU transfers
when: PIO
When transfers are tiny or rare, and simplicity matters more than CPU time.
DMA
When transfers are large or continuous and you do not want the CPU tied up: storage, networking, streaming data.
Watch out
With DMA, make sure the CPU cache and memory agree before the device reads or after it writes (flush or invalidate the cache, or use coherent memory).
faq: Why does DMA reduce the CPU load?
A DMA controller moves the data itself, so the CPU only sets up the transfer and is notified when it is done.
Is DMA always faster?
No. For tiny transfers the setup cost can outweigh the benefit, and programmed I/O can be faster.
What is a DMA descriptor ring?
A ring of descriptors in memory, each describing a buffer. The device and the driver pass buffers back and forth through it, as in network cards and NVMe drives.
Why does cache coherency matter with DMA?
The device reads and writes memory directly, so the CPU cache may hold stale data. Software must flush or invalidate the cache, or use coherent memory.

ddr4-vs-ddr5.title: DDR4 vs DDR5: Differences and Is It Worth Upgrading
ddr4-vs-ddr5.description: DDR4 vs DDR5 compared in a table: speed, voltage, channel structure, burst length, banks, on-die ECC, power management, latency, bandwidth and compatibility.
ddr4-vs-ddr5.lead: DDR5 is the successor to DDR4 and roughly doubles the starting data rate, lowers the voltage and changes how a memory module is organized: each module has two independent 32-bit subchannels, and the power regulator moves onto the module. It also adds error correction inside the chip. The catch is that DDR5 and DDR4 are not interchangeable, and the higher latency measured in clock cycles means real-world gains depend on the workload.
rows: Introduced
About 2014
About 2020 to 2021
Supply voltage
Data rate
1,600 to 3,200 MT/s (standard speeds)
Starts at 4,800 MT/s; standard speeds reach 6,400 MT/s and beyond
Bandwidth of a 64-bit channel
About 25.6 GB/s at 3,200 MT/s
About 51.2 GB/s at 6,400 MT/s
Channels per module
One 64-bit channel
Two independent 32-bit subchannels
Prefetch and burst length
8n prefetch, burst length 8
16n prefetch, burst length 16
Banks
16 banks in 4 bank groups (typical x8 chips)
32 banks in 8 bank groups
Chip capacity
Up to 16 Gbit per die
Specification allows up to 64 Gbit per die
Error correction
No built-in correction (ECC modules add extra chips)
On-die ECC built into every chip
Power management
On the motherboard
On the module (a PMIC)
Latency
Lower in clock cycles
Higher in clock cycles, so latency in nanoseconds is similar at first
Compatibility
Its own slot
A different slot: not interchangeable with DDR4
when: DDR4
Still a sound, cheaper choice for existing systems and for workloads that are not bandwidth-limited.
DDR5
The choice for new systems, high core counts, integrated graphics and anything that needs memory bandwidth: servers, content creation, modern gaming platforms.
Note
You cannot mix them: the platform (CPU and motherboard) decides which type you can use.
faq: Is DDR5 faster than DDR4?

Its data rate is higher: DDR5 starts at 4,800 MT/s while standard DDR4 tops out around 3,200 MT/s, which doubles the bandwidth per channel. Latency in nanoseconds is similar at first, so everyday tasks may not feel much faster.
Can I use DDR5 in a DDR4 slot?
No. The slots are keyed differently and the electrical design is different, so the two types are not interchangeable. Your CPU and motherboard decide which type you can use.
What is on-die ECC in DDR5?
Every DDR5 chip has error correction built into the chip itself, which improves reliability at high densities. It is not the same as full ECC memory, which protects the data on the module bus.
Why does DDR5 have two subchannels per module?
Each DDR5 module has two independent 32-bit subchannels instead of one 64-bit channel. This improves efficiency, because two accesses can be in flight at the same time.

pcie-3-vs-4-vs-5-vs-6.title: PCIe 3.0 vs 4.0 vs 5.0 vs 6.0: Speed and Differences
pcie-3-vs-4-vs-5-vs-6.description: PCIe 3.0, 4.0, 5.0 and 6.0 compared in a table: transfer rate, bandwidth per lane and per x4 and x16 link, encoding, signaling and typical devices.
pcie-3-vs-4-vs-5-vs-6.lead: PCI Express doubles its per-lane transfer rate with each generation, so a link of the same width gets twice the bandwidth: 3.0 runs at 8 GT/s, 4.0 at 16 GT/s, 5.0 at 32 GT/s and 6.0 at 64 GT/s. Generations 3 to 5 use simple two-level signaling, while 6.0 switches to four-level PAM4 with forward error correction. Every generation is backward and forward compatible, so a device simply runs at the highest speed that both sides support.
rows: Introduced
2022 (specification)
Transfer rate per lane
8 GT/s
16 GT/s
32 GT/s
64 GT/s
Signaling and encoding
PAM4 with forward error correction and fixed-size FLIT packets
Bandwidth per lane (one direction)
About 1 GB/s
About 2 GB/s
About 4 GB/s
About 7.5 GB/s
x4 link (one direction)
About 4 GB/s
About 8 GB/s
About 16 GB/s
About 30 GB/s
x16 link (one direction)
About 16 GB/s
About 32 GB/s
About 63 GB/s
About 121 GB/s
Typical devices
Older NVMe SSDs and graphics cards
Current graphics cards and NVMe SSDs (about 7 GB/s)
Newest NVMe SSDs (up to about 14 GB/s) and high-end graphics cards
Data-center accelerators, high-speed networking and AI systems
when: PCIe 3.0
Still adequate for most graphics cards and for everyday SSD use.
PCIe 4.0
The mainstream today for fast NVMe SSDs and graphics cards.
PCIe 5.0
For the fastest SSDs and the most demanding devices, where bandwidth is the limit.
PCIe 6.0
For servers and AI infrastructure, where very high bandwidth per link is needed.
faq: Does each PCIe generation double the speed?
Yes. 3.0 runs at 8 GT/s, 4.0 at 16 GT/s, 5.0 at 32 GT/s and 6.0 at 64 GT/s per lane, so the same link width gets twice the bandwidth.
Can I put a PCIe 4.0 card in a PCIe 3.0 slot?
Yes. PCIe is backward and forward compatible, and the link runs at the highest speed that both sides support.
What does x4 or x16 mean?
It is the number of lanes in the link. Each lane carries data in both directions, so an x16 link has four times the bandwidth of an x4 link of the same generation.
What is PAM4 in PCIe 6.0?
PAM4 uses four voltage levels per symbol instead of two, carrying two bits at once. PCIe 6.0 uses it, together with forward error correction, to double the rate without doubling the signal frequency.

arm-vs-risc-v-vs-x86.title: ARM vs RISC-V vs x86: Instruction Set Architectures Compared
arm-vs-risc-v-vs-x86.description: ARM vs RISC-V vs x86 compared in a table: design style, instruction length, licensing, registers, ecosystem, strengths and typical uses.
arm-vs-risc-v-vs-x86.lead: ARM, RISC-V and x86 are three instruction set architectures (ISAs): the contract between software and a processor. ARM and RISC-V are RISC designs, while x86 is a CISC design that has grown over decades. The biggest differences are in who may build them and how big the software ecosystem is. x86 dominates PCs and servers, ARM dominates phones and is growing in laptops and servers, and RISC-V is an open standard that is spreading fast in embedded systems.
rows: Design style
RISC, load/store architecture
RISC, load/store architecture, modular
CISC, with many complex instructions and memory operands
Instruction length
Fixed 32 bits in the 64-bit mode (AArch64)
32 bits, plus optional 16-bit compressed instructions
Variable, 1 to 15 bytes
General-purpose registers
31 (AArch64)
32 (x0 always reads as zero)
Licensing
Proprietary: companies license it from Arm Ltd and pay fees and royalties
Open standard: anyone can build a chip without license fees
Proprietary: in practice only Intel and AMD build x86 processors
Modularity
Profiles for applications (A), real-time (R) and microcontrollers (M)
A small base plus optional extensions (such as multiply, floating point, vector)
Extensions added over decades (SSE, AVX and more), keeping old software working
Software ecosystem
Mature: mobile, Linux, macOS on Apple silicon, Windows on Arm
Growing quickly, strongest in embedded systems and Linux
The largest, especially for Windows and legacy desktop and server software
Main strengths
Power efficiency and a wide range from microcontrollers to servers
Customization and no license cost
High single-thread performance and software compatibility
Typical uses
Smartphones, tablets, Apple Macs, cloud servers, embedded
Embedded and IoT, accelerators, education, emerging servers
PCs, servers, workstations
when: ARM
When power efficiency matters and you want a proven ecosystem, from phones to cloud servers.
RISC-V
When you want to design your own processor, avoid license fees, or add custom instructions.
When compatibility with existing PC and server software is the priority.
faq: Is ARM faster than x86?

Not inherently. Performance depends on the specific processor design and manufacturing process. ARM designs tend to be more power-efficient, while x86 designs have often led in peak single-thread performance.
Why is RISC-V free?
RISC-V is an open standard managed by RISC-V International, so anyone can build a chip with it without paying license fees. ARM and x86 are proprietary.
Can ARM software run on x86, and the reverse?
Not directly, because the instruction sets differ. Programs must be recompiled, or run through an emulator or a translation layer.
Which processors do Apple Macs use?
Apple silicon Macs use ARM-based processors designed by Apple.

ssd-vs-hdd.title: SSD vs HDD: Differences in Speed, Durability and Cost
ssd-vs-hdd.description: SSD vs HDD compared in a table: how each stores data, speed, latency, durability, noise, power, cost per terabyte, capacity, lifespan and best uses.
ssd-vs-hdd.lead: A hard disk drive (HDD) stores data magnetically on spinning platters read by a moving head. A solid-state drive (SSD) stores data in NAND flash chips with no moving parts. SSDs are many times faster, silent and more resistant to shock; HDDs cost much less per terabyte and reach larger capacities, so the two are often used together: an SSD for the system and active files, and an HDD for bulk storage.
rows: How it stores data
Magnetic platters spinning under a moving read/write head
NAND flash memory chips, with no moving parts
Sequential speed
About 100 to 250 MB/s
About 500 MB/s (SATA) up to 14 GB/s (fast NVMe)
Random access and latency
Slow: milliseconds for the head to move and the disk to rotate
Fast: tens of microseconds, and hundreds of thousands of operations per second or more
Shock resistance
Vulnerable to drops and vibration while running
Resistant, because nothing moves
Noise
Audible spinning and seeking
Silent
Power
Higher: a motor and head actuator
Lower, especially at idle
Cost per terabyte
Low
Higher, but falling
Capacity
Tens of terabytes per drive
Consumer drives of 1 to 8 TB; larger enterprise drives
Wear
Mechanical wear; no write-cycle limit
Limited program/erase cycles, managed by wear leveling and rated in TBW
Special maintenance
Fragmentation slows it down
Needs TRIM and spare area; fragmentation hardly matters
Best for
Bulk storage, backups, network storage, surveillance and archives
Operating system drives, laptops, phones, gaming, databases
when: SSD
For anything where speed and responsiveness matter: the system drive, applications, laptops and mobile devices.
HDD
For large amounts of rarely accessed data at the lowest cost per terabyte: backups, media libraries, archives.
Both
A common setup is a fast SSD for the system and active work, and a large HDD for storage.
faq: Is an SSD always faster than an HDD?
For almost all tasks, yes. SSDs have access times of tens of microseconds versus milliseconds, and sequential speeds from about 500 MB/s up to 14 GB/s, against about 100 to 250 MB/s for an HDD.
Do SSDs wear out?
Flash cells survive a limited number of program/erase cycles. Wear leveling and spare area spread the wear, and drives are rated in TBW, which is far more than most users write.
Why are HDDs still used?
They are much cheaper per terabyte and reach larger capacities, so they remain the choice for bulk storage, backups and archives.
What is TRIM?
A command that tells the SSD which blocks the operating system no longer uses, so garbage collection can erase them in advance and keep write performance up.

bga-vs-qfp-vs-qfn.title: BGA vs QFP vs QFN: IC Package Types Compared
bga-vs-qfp-vs-qfn.description: BGA vs QFP vs QFN packages compared in a table: terminals, pin count, pitch, size, electrical and thermal performance, inspection and typical uses.
bga-vs-qfp-vs-qfn.lead: These are three common surface-mount IC packages that differ in where the connections are. A QFP has gull-wing leads sticking out of all four sides. A QFN has flat pads on the underside edges with no leads. A BGA has a grid of solder balls across the whole underside. BGAs give the most connections in the smallest area, QFNs are compact with excellent heat dissipation, and QFPs are the easiest to inspect and solder by hand.
rows: Terminals
A grid of solder balls on the bottom
Gull-wing leads on all four sides
Flat pads on the bottom edges, plus an exposed thermal pad in the center
Typical pin count
Hundreds to thousands
About 32 to 300
About 8 to 100
Typical pitch
About 0.4 to 1.27 mm
About 0.4 to 0.8 mm
About 0.4 to 0.65 mm
Size
Compact for the pin count
Largest: the leads extend beyond the body
Small and thin
Electrical performance
Short paths, low inductance
Longer leads, higher inductance
Short paths, low inductance
Heat dissipation
Good, through the balls and thermal vias
Moderate
Excellent, through the exposed pad
Inspection and rework
Joints are hidden, so X-ray inspection is needed and rework is hard
Easy: leads are visible and can be hand-soldered
Harder: joints are partly hidden under the package
Narrow pitch problem
Needs fine vias and many board layers
Leads can bend or bridge when the pitch is very narrow
Moderate
Typical uses
CPUs, GPUs, FPGAs, SoCs and memories
Microcontrollers and older ASICs
Microcontrollers, RF, power management and sensors
when: BGA
When you need a lot of pins in a small area with good electrical performance, as in processors and memories.
QFP
When ease of assembly, inspection and prototyping matter more than size.
QFN
When you need a small, thin package with good heat dissipation and moderate pin count.
faq: Why is BGA used for CPUs?
A BGA places a grid of solder balls across the whole underside, giving hundreds to thousands of connections in a small area, with short, low-inductance paths.
Is QFN easier to solder than BGA?
Generally yes, but QFN is harder than QFP because its joints are partly hidden under the package. BGA joints are completely hidden and need X-ray inspection.
What is the exposed pad on a QFN?
A metal pad in the center of the underside that is soldered to the board to carry heat away, and it often serves as the ground connection.
Which package is best for hand soldering?
QFP, because its leads are visible and easy to reach.

combinational-vs-sequential-logic.title: Combinational vs Sequential Logic: Differences Explained
combinational-vs-sequential-logic.description: Combinational vs sequential logic compared in a table: what the output depends on, memory elements, clock, feedback, examples, timing and how each is written in HDL.
combinational-vs-sequential-logic.lead: In combinational logic the output depends only on the present inputs, so the same inputs always give the same output. In sequential logic the output also depends on stored state, which means on the history of past inputs. Sequential circuits add memory elements such as flip-flops, and are usually controlled by a clock. Real digital systems alternate the two: combinational logic computes between registers that hold the state.
rows: Output depends on
Present inputs only
Present inputs and the stored state (history)
Memory elements
None
Flip-flops or latches
Clock
Not needed
Usually clocked (synchronous design)
Feedback
None: a feedback loop would be a design error
Feedback through the state elements
Examples
Adders, multiplexers, decoders, encoders, comparators
Registers, counters, shift registers, state machines
Timing concerns
Propagation delay, and glitches (hazards) while inputs change
Setup and hold times, clock period and clock skew
Design tools
Truth tables, Boolean algebra, Karnaugh maps
State tables and state diagrams
In Verilog
Continuous assignments or always blocks that set every output in every branch
Clocked always blocks (on the clock edge)
when: Combinational
For calculation and decoding that should depend only on the present values, such as arithmetic and selection.
Sequential
For anything that remembers: counters, registers, controllers, and any circuit that follows a sequence of steps.
HDL tip
In a combinational always block, assign every output in every branch. Otherwise synthesis infers an unintended latch.
faq: Is a flip-flop combinational or sequential?
Sequential. It stores a bit, so its output depends on the stored state, not only on its inputs.
Is an adder combinational or sequential?
Combinational. Its outputs depend only on the current inputs. A counter, in contrast, is sequential.
Can a circuit be both?
Yes. Real digital systems alternate combinational logic between registers, so the whole system is sequential and built from combinational blocks.
Why are feedback loops a problem in combinational logic?
A combinational circuit should have no loops. A loop makes the output depend on itself, which can oscillate or hold a state unintentionally.

compiler-vs-interpreter-vs-jit.title: Compiler vs Interpreter vs JIT: Differences Explained
compiler-vs-interpreter-vs-jit.description: Compiler vs interpreter vs JIT compared in a table: when code is translated, start-up, speed, portability, error detection, memory use and example languages.
compiler-vs-interpreter-vs-jit.lead: There are three main ways to run source code. A compiler (ahead-of-time, or AOT) translates the whole program into machine code before it runs. An interpreter reads and executes the program as it runs, without producing a separate machine-code file. A just-in-time (JIT) compiler starts by interpreting and then compiles the frequently used parts into machine code while the program is running. Many languages mix these approaches.
rows: When code is translated
Before running: the whole program becomes machine code
While running: the program is read and executed step by step
While running: frequently used code is compiled into machine code
Start-up
Fast to start (but needs a build step first)
Fast to start, with no build step
Slower at first, until the code is warmed up
Execution speed
Fastest and most predictable
Slowest, often many times slower than compiled code
Close to compiled speed after warm-up, sometimes faster by using run-time information
Portability
A binary for each platform
Portable: runs wherever the interpreter exists
Portable bytecode, with a platform-specific runtime
Error detection
Many errors are caught at compile time
Errors appear when the faulty line runs
Depends on the language
Memory use
Low run-time overhead
The interpreter itself stays in memory
Extra memory for the compiler and compiled-code cache
Development cycle
Edit, build, run
Edit and run immediately
Usually edit and run, or build to bytecode
Example languages
C, C++, Rust, Go
Classic Python (CPython), Ruby, shell scripts
Java (HotSpot), JavaScript (V8), C# (.NET), PyPy
when: Compiler
When performance, small size and predictable behavior matter: operating systems, games, embedded firmware.
Interpreter
For quick experiments, scripting and learning, where fast development matters more than speed.
JIT
For long-running programs on a portable platform that need speed, such as web browsers and server applications.
faq: Is Python compiled or interpreted?
The standard implementation, CPython, compiles source code to bytecode and then interprets it. Other implementations such as PyPy add a JIT compiler for more speed.
Is Java compiled or interpreted?
Both. Java is compiled ahead of time to bytecode, which the JVM then interprets and JIT-compiles to machine code while the program runs.
Why is compiled code faster?
The whole program is translated into optimized machine code before it runs, so nothing needs to be interpreted at run time.
What is the warm-up of a JIT compiler?
At first the program runs in an interpreter, and the JIT compiles the hot code once it has seen it run often. Until then the speed is lower.

stack-vs-heap.title: Stack vs Heap Memory: Differences Explained
stack-vs-heap.description: Stack vs heap memory compared in a table: what each is used for, allocation, speed, lifetime, size limits, layout, fragmentation and common errors.
stack-vs-heap.lead: A running program uses two main regions of memory for its data. The stack holds function call frames: local variables, arguments and return addresses. It is managed automatically and is very fast, but small and tied to the lifetime of each function call. The heap holds memory that the program requests explicitly, such as with malloc or new, and it lives until it is freed. The heap is flexible and large but slower, and it is where leaks and fragmentation happen.
rows: Used for
Function call frames: local variables, arguments, return addresses
Dynamically allocated data that must outlive a function or whose size is not known in advance
Allocation
Automatic: the stack pointer moves on each call and return
Explicit: malloc and free, new and delete, or a garbage collector
Speed
Very fast: just adjusting a pointer
Slower: the allocator must find a free block and keep records
Lifetime
Until the function returns
Until the memory is freed (or garbage collected)
Size
Limited (typically a few megabytes per thread)
Limited only by the available memory
Layout
Usually grows downward from high addresses
Usually grows upward from lower addresses, so the two grow toward each other
Fragmentation
None
Possible: repeated allocation and freeing can leave unusable gaps
Threads
Each thread has its own private stack
Shared by all threads, so the allocator must be thread-safe
Typical errors
Stack overflow from deep recursion or large local arrays
Memory leaks, use after free, double free and running out of memory
when: Stack
For small, short-lived data whose size is known at compile time: ordinary local variables.
Heap
For large data, data whose size changes at run time, and data that must outlive the function that created it.
faq: Why is stack allocation faster than heap allocation?
Stack allocation only moves the stack pointer, while heap allocation must find a free block and update the records of the allocator.
What causes a stack overflow?
Using too much stack, typically through deep or infinite recursion or very large local arrays, which exceeds the stack size limit and crashes the program.
What is a memory leak?
Heap memory that was allocated but never freed, so it cannot be reused. Repeated leaks make a program use more and more memory.
Do threads share the stack?
No. Each thread has its own stack, while all threads share the heap.

planar-mosfet-vs-finfet.title: Planar MOSFET vs FinFET: Why the Industry Switched
planar-mosfet-vs-finfet.description: Planar MOSFET vs FinFET compared in a table: structure, gate control, short-channel effects, leakage, subthreshold swing, drive current, doping and where each is used.
planar-mosfet-vs-finfet.lead: A planar MOSFET has its gate on top of a flat channel, so the gate controls the channel from only one side. As gates became shorter than about 20 nm, the drain began to influence the channel too much, and leakage and short-channel effects grew. A FinFET raises the channel into a thin vertical fin and wraps the gate over three sides, which gives much tighter control. That is why logic moved from planar transistors to FinFETs starting at the 22 nm and 16/14 nm nodes.
rows: Structure
The gate lies on top of a flat channel
The gate wraps a thin vertical silicon fin on three sides
Gate control
From one side only: weaker at short gate lengths
From three sides: much stronger
Short-channel effects (such as DIBL)
Severe at small dimensions
Strongly suppressed
Leakage current
Higher in scaled devices
Lower
Subthreshold swing
Degrades as the device shrinks
Close to the ideal of about 60 mV per decade
Drive current per footprint
Lower
Higher: the channel width includes both fin sides and the top
Channel doping
Heavy, which causes random dopant fluctuation
Light or undoped, so less variation
Width adjustment
Continuous: any width can be drawn
In steps: set by the number of fins
Manufacturing
Simpler and cheaper
More complex: fin patterning and 3D gate formation
Where it is used today
Mature nodes (28 nm and larger): analog, microcontrollers, RF, IoT
Advanced logic from 16/14 nm down to about 3 nm
when: Planar
When cost matters more than the last bit of speed, and the design does not need the smallest nodes: analog, mixed-signal and many microcontrollers.
FinFET
When performance and low leakage at small dimensions are essential: smartphones, PCs and data-center processors.
faq: Why did planar transistors stop scaling?
Below a gate length of about 20 nm the drain began to influence the channel too much (short-channel effects such as DIBL), causing leakage that gate control from one side could not stop.
How does a FinFET reduce leakage?
The gate wraps three sides of a thin vertical fin, so it controls the channel better and the transistor turns off more completely.
Is planar technology obsolete?
No. Mature nodes at 28 nm and larger still use planar transistors for analog, microcontroller, RF and IoT chips, where cost matters more.
Why can FinFET channels be left undoped?
Strong gate control makes heavy channel doping unnecessary, which avoids random dopant fluctuation and reduces variation between transistors.

von-neumann-vs-harvard.title: Von Neumann vs Harvard Architecture: Differences Explained
von-neumann-vs-harvard.description: Von Neumann vs Harvard architecture compared in a table: memory, buses, throughput, flexibility, complexity, typical devices and the modified Harvard design.
von-neumann-vs-harvard.lead: In a von Neumann architecture, instructions and data share one memory and one bus, so the processor cannot fetch an instruction and access data at the same moment. This limit is the von Neumann bottleneck. In a Harvard architecture, instructions and data live in separate memories with separate buses, so both can be accessed at once. Most modern CPUs combine the two: main memory is unified, but the L1 cache is split into separate instruction and data caches. This is called a modified Harvard architecture.
rows: Memory
One memory holds both instructions and data
Separate memories for instructions and for data
Buses
One shared bus
Separate buses
Instruction fetch and data access
Compete for the same bus (the von Neumann bottleneck)
Can happen at the same time
Throughput
Lower for the same bus speed
Higher, because of parallel access
Flexibility
High: programs are data, so they can be loaded, generated and modified easily
Lower: code and data are kept apart
Memory allocation
Flexible split between code and data
Fixed sizes for each memory
Hardware complexity
Simpler
More complex: two memories and two buses
Typical devices
General-purpose computers
Digital signal processors and many microcontrollers (such as AVR and PIC)
In modern CPUs
Unified main memory
Split L1 instruction and data caches (modified Harvard)
when: Von Neumann
For general-purpose computing, where programs are loaded from storage and flexibility is important.
Harvard
For signal processing and embedded devices, where predictable, high-throughput access to instructions and data matters.
faq: What is the von Neumann bottleneck?
Instructions and data share one memory and one bus, so the processor cannot fetch an instruction and access data at the same time. This limits throughput.
Do modern CPUs use the Harvard architecture?
Partly. Main memory is unified, but the L1 cache is split into separate instruction and data caches. This is called a modified Harvard architecture.
Which microcontrollers use the Harvard architecture?
Many do, including AVR and PIC chips, which keep program memory and data memory separate.
Can a Harvard machine run self-modifying code?
Not easily, because code and data are kept in separate memories. That separation is one reason von Neumann machines are more flexible.

cmos-vs-ttl.title: CMOS vs TTL Logic: Differences Explained
cmos-vs-ttl.description: CMOS vs TTL logic compared in a table: transistors, static power, supply voltage, logic levels, noise margin, speed, inputs and where each is used.
cmos-vs-ttl.lead: TTL (transistor-transistor logic) builds gates from bipolar transistors and was the standard digital family from the 1960s. CMOS builds gates from complementary MOS transistors and has since replaced it almost everywhere. The big difference is power: a CMOS gate draws almost no current when it is not switching, while a TTL gate draws current all the time. CMOS also tolerates a wide supply range, has larger noise margins and can be packed by the billions on a chip.
rows: Transistors
Bipolar transistors, with multi-emitter input transistors
Complementary nMOS and pMOS transistors
Static power
High: current flows even when idle
Very low: only leakage current
Supply voltage
Fixed 5 V (about plus or minus 5 percent)
Wide range, from about 1 V to 15 V depending on the family
Logic levels
Low up to about 0.8 V and high from about 2.0 V
About 30 percent and 70 percent of the supply voltage
Noise margin
Small (about 0.4 V)
Large (about 30 percent of the supply)
Output swing
Does not reach the supply rails fully
Swings fully between ground and the supply
Inputs
Draw current; an unconnected input floats high
Draw almost no current, but unused inputs must be tied to a level
Speed
Fast in its day (74S, 74F families)
Equal or faster in modern families
Integration density
Low, because of its power draw
Very high: the basis of VLSI
Typical uses
Legacy systems, education and old equipment
Nearly all modern digital chips, including processors and memories
when: TTL
Mostly found in legacy designs and when repairing old equipment.
CMOS
The choice for essentially every new digital design.
Mixed
Some CMOS families (such as 74HCT) accept TTL input levels, so they can connect to older TTL parts.
faq: Why does CMOS use less power than TTL?
A CMOS gate draws almost no current when it is not switching, because one of its two complementary transistors is always off. A TTL gate draws current all the time.
What does 74HCT mean?
It is a CMOS family with TTL-compatible input levels, so it can be connected to older TTL parts.
Do unused CMOS inputs need to be connected?
Yes. CMOS inputs draw almost no current, so an unconnected input floats and can cause erratic behavior and extra power use. Tie it to ground or to the supply.
Is TTL still used?
Rarely. It appears in legacy designs and old equipment, while nearly all modern digital chips use CMOS.

rie-vs-icp-vs-ale.title: RIE vs ICP-RIE vs ALE: Plasma Etching Methods Compared
rie-vs-icp-vs-ale.description: Capacitively coupled RIE, ICP-RIE and ALE compared: plasma source, pressure, density, ion energy control, etch rate, damage, depth control, uses.
rie-vs-icp-vs-ale.lead: All three are dry etching methods that use a plasma, but they differ in how the plasma is generated and how material is removed. Capacitively coupled (CCP) RIE applies RF power to parallel-plate electrodes; it is simple, but plasma density and ion energy are hard to set independently. ICP-RIE generates a high-density plasma with a coil and sets the ion energy with a separate power supply on the wafer side, so it etches fast with limited damage. ALE alternates surface modification and removal, taking off only an atomic-layer amount per cycle; it is slow, but gives extremely precise depth control.
rows: Plasma generation
RF power is applied between parallel-plate electrodes, typically at 13.56 MHz. Many tools use two frequencies
RF current flows through a coil outside a dielectric window, and the induced electric field accelerates electrons. A separate bias supply is connected on the wafer side
No fixed method. It is usually done in an etch tool such as an ICP type, switching gas supply and bias step by step (plasma ALE)
Typical pressure
About a few Pa to a few tens of Pa
Low pressure, about 0.1 Pa to a few Pa
Set for each step: gas is adsorbed in the modification step, and ions are applied in the removal step
Plasma density
Lower (about 10⁹ to 10¹⁰ cm⁻³)
High (about 10¹¹ to 10¹² cm⁻³)
Depends on the tool. What matters more than density is that each step stops in a self-limiting way
Ion energy control
A single power sets both density and self-bias, so they are hard to control separately. Dual frequency partly decouples them
Coil source power sets the density and wafer-side bias power sets the ion energy, almost independently
The ion energy in the removal step is set within a narrow window (typically a few tens of eV) that removes only the modified layer without sputtering the underlying material
Etch rate
Moderate (about tens to hundreds of nm/min depending on conditions)
Fast (about hundreds of nm/min to several µm/min for silicon)
Very slow: about 0.1 to 0.5 nm per cycle, and gas switching and purging take time
Directionality
Anisotropy comes from ion bombardment and sidewall protection
At low pressure, ions arrive almost vertically, which favors high-aspect-ratio anisotropic etching
Plasma ALE is directional and can etch only the bottom surface. Thermal ALE is isotropic
Damage
Ion energy tends to be high, so damage to the underlying layer and charging are more likely
Lowering the bias reduces damage while keeping the etch rate
Lowest. Ions have low energy, and the surface stays smooth
Depth control
Set by time and endpoint detection. Stopping within a few nm is difficult
Set by time and endpoint detection. Conditions are switched near the underlying layer to raise selectivity
Set by the number of cycles. It can stop at the atomic-layer level, with little difference between dense and sparse patterns
Throughput
High
High
Low. Used only for the critical final part of a process
Typical uses
Etching oxide and nitride films with fluorocarbon gases, and patterning dielectrics such as contact holes
Silicon and polysilicon gates, STI, metal interconnects, compound semiconductors, deep MEMS etching (Bosch process)
Steps that must stop within a few nm, such as around GAA nanosheets and gates, patterning extremely thin films, low-damage recesses
when: Capacitively coupled RIE (CCP)
When etching dielectric films such as oxide and nitride with fairly high ion energy. The structure is simple, and large electrodes give a uniform plasma.
ICP-RIE
When you want to etch fast but tune the ion energy separately to control damage and profile: silicon, metals, compound semiconductors and deep trenches.
ALE (atomic layer etching)
When you need to stop precisely within a few nm, or etch a film only a few atomic layers thick without damaging it.
Combined

In real processes, most of the material may be removed with fast conditions such as ICP, then the recipe switches to high-selectivity conditions near the underlying layer, and only the last few nm are finished with ALE. Both can also be done in the same tool.
faq: Is ICP-RIE a kind of RIE?

Yes. RIE is the name of the method that etches by combining chemical reactions and ion bombardment in a plasma of reactive gases, and capacitively coupled (CCP) and inductively coupled (ICP) describe different ways of generating that plasma. ICP-RIE is RIE with a high-density plasma and independently controlled ion energy.
What is the difference between ICP and CCP?

In CCP, the single power applied to the electrode sets both plasma density and ion energy. ICP sets the density with a coil and the ion energy with the wafer-side bias, so it can create a high-density plasma at low pressure while keeping the ion energy low.
Why is ALE used when it is so slow?

Each step stops in a self-limiting way, so the amount removed is set by the number of cycles rather than by time, and etching can stop precisely at the atomic-layer level. Damage is also low, so it is used in advanced processes where transistor dimensions are a few nm, only in parts where over-etching cannot be tolerated.

fsi-vs-bsi-vs-stacked-image-sensor.title: FSI vs BSI vs Stacked Image Sensors: Key Differences
fsi-vs-bsi-vs-stacked-image-sensor.description: FSI, BSI and stacked CMOS image sensors compared: structure, sensitivity, wiring, chip area, speed, manufacturing and uses.
fsi-vs-bsi-vs-stacked-image-sensor.lead: CMOS image sensors fall into three structures depending on which side light enters from and where the circuits are placed. Front-side illumination (FSI) brings light in through the front surface, where the wiring layers are, so part of the light is blocked by the wiring. Back-side illumination (BSI) flips the wafer, thins it to a few µm and brings light in through the back, which has no wiring, so even small pixels keep their sensitivity. A stacked sensor bonds a BSI pixel chip to a logic chip that carries the readout and image-processing circuits, making the chip smaller and the readout faster.
rows: Side where light enters
The front side, where the wiring layers are. Light passes through microlenses, color filters and gaps between several wiring layers to reach the photodiode
The side opposite the wiring layers (back side). Light reaches the photodiode without passing through wiring
Back side. The pixel chip has a BSI structure
Basic structure
Pixels and peripheral circuits are made on a single silicon substrate
After front-side processing, the wafer is bonded to a support wafer and the original substrate is thinned to a few µm
A pixel wafer is bonded to a logic wafer that performs readout, AD conversion and image processing. The logic wafer replaces the support wafer
Fill factor and sensitivity
Wiring blocks part of the light, and sensitivity tends to drop as pixels get smaller
Almost the entire pixel area can receive light, so sensitivity is high
Same as BSI
Light at oblique angles
The layers that light passes through are thick, so oblique light is easily lost
The optical path is short, so it handles oblique light well
Same as BSI
Wiring flexibility
Wiring must be kept out of the light path, which limits the number of layers and layout
No optical constraints, so more wiring layers can be used
Much of the circuitry can be moved to the logic chip
Location of peripheral circuits
Around the pixel array, made in the same process as the pixels
Around the pixel array, made in the same process as the pixels
On the logic chip under the pixels, which can use a finer process suited to logic. Some three-layer designs add a memory chip
Chip area
Larger than the pixel area by the amount of peripheral circuitry
Larger than the pixel area by the amount of peripheral circuitry
Can be smaller, because circuits sit under the pixels
Readout speed and features
Standard
Standard
Easy to add more circuitry, so high-speed readout, high frame rates and processing such as HDR are easier to include
Manufacturing difficulty
Simplest and cheapest
Requires bonding, thinning and back-surface treatment (passivation)
In addition to the BSI steps, requires wafer-to-wafer bonding and electrical connections (TSVs or Cu-Cu hybrid bonding), so it is the most complex
Main challenges
There is a limit to pixel shrinking
Dark current from back-surface defects, crosstalk to neighboring pixels in thin silicon (suppressed with DTI), and lower sensitivity in red and near-infrared
In addition to the BSI challenges, bonding yield and the effect of heat from the logic on dark current and noise
Typical uses
Industrial and low-cost sensors with large pixels
Sensors that need sensitivity with small pixels, such as in smartphones and digital cameras
Sensors that need speed and small size, such as high-end smartphones, high-speed cameras and automotive
when: Front-side illumination (FSI)
When pixels are large and light loss from the wiring is small, or when cost must be kept as low as possible.
Back-side illumination (BSI)
When you need to keep sensitivity even as pixels shrink to around 1 µm. It is the standard structure for smartphone cameras.
Stacked
When you want a smaller chip, or want to put high-speed readout and image-processing functions in the sensor.
How they relate
The three structures evolved in sequence. BSI needs a support wafer for bonding, and replacing that support wafer with a logic chip containing circuits gives the stacked sensor.
faq: Why is back-side illumination more sensitive?

In front-side illumination, light passes between several wiring layers before reaching the photodiode, so part of it is blocked or reflected. Back-side illumination brings light in through the back, which has no wiring, so almost the entire pixel area receives light and oblique light is less likely to be lost.
Is a stacked sensor also back-side illuminated?

Yes. The pixel chip of a stacked sensor has a back-side illuminated structure, and a logic chip with readout and image-processing circuits is bonded underneath it. Back-side illumination describes how light enters, while stacked describes where the circuits are placed.
Is front-side illumination no longer used?

It is still used. With large pixels, light loss from the wiring is small, and the process is simple and cheap, so front-side illumination is still sometimes chosen for large-pixel and low-cost sensors.

rolling-vs-global-shutter.title: Rolling vs Global Shutter: Key Differences Explained
rolling-vs-global-shutter.description: Rolling vs global shutter compared: exposure timing, readout, motion distortion, flicker, pixel circuit, pixel size, noise, cost and typical uses.
rolling-vs-global-shutter.lead: Both are electronic shutter methods for image sensors. A rolling shutter exposes each row of pixels slightly later than the previous one and reads them out in order. The pixel circuit is simple and noise can be kept low, but because the top and bottom rows are captured at different times, fast-moving subjects are skewed. A global shutter exposes all pixels at the same time and temporarily holds the charge inside each pixel before readout, so there is no distortion. In exchange, the pixel needs more circuitry and tends to be larger.
rows: Exposure timing
Each row starts and ends exposure slightly later than the previous one
All pixels start and end exposure at the same time
Readout sequence
Rows are read out in order as each finishes exposure
The charge of all pixels is transferred at once to in-pixel storage, then read out row by row
Capture time offset
The top and bottom of the frame differ by one frame readout time (a few ms to a few tens of ms)
None
Moving subjects
Fast-moving objects, or panning the camera, cause skewed distortion
No distortion
Flickering light and flash
Lighting flicker tends to appear as horizontal bands. A short flash may light up only part of the frame
The whole frame receives light at the same time, so there are no bands, and it is easy to synchronize with pulsed light
Pixel circuit
Typically a four-transistor pixel
Needs an extra element to temporarily hold the charge, plus transistors for it
Pixel size and sensitivity
Easy to make small pixels
The storage element tends to make the pixel larger and reduce the light-receiving area
Noise
Correlated double sampling (CDS), which takes the difference between the reset level and the signal, makes it easy to keep readout noise low
Depending on the method, CDS may be difficult and noise tends to increase. Dark current during storage and light leaking into the storage element are also problems
Cost
Low
Higher
Typical uses
Smartphones, digital cameras, video recording, security cameras
Factory inspection cameras (machine vision), barcode reading, automotive driver monitoring, distance measurement such as ToF, tracking for robots and AR/VR
when: Rolling shutter
When the subject does not move too fast and small pixels, sensitivity, low noise and cost come first. It is the standard in most cameras.
Global shutter
When you need to capture fast-moving objects with accurate shapes, or precisely align exposure with pulsed light or a flash: inspection, measurement and applications where machines judge images.
Reducing distortion
Even with a rolling shutter, shortening the time to read out one frame reduces distortion. Methods include faster readout with a stacked sensor and combining it with a mechanical shutter.
faq: Why do moving objects look distorted with a rolling shutter?

Pixels are exposed and read out one row at a time, so the top and bottom rows of the frame are captured a few ms to a few tens of ms apart. If the subject moves in that time, each row records a different position, and the whole image is skewed.
Is a global shutter always better?

Not necessarily. A global shutter needs storage in each pixel, so pixels tend to be larger, and it is often at a disadvantage in sensitivity, noise and cost. Where motion distortion is not a problem, a rolling shutter is chosen.
Why does lighting flicker appear as bands?

With a rolling shutter, each row is exposed at a different time, so rows exposed while a flickering light is changing brightness differ in brightness from other rows, and this shows up as horizontal bands. With a global shutter, all pixels are exposed at the same time, so there are no bands.

ball-vs-wedge-bonding.title: Ball vs Wedge Bonding: Key Differences Explained
ball-vs-wedge-bonding.description: Ball vs wedge bonding compared: bond shape, tool, bonding energy, wire (Au, Cu, Al, ribbon), diameter, direction, speed, loops, reliability and uses.
ball-vs-wedge-bonding.lead: Both are wire bonding methods that connect the electrode pads of a chip to a lead frame or substrate with a thin metal wire. Ball bonding melts the tip of the wire with an electrical discharge to form a ball, then bonds it with heat, force and ultrasound. The ball has no direction, so the wire can be led out in any direction and bonding is fast, which makes it the most widely used method for IC packages. Wedge bonding presses the wire flat from the side and bonds it mainly with ultrasound. It can use aluminum wire and ribbon directly, so it is common in power semiconductors that carry large currents.
rows: Bond shape
The first bond is a ball; the second bond is a stitch where the wire is pressed flat
Both the first and second bonds are wedge-shaped, with the wire pressed flat
Tool
Capillary (a thin ceramic tube with a hole in the center)
Wedge tool (feeds the wire at an angle from behind and presses it with the tip)
Bonding energy
Thermosonic, combining heat, force and ultrasound. The substrate is heated to about 150 to 200 °C
Mainly ultrasound and force. Aluminum wire can be bonded at room temperature
Wire material
Gold, copper (including palladium-coated copper)
Aluminum (thin and thick wire), aluminum ribbon, gold. Thick copper wire is also used for power
Wire diameter
About 15 to 50 µm
Tens of µm for thin wire, about 100 to 500 µm for thick power wire. Flat ribbon is also used
Directionality
The ball has no direction, so the wire can be led out in any direction
Bonds are made along the wire feed direction, so the direction is fixed. The head or workpiece is rotated for each bond to align the direction
Speed
Fast. Bonds can be made continuously without regard to direction
