Slower. Requires motion to align the direction
Bond size and pitch
The ball is about twice the wire diameter. Supports narrow pad pitches of a few tens of µm
The bond is narrower than a ball, so thin wire also suits narrow pitches
Loop shape
The wire rises from the ball, so some height is needed. There are techniques to lower it
Low loops are easy to make
Reliability concerns
With gold wire on aluminum pads, growth of intermetallic compounds and voids. With copper wire, cracking under the pad (cratering)
With thick aluminum wire, bond lift-off and heel cracks caused by repeated temperature cycling
Typical uses
IC packages in general, such as QFP, BGA and stacked memory chips
Power semiconductors and power modules, automotive electronics, RF and optical devices, connections with aluminum wire
when: Ball bonding
When you want to connect an IC with many pads quickly using thin gold or copper wire. It is the standard method for IC packages.
Wedge bonding
When you want to use thick aluminum wire or ribbon to carry large currents, when you want to avoid heating, or when you need low loops.
Telling them apart
If the first bond has a round ball, it is ball bonding; if both ends are pressed flat, it is wedge bonding.
faq: What is the main difference between ball bonding and wedge bonding?

The shape of the wire bond. Ball bonding forms a ball on the wire tip with an electrical discharge and bonds it, so it has no direction and the wire can be led out in any direction. Wedge bonding presses the wire flat from the side, so the direction is fixed.
Why is aluminum wedge bonding common in power semiconductors?

Carrying large currents requires thick wire or ribbon about 100 to 500 µm in diameter. Thick aluminum wire can be bonded ultrasonically at room temperature without forming a ball, and the material is cheap, so it is widely used in power modules.
Why is aluminum wire not used for ball bonding?

Aluminum readily forms a tough oxide film on its surface, which makes it hard to form a stable round ball with an electrical discharge. So aluminum wire is mainly bonded by wedge bonding, and ball bonding uses gold or copper wire.

capacitive-vs-piezoresistive-mems.title: Capacitive vs Piezoresistive MEMS Sensors: Key Differences
capacitive-vs-piezoresistive-mems.description: Capacitive vs piezoresistive MEMS sensors compared: accelerometer and pressure sensor structure, readout, power, temperature effects, sensitivity and uses.
capacitive-vs-piezoresistive-mems.lead: MEMS accelerometers and pressure sensors convert how much a proof mass or diaphragm moves or bends under force into an electrical signal. Capacitive sensors measure displacement from the change in capacitance between movable and fixed electrodes. Power consumption is low and temperature has little effect, but the change is tiny, so a dedicated high-sensitivity circuit is needed. Piezoresistive sensors use the effect that silicon's resistivity changes under stress and read it with a bridge circuit. The circuit is simple and the output is easy to handle, but current flows continuously, so power consumption is higher, and compensation for temperature-induced changes is essential.
rows: Sensing principle
Change in capacitance between movable and fixed electrodes
Change in resistivity caused by stress (piezoresistive effect)
Accelerometer structure
Comb-shaped movable electrodes are attached to a spring-supported proof mass, and the difference in capacitance to fixed electrodes on both sides is measured (differential)
Resistors are built into the beams that support the proof mass, and the stress when the beams bend is measured
Pressure sensor structure
Measures the capacitance between a diaphragm that bends under pressure and an opposing electrode
Four resistors are built into the edges of a thin diaphragm to form a Wheatstone bridge
Signal read
Very small capacitance changes (in accelerometers, sometimes below a fF). A dedicated ASIC that converts capacitance to voltage is required
The resistance change is taken out as a bridge voltage. The circuit is simple
Power consumption
Low. No DC current flows
Higher. DC current flows through the bridge continuously
Temperature effects
Little affected
Resistance and sensitivity change significantly with temperature, so temperature compensation is essential
Sensitivity and resolution
Differential electrodes and a high-sensitivity circuit make it easy to measure small accelerations and tiny pressures with high resolution
Good output linearity. Sensitivity is relatively low, but it also suits measuring high pressures and shocks
Static (constant force) measurement
Possible (can also measure gravity)
Possible (can also measure gravity)
Robustness to disturbances
Susceptible to parasitic capacitance of the wiring and electrical noise, so the circuit is placed close to the sensor
Low impedance, so it is hardly affected by parasitic capacitance
Manufacturing
Made by surface micromachining and similar methods, and easy to put in a small package together with the circuit chip
Diaphragms and beams are made mainly by bulk micromachining, and resistors are formed by ion implantation or diffusion
Typical uses
Accelerometers and gyroscopes in smartphones and similar devices, MEMS microphones, low-power barometric pressure sensors
Automotive engine and tire pressure, blood pressure monitors, industrial pressure gauges, shock accelerometers
when: Capacitive
When you want low power consumption in battery-powered devices, stability in environments with large temperature changes, or high-resolution measurement of small changes.
Piezoresistive
When you want a simple circuit, value output linearity and ease of use, or need to measure high pressures or shocks.
When choosing

The performance of a real product depends heavily not only on the sensor structure but also on the accompanying circuit, temperature compensation and package. Compare power consumption, measurement range, accuracy and temperature range in the datasheets.
faq: Are piezoresistive and piezoelectric the same?

No. The piezoresistive effect is a change in resistivity caused by stress, measured by passing a current and detecting the resistance change. The piezoelectric effect is the generation of charge in a material under stress. Under a sustained constant force, the charge in a piezoelectric sensor leaks away, so it has difficulty measuring constant accelerations such as gravity, whereas a piezoresistive sensor can measure them.
Why are smartphone accelerometers capacitive?

Because they consume little power, are little affected by temperature and are easy to put in a small package together with the circuit chip. The capacitance change is tiny, but it is read with differential electrodes and a high-sensitivity circuit.
Why do piezoresistive sensors need temperature compensation?

Both the resistance of silicon and the size of the resistance change per unit stress (sensitivity) vary with temperature. Connecting four resistors in a bridge cancels part of the effect, and the rest is corrected with compensation circuits or calibration.

static-vs-dynamic-burn-in.title: Static vs Dynamic vs Wafer-Level Burn-In: Differences Explained
static-vs-dynamic-burn-in.description: Static, dynamic and wafer-level burn-in compared: stress method, stage, typical conditions, stress coverage, equipment, monitoring, cost and uses.
static-vs-dynamic-burn-in.lead: Burn-in is a screen that powers products at high temperature and above their rated voltage to remove units prone to early failure before shipment. Static burn-in only applies power and fixed bias without operating the circuit, so the equipment is simple, but stress reaches only limited parts. Dynamic burn-in applies clocks and test patterns to operate the internal circuits, so stress reaches a wider area. Wafer-level burn-in differs in the stage at which it is done: stress is applied to the whole wafer before dicing, finding defective chips before they are packaged.
rows: How stress is applied
Only supply voltage and fixed bias are applied at high temperature. The circuit is not operated
At high temperature and high voltage, clocks and test patterns are applied, operating the circuit while toggling internal nodes between 0 and 1
Power and signals are applied at once to many chips on the wafer through contactors
Stage
After packaging
After packaging
Before dicing (in wafer form)
Typical conditions
About 125 °C, supply voltage above rated, for a few hours to a few tens of hours
About 125 °C, supply voltage above rated, for a few hours to a few tens of hours
The same idea of acceleration by temperature and voltage. Conditions are set for the product and equipment
Stress coverage
Limited to parts biased by the fixed inputs; many internal nodes stay in fixed states
Operating the internals with scan, BIST and similar means stresses more transistors and interconnects
Depends on the method: some apply only power and bias, others operate the chip using on-chip self-test circuits and similar means
Defects easily found
Voltage-accelerated defects in biased parts, such as weak spots in oxides and junction leakage
Early failures can be found more comprehensively, including in parts stressed only during operation
Chips that would fail early can be found before packaging
Equipment and fixtures
Simple: burn-in boards, oven, power supply
Requires boards with signal-generating drivers and the equipment for them
Requires dedicated contactors that contact the entire wafer surface and dedicated equipment, which are expensive
Operation monitoring
Usually none. Pass/fail is judged by electrical testing after burn-in
Some methods monitor the outputs during burn-in
Depends on the method
Cost
Low
Higher
Fixtures and equipment are expensive, but defective chips do not have to be packaged
Main challenges
Low stress coverage
In high-power products, heat generation is large and temperature control is difficult
Reliable contact with many chips, power capacity and heat across the whole wafer, isolating defective chips
Typical uses
Products with simple structures, or where voltage stress is the main concern
High-reliability products for automotive and servers, such as logic ICs, memory and processors
Multi-chip packages that need known good die (KGD), stacked memory, products shipped as bare die
when: Static burn-in
For products where the main defects can be accelerated by voltage stress without operating the circuit, when you want to keep equipment and cost down.
Dynamic burn-in
When you want more reliable screening of products with complex internal circuits, where many parts receive no stress unless the circuit is operated.
Wafer-level burn-in
When you need die confirmed good before packaging (KGD), such as packages stacking multiple chips, where one defective chip makes the whole package defective.
Place in the test flow
The usual flow is wafer test, assembly, final test, then shipment, and package burn-in is inserted before or after final test. Wafer-level burn-in applies stress at the wafer test stage.
faq: What is the difference between static and dynamic burn-in?

Static burn-in only applies power and fixed bias without operating the circuit. Dynamic burn-in operates the circuit, toggling internal nodes with clocks and test patterns, so it stresses more transistors and interconnects and finds early failures more easily.
Why is burn-in done in wafer form?

When multiple chips go into a single package, even one defective chip makes the whole package defective. Burning in at the wafer level and removing chips that would fail early lets you assemble only die confirmed good (KGD).
Doesn't burn-in shorten the life of good units?

It uses up a little, but conditions are chosen so that good units lose only a tiny fraction of their wear-out life. The purpose of burn-in is to get through the early failure period of the bathtub curve before shipment, so that products ship in the low-failure-rate random failure period.

setup-vs-hold-time.title: Setup Time vs Hold Time: Key Differences Explained
setup-vs-hold-time.description: Flip-flop setup vs hold time compared: definition, max or min delay, clock frequency, clock skew, how to fix violations and which corners to check.
setup-vs-hold-time.lead: Both are timing conditions for a flip-flop to capture data correctly, but they guard in opposite directions. Setup time is how long data must be stable before the clock edge, and checks that data is not too slow. Hold time is how long data must stay unchanged after the edge, and checks that data is not too fast. The setup condition includes the clock period, so slowing the clock fixes it, but hold compares the same edge, so lowering the frequency does not fix it.
rows: Definition
The minimum time data must be stable before the active clock edge
The minimum time data must stay unchanged after the active clock edge
What it checks
Whether data is too slow: does it arrive in time for the next edge
Whether data is too fast: does new data slip in at the same edge
Edges compared
The launch edge and the capture edge one period later
The same edge at launch and capture
Delay used for the check
Maximum (max) delay: the slowest path
Minimum (min) delay: the fastest path
Condition (rough)
tcq(max) + tlogic(max) + tsu ≤ T + tskew
tcq(min) + tlogic(min) ≥ th + tskew (tskew is positive when the capture clock is late)
Relation to clock frequency
The period T appears in the equation. It sets the maximum operating frequency
The period does not appear in the equation. Independent of frequency
Effect of clock skew
A late capture clock increases the margin
A late capture clock reduces the margin
How to fix violations
Reduce logic levels, switch to stronger or faster low-threshold cells, place cells closer, split the path with pipelining, slow the clock
Insert delay buffers in the data path, switch to slower high-threshold cells, adjust clock skew
Corners where violations are likely
Slow conditions: slow process, low voltage, high temperature (in advanced processes, low temperature may be slower)
Fast conditions: fast process, high voltage, low temperature, etc.
If found after the chip is made
The chip works if the clock is slowed, at lower performance
Lowering the frequency does not fix it, and the chip does not work correctly. A fix often requires a design change
when: Setup time
When determining the maximum operating frequency, or finding and speeding up slow paths. In static timing analysis, it is checked with max delay and slow corners.
Hold time
When paths between flip-flops are short or clock skew is large. It is checked with min delay and fast corners, and is usually fixed after building the clock tree.
Both together
Fixing one can make the other worse. Inserting too many buffers to fix hold reduces setup margin, so both must be met at the same time in all corners.
faq: Why can't a hold violation be fixed by slowing the clock?

The hold condition compares the same clock edge at launch and capture, so the clock period does not appear in the equation. It is fixed by changing the path delay itself, for example by inserting buffers in the data path to delay it.
Why is max delay used for setup checks and min delay for hold checks?

For setup, the question is whether data arriving at its slowest still makes it before the next edge, so maximum delay is checked. For hold, the question is whether new data arriving at its fastest corrupts the previous data, so minimum delay is checked.
What happens if setup or hold time is not met?

The flip-flop captures a wrong value, or its output enters a metastable state, staying neither 0 nor 1 for a while. This cannot be completely avoided for asynchronous signals, so they are received through a synchronizer of two or more flip-flops.

blocking-vs-nonblocking-assignment.title: Blocking vs Non-Blocking Assignment in Verilog: Key Differences
blocking-vs-nonblocking-assignment.description: Verilog blocking (=) vs non-blocking (<=) assignment compared: update timing, order dependence, where to use each, and simulation-synthesis mismatches.
blocking-vs-nonblocking-assignment.lead: Both are assignments used inside Verilog always blocks, but they differ in when the left-hand side is updated. A blocking assignment (=) updates the left-hand side as soon as the line executes, and the next line sees the new value. A non-blocking assignment (<=) first evaluates all right-hand sides at the same time step, then updates the left-hand sides together. The basic guideline is <= for clocked sequential logic and = for combinational always blocks.
rows: Syntax
a = b;
a <= b;
When the left-hand side is updated
Immediately, when the line executes
Together, after all right-hand sides at the same time step have been evaluated
Value seen by the next line
The new, updated value
The old value before the update
Dependence on statement order
Yes. Swapping lines changes the result
Almost none. However, if the same variable is assigned twice, the later assignment wins
Corresponding hardware behavior
Combinational logic that computes intermediate values in order from top to bottom
Flip-flops that all capture values at the same clock edge
Where it is mainly used
Combinational always @(*), testbench procedures
Clocked sequential always @(posedge clk)
Two-stage shift register (clocked block)
With q1 = d; q2 = q1; q2 also gets d at the same edge, giving only one stage of delay
With q1 <= d; q2 <= q1; q2 gets q1 from before the edge, giving two stages
Swapping values (clocked block)
With a = b; b = a; a and b end up with the same value
With a <= b; b <= a; a and b are swapped
Across multiple always blocks
Blocks triggered by the same edge are prone to races where the result depends on execution order
All right-hand sides are evaluated first, so races are unlikely
When misused
In sequential logic, the result depends on block execution order and may differ from the synthesized circuit
In combinational logic, intermediate values are read while still stale, so simulation may differ from the synthesized circuit or blocks re-execute unnecessarily
when: Blocking assignment (=)
When computing intermediate values in order inside a combinational always @(*), or writing step-by-step procedures in a testbench.
Non-blocking assignment (<=)
When describing clocked flip-flops, as in always @(posedge clk): registers, counters and state machine state updates.
Don't mix them
Do not mix = and <= inside one always block, and do not assign the same variable from multiple always blocks. In SystemVerilog, always_ff and always_comb tell the tools your intent.
faq: What happens if you use blocking assignments in sequential logic?

Depending on line order, a value updated at an edge passes straight to the next line, giving a circuit with fewer stages than intended. It can also cause races with other always blocks on the same clock, where the result depends on execution order, making simulation differ from the synthesized circuit.
Why does a <= b; b <= a; swap the values with non-blocking assignment?
Both right-hand sides are evaluated first using the old values, and then the left-hand sides are updated together. This behaves like two flip-flops whose outputs are connected to each other's inputs.
Which should be used in a testbench?

Blocking assignments are fine for parts that describe steps in order. However, if inputs to the circuit change at the same time as the clock edge, whether the old or new value is captured depends on execution order, so change them slightly away from the edge or use non-blocking assignments.

synchronous-vs-asynchronous-reset.title: Synchronous vs Asynchronous Reset: Key Differences Explained
synchronous-vs-asynchronous-reset.description: Synchronous vs asynchronous reset compared: when reset acts, clock needs, glitch immunity, timing analysis, reset release, area and Verilog coding.
synchronous-vs-asynchronous-reset.lead: Both are mechanisms for putting flip-flops into a defined initial value, but they differ in when the reset takes effect. A synchronous reset captures the reset signal at the clock edge, just like other data. An asynchronous reset uses the flip-flop's reset pin directly and takes effect immediately, regardless of the clock. In practice, a common approach is to assert the reset asynchronously so it acts at once, and synchronize only its release to the clock.
rows: When it takes effect
When a clock edge arrives while reset is active
The instant reset becomes active. It does not wait for the clock
Clock required
Yes. If the clock is stopped, the circuit cannot be reset
No. It works even before the clock starts or while it is stopped
Verilog coding
always @(posedge clk) if (!rst_n) q <= 0; else q <= d;
always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) if (!rst_n) q <= 0; else q <= d;
Circuit implementation
Reset logic is placed before the data input
Uses flip-flops with a reset pin
Area and data path
Gates are added to the data path, which can increase delay and area
The cell is larger by the reset pin, but no logic is added to the data path
Glitch immunity
Strong. Glitches other than at the edge instant are not captured
Weak. A glitch on the reset line can cause a false reset
Reset pulse width
Must stay active for at least one clock period
Even a short pulse works
Timing analysis
Can be analyzed with setup and hold as an ordinary data input
Release timing (recovery and removal times) is checked separately
Care at reset release
Synchronized to the clock, so problems are unlikely within the same clock domain
If release is close to a clock edge, flip-flops may leave reset in different cycles or go metastable. A reset synchronizer aligns the release to the clock
Suited to
Circuits whose clock always runs, circuits where the reset signal is prone to noise
Circuits that must be initialized right after power-up, circuits whose clock may stop
when: Synchronous reset
When the clock always runs and the reset signal may pick up glitches, or when you want to time the reset like an ordinary data path.
Asynchronous reset
When you need to initialize immediately even before the clock runs or while it is stopped, such as circuits whose outputs must quickly go to a safe state.
Combined
Asynchronous assertion with synchronous release (a reset synchronizer) is widely used. Assertion acts at once, and release is aligned to the clock edge by two flip-flops.
faq: Why synchronize the release of an asynchronous reset to the clock?

If release happens near a clock edge, recovery or removal time is violated, and one flip-flop may start in the current cycle while another starts in the next, or metastability may occur. This can make a state machine start in an illegal state, so the release is aligned to the clock with two flip-flops before being distributed.
What happens with a synchronous reset if the clock is stopped?
Even if the reset signal is asserted, the flip-flops are not initialized. For circuits that need a safe state before the clock stabilizes, such as right after power-up, an asynchronous reset is used.
Does every flip-flop need a reset?

No. Registers that are always written before use, such as in the data path, may omit reset to save area and wiring. Things whose initial value affects operation, such as state machines and control signals, are reset.

ldo-vs-switching-regulator.title: LDO vs Switching Regulator: Key Differences Explained
ldo-vs-switching-regulator.description: LDO (linear) vs switching regulator (DC-DC converter) compared: operation, efficiency, heat, noise, part count, boost capability, load response and uses.
ldo-vs-switching-regulator.lead: Both produce a stable voltage from a DC input voltage, but they handle the excess voltage differently. Linear regulators such as LDOs use a transistor like a variable resistor and dissipate the difference between input and output voltage as heat. Switching regulators turn transistors on and off at high speed and transfer energy through an inductor and capacitor, so they stay efficient even with a large voltage difference and can also boost. In exchange, switching produces ripple and noise.
rows: How it works
The output transistor operates in its linear region and drops the difference between input and output voltage
Transistors switch on and off, and an inductor and capacitor transfer energy
Efficiency
Roughly output voltage ÷ input voltage. Producing 1.0 V from 1.8 V gives about 56%
About 80 to 95% depending on conditions, even with a large voltage difference
Heat
(input voltage − output voltage) × current all becomes heat
Losses are small, so little heat is generated
Output noise
Very low. No switching noise
Ripple at the switching frequency and harmonic noise (EMI)
Switching frequency
None
About a few hundred kHz to a few MHz
Part count
Few: about an IC plus input and output capacitors
Many: inductor, capacitors and, depending on the topology, diodes
Board design
Small and simple
The inductor takes space, and layout must be careful to keep noise down
Boost and inversion
Not possible. Step-down only, and the input must exceed the output by at least the dropout voltage
Step-down, step-up, buck-boost and inversion are possible
Response to load changes
Fast
Set by the control loop bandwidth, and often slower than an LDO
Cost
Low
Higher, because of the extra parts
Typical uses
Supplies for noise-sensitive circuits such as ADCs, PLLs and RF circuits, small voltage differences, low currents
CPU and SoC core supplies, high currents, efficient conversion from batteries, when boosting is needed
when: LDO (linear regulator)
When the input-output voltage difference is small, the current is low, or for supplies to circuits where low noise matters, such as ADCs, PLLs and RF circuits.
Switching regulator
When the voltage difference is large, the current is high, you want long battery life, or you need a voltage higher than the input.
Combined

A common arrangement steps the voltage down efficiently with a switching regulator and then places an LDO after it to remove ripple. The LDO's input-output voltage difference is small, so its loss stays small too.
faq: How do you calculate LDO efficiency?

The same current flows at the input and output, so ignoring the LDO's own current consumption, efficiency is roughly output voltage ÷ input voltage. From 5 V to 3.3 V it is about 66%, and from 3.6 V to 3.3 V about 92%; the smaller the voltage difference, the higher the efficiency.
Why are switching regulators so efficient?

The transistors are used fully on or fully off. When on, the voltage across them is almost zero, and when off, the current is almost zero, so the loss, which is the product of voltage and current, is small except during transitions and similar moments.
What is the dropout voltage of an LDO?

It is the minimum difference between input and output voltage needed to keep the output at its specified voltage. In an LDO it can be as small as about 0.1 to 0.3 V, and if the input falls below that, the output voltage drops as well.

static-vs-dynamic-power.title: Static vs Dynamic Power in CMOS: Key Differences
static-vs-dynamic-power.description: Static (leakage) vs dynamic power in CMOS compared: causes, equations, voltage, frequency and temperature dependence, reduction and scaling.
static-vs-dynamic-power.lead: Power in CMOS circuits divides into dynamic power, used when signals switch, and static power, used continuously even without switching. Dynamic power comes from charging and discharging wire and gate capacitance and is expressed as P = αCV²f. Static power comes from leakage current through off transistors and other paths, and it rises sharply as temperature goes up. As scaling lowered supply voltage and threshold voltage, static power grew to a larger share.
rows: Also called
Leakage power
Switching power
Cause
Subthreshold leakage of off transistors, gate leakage, junction leakage, etc.
Charging and discharging of load capacitance. Sometimes includes short-circuit current when pMOS and nMOS are on at the same time during switching
Rough equation
P = V × Ileak (Ileak: leakage current)
P = αCV²f (α: activity factor, C: capacitance, V: supply voltage, f: frequency)
When the circuit is idle
Consumed as long as power is on
Almost zero if signals do not switch
Dependence on supply voltage
Increases faster than proportionally to voltage, because leakage current itself also increases due to DIBL and other effects
Proportional to the square of the voltage
Dependence on frequency
Almost none
Proportional to frequency
Dependence on temperature
Strong. Increases exponentially with temperature and can also cause thermal runaway
Weak
Dependence on threshold voltage
Strong. Lowering the threshold increases subthreshold leakage exponentially (roughly 10 times for every 60 to 100 mV decrease at room temperature)
No direct dependence. However, a high threshold makes the circuit slower
Reduction techniques
Power gating, high-threshold transistors (multi-Vt), lowering voltage in standby, suppressing gate leakage with high-k/metal gates
Clock gating, DVFS, lowering supply voltage, reducing capacitance, reducing activity factor
Change with scaling
Rose sharply because threshold voltage was lowered along with supply voltage, becoming a non-negligible share. Structures with better gate control such as FinFETs keep it in check
Under Dennard scaling, shrinking dimensions and voltage by the same ratio kept power density constant. As voltage became hard to lower, rising power density became a problem
When it matters
Devices that spend long periods in standby, chips that run at high temperature
When running actively at high frequency
when: Reducing static power
Devices that spend long periods in standby, and chips that run at high temperature. Power gating cuts power to unused blocks, and high-threshold transistors are used on paths that do not need speed.
Reducing dynamic power
Processors running actively at high frequency. Clock gating stops unnecessary switching, and DVFS lowers voltage and frequency according to the load.
Combined

Lowering the voltage reduces dynamic power with its square, but the circuit becomes slower and processing takes longer, increasing the leakage energy during that time. So there is a voltage at which the energy per operation is minimized.
faq: What happens to dynamic power if the supply voltage is halved?

If other conditions are the same, it falls to 1/4, because it is proportional to the square of the voltage. However, lowering the voltage makes the circuit slower, so it may not run at the same frequency.
Why does static power increase with temperature?

Subthreshold leakage, which flows below the threshold, increases sharply because a higher temperature broadens the energy distribution of carriers and also lowers the threshold voltage. Watch out for the vicious cycle in which more heat raises the temperature further.
Does clock gating reduce static power?

Hardly at all. Stopping the clock eliminates switching and reduces dynamic power, but power stays connected, so leakage current keeps flowing. To reduce leakage as well, use power gating, which cuts the power.

ccp-vs-icp-plasma.title: CCP vs ICP Plasma: Key Differences Explained
ccp-vs-icp-plasma.description: Capacitively vs inductively coupled plasma: electrodes and coil, density, independent ion energy control, pressure, etching uses and PECVD/HDP-CVD.
ccp-vs-icp-plasma.lead: Both create a plasma by ionizing gas with RF power, but they differ in how the power is delivered to the plasma. CCP applies an RF voltage between two facing electrodes, and the electric field accelerates electrons. ICP passes RF current through a coil, and the induced electric field created by the changing magnetic field accelerates electrons, so it can create a high-density plasma at low pressure. ICP has a separate bias supply on the wafer side, allowing plasma density and ion energy to be adjusted separately.
rows: Plasma generation
An RF voltage is applied to parallel-plate electrodes, and the electric field between them accelerates electrons
RF current flows through a coil, and the induced electric field accelerates electrons
Tool structure
Two electrodes facing each other top and bottom. The wafer sits on one electrode
A coil is placed outside (above or around) a dielectric window, and a separate bias supply is connected to the wafer stage
Plasma density (typical)
Moderate, about 10⁹ to 10¹⁰ cm⁻³
High, about 10¹¹ to 10¹² cm⁻³
Operating pressure (typical)
Often about a few Pa to a few tens of Pa
Low pressure, about 0.1 Pa to a few Pa
Control of density and ion energy
With a single supply, raising power changes density and self-bias together, so they are hard to control independently. Dual-frequency designs split the roles
Coil power sets density and wafer-side bias power sets ion energy, so they are easy to adjust separately
Ion energy
Large self-bias makes high ion energy easy to obtain
Lowering the bias delivers many ions at low energy, making damage easy to limit
Gas dissociation
Relatively low. Source molecules and their fragments tend to remain
High. The gas is well decomposed, with many radicals and ions
Etching strengths
Dielectric films such as oxide and low-k films. Strong ion bombardment and fluorocarbon polymers provide selectivity. High-aspect-ratio contact holes
Fast, highly anisotropic etching of silicon (gates and isolation trenches), metals (such as aluminum interconnects) and compound semiconductors
Deposition applications
Parallel-plate plasma CVD (PECVD). The ratio of high- and low-frequency power adjusts film stress
High-density plasma CVD (HDP-CVD). Ion sputtering trims the trench opening during deposition to fill narrow trenches
Equipment configuration
Relatively simple: electrodes and an RF supply
Needs a coil, a dielectric window, two supplies and more, so it is somewhat complex
when: CCP (capacitively coupled plasma)
Etching dielectric films such as oxide, nitride and low-k films, including deep contact holes that need high ion energy and polymer-based selectivity. Parallel-plate plasma CVD.
ICP (inductively coupled plasma)
Fast, highly anisotropic etching of silicon and metals. When you want a high-density plasma with low ion energy to limit damage. HDP-CVD for filling narrow trenches.
Trend
Even in CCP, dual-frequency designs in which a high frequency sets density and a low frequency sets ion energy are widely used, offsetting the weakness of hard-to-separate control.
faq: Why can ICP control plasma density and ion energy separately?

Because the supply that powers the coil to create the plasma and the supply that biases the wafer are separate. Coil power adjusts plasma density, and wafer-side RF power adjusts self-bias and ion energy.
Why is CCP often used for oxide etching?

SiO2 has strong bonds, so etching it requires high ion energy. CCP easily produces a large self-bias, and gas dissociation is relatively low, so fluorocarbon polymers make it easy to obtain selectivity against the underlying nitride or silicon.
Are CCP and ICP used for anything besides etching?

Yes. Parallel-plate CCP is widely used in plasma CVD (PECVD) tools, and high-density plasmas such as ICP have been used in HDP-CVD, which deposits and sputters at the same time to fill narrow trenches.

dry-vs-wet-oxidation.title: Dry vs Wet Oxidation: Key Differences Explained
dry-vs-wet-oxidation.description: Dry vs wet thermal oxidation of silicon in one table: oxidant, growth rate, film quality, temperature, thickness control, Deal-Grove model and uses.
dry-vs-wet-oxidation.lead: Both are thermal oxidation processes that oxidize silicon at high temperature to form SiO2, but they use different oxidants. Dry oxidation uses dry oxygen (O2). It grows slowly, but produces a dense, high-quality film with few interface states, so it has been used for thin gate oxides. Wet oxidation uses water vapor (H2O). Because H2O dissolves in SiO2 far more than O2 does, the oxide grows several to about 10 times faster. That is why wet oxidation is used for thick films such as LOCOS field oxides and masks.
rows: Oxidant
Dry oxygen (O2)
Water vapor (H2O). It is commonly produced by burning hydrogen and oxygen at the furnace inlet (pyrogenic oxidation)
Reaction
Si + O2 → SiO2
Si + 2H2O → SiO2 + 2H2
Growth rate
Slow. Example: about 70 nm in 1 hour at 1000 °C
Fast (several to about 10 times faster than dry). Example: about 400 nm in 1 hour at 1000 °C
Why it is fast or slow
O2 dissolves only a little in SiO2
H2O dissolves in SiO2 several hundred times more than O2, so much more oxidant reaches the interface
Film quality and density
Dense, with few interface states and high resistance to dielectric breakdown
Slightly less dense than dry oxide; hydrogen and OH groups tend to remain in the film
Temperature (typical range)
About 800–1200 °C
About 800–1200 °C. Because it is fast, the same thickness can be grown at a lower temperature or in a shorter time
Thickness control
Slow growth makes it easy to precisely control thin films from a few nm to tens of nm
Fast growth makes it unsuitable for precise control of thin films
Treatment in the Deal-Grove model
Described by x² + Ax = B(t + τ). Initial oxidation below tens of nm is faster than the model predicts, so the initial thickness (about 25 nm) is converted into a time τ as a correction
Same equation; it fits the model well. τ ≈ 0 is often assumed. The rate constants B and B/A are much larger than for dry oxidation
Typical thickness
A few nm to tens of nm
Hundreds of nm to about 1 µm
Typical uses
Gate oxides, tunnel oxides, thin pad oxides
LOCOS field oxides, masks for ion implantation and diffusion, thick insulating films
when: Dry oxidation
When the film can be thin but interface quality and thickness accuracy come first: for example, MOSFET gate oxides and the thin pad oxide placed under a nitride film.
Wet oxidation
When you need a thick oxide in a short time: for example, LOCOS field oxides, diffusion and implantation masks, and thick insulating films around devices.
Combined
The two are sometimes combined in sequence: dry oxidation to form the interface, wet oxidation to build up thickness, and a final dry oxidation to finish.
faq: Why is wet oxidation faster than dry oxidation?

Oxidation takes place at the SiO2/silicon interface, so the oxidant must diffuse through the film to reach it. H2O dissolves in SiO2 several hundred times more than O2, so the oxidant concentration in the film is higher and more of it reaches the interface. In the Deal-Grove model, this shows up as larger rate constants B and B/A.
Why has dry oxidation been used for gate oxides?

Dry oxide is dense, has few interface states at the silicon interface, and is highly resistant to dielectric breakdown. Its slow growth also makes it easy to control a thickness of a few nm precisely. Advanced gates have moved to high-k films, but the very thin SiO2 interfacial layer beneath them is still important.
Why does only dry oxidation need a correction in the Deal-Grove model?

In dry oxidation, the film is known to grow faster than the model predicts while it is thinner than tens of nm. To correct for this, the fast initial growth is treated as having formed about 25 nm of oxide, and that amount is added to the equation as a time τ. Wet oxidation fits the model well, so τ ≈ 0 is often assumed.
How much silicon is consumed in thermal oxidation?
The same for both dry and wet oxidation: silicon equal to about 44% of the resulting oxide thickness is consumed. The oxide grows about 56% above the original surface and about 44% below it.

lpcvd-vs-pecvd.title: LPCVD vs PECVD: Key Differences Explained
lpcvd-vs-pecvd.description: LPCVD vs PECVD in one table: temperature, film quality, hydrogen content, step coverage, film stress, processing style, throughput and uses.
lpcvd-vs-pecvd.lead: Both are CVD processes that form films by reacting gaseous precursors, but they supply the reaction energy differently. LPCVD drives the reaction with heat alone, at about 600–800 °C in a low-pressure furnace, so it deposits dense, low-hydrogen films that cover steps uniformly. PECVD decomposes the precursor gases with a plasma, so it can deposit at low temperatures of about 300–400 °C and can be used even after interconnects have been formed. However, its films contain much hydrogen and have lower density.
rows: Reaction energy
Heat only
A plasma (RF discharge) decomposes and activates the precursor gases
Temperature (typical range)
About 600–800 °C
About 300–400 °C
Pressure (typical range)
Tens to hundreds of Pa
About hundreds of Pa
Processing style
Batch processing in a vertical furnace. 100 or more wafers are stacked and coated at once
Mainly single-wafer. Wafers are processed one at a time under a showerhead electrode
Film quality
Dense, with near-stoichiometric composition. Slow etch rate
Lower density, and composition tends to deviate. Fast etch rate
Hydrogen content (nitride example)
A few % or less
About 10–30%, as Si-H and N-H
Step coverage
Surface-reaction-limited, so films are nearly uniform in thickness even over steps
Often worse than LPCVD. Can be improved depending on the precursors and conditions
Film stress
Nitride has a large tensile stress of about 1 GPa. Thick films crack easily
Can be tuned from compressive to tensile, for example by the ratio of high-frequency to low-frequency power
Throughput
Each run is long, including ramp-up and ramp-down, but many wafers are processed at once
High deposition rate and short processing time per wafer
Usable process stage
Before interconnects are formed (while the wafer can withstand high temperature)
Can be used even after interconnects are formed
Main films and uses
Polysilicon, nitride for LOCOS/STI masks and spacers, TEOS oxide
Interlayer dielectrics, passivation films, copper diffusion barriers, SiON anti-reflective coatings, hard masks
when: LPCVD

When the process can withstand high temperature and density, purity and step coverage come first: gate polysilicon, nitride for isolation and spacers, and other front-end steps that build the transistors.
PECVD

When the underlying layers cannot withstand high temperature: interlayer dielectrics and protective films after aluminum or copper interconnects are formed, and nitride films whose stress needs to be tuned.
Rule of thumb
The thermal budget (how high the temperature can go) first determines which method is usable. Then compare the required film quality, coverage, stress and processing speed to choose.
faq: Why can PECVD deposit films at low temperature?

High-energy electrons in the plasma collide with the precursor gases and break them into reactive radicals and ions. The reaction proceeds without heating the gas or the wafer itself to high temperature, so deposition is possible at about 300–400 °C, compared with 600–800 °C for thermal CVD.
Why can't LPCVD be used after interconnects are formed?

It requires high temperatures of about 600–800 °C, which would melt or deform aluminum interconnects and degrade copper interconnects and low-k films. Interconnect processing generally has to stay below about 400 °C, so PECVD is used.
What problems does a high hydrogen content in PECVD films cause?

It lowers film density and increases the wet etch rate. In addition, if hydrogen escapes during later heat treatment, the film can shrink and its stress can change. That is why LPCVD is chosen for films that must be dense or pure.
Why is the film thickness uniform even when LPCVD processes many wafers at once?

At low pressure, gas molecules diffuse quickly, so the deposition rate is set by the surface reaction rather than by gas supply (surface-reaction-limited). As long as the surface temperature is uniform, films of nearly the same thickness form everywhere, even with wafers spaced a few mm apart.

amdahl-vs-gustafson.title: Amdahl's Law vs Gustafson's Law: Key Differences
amdahl-vs-gustafson.description: Amdahl's law vs Gustafson's law in one table: assumptions, formulas, how fractions are measured, limits, strong vs weak scaling and worked examples.
amdahl-vs-gustafson.lead: Both laws estimate how much faster a program gets when you add processors, but they rest on different assumptions. Amdahl's law fixes the problem size and asks how fast the same work can be finished, so the part that cannot be parallelized sets the upper limit on speedup. Gustafson's law fixes the run time and solves a larger problem as processors are added, so speedup grows nearly in proportion to the number of processors. The two do not contradict each other; they answer different questions.
rows: What is fixed
Problem size (total amount of work)
Run time (amount of work per processor)
Question
How much faster can the same problem be solved?
How much larger a problem can be solved in the same time?
Formula (N is the number of processors)
How the fraction is measured
p is the fraction of time taken by the parallelizable part when run on one processor
s is the fraction of time taken by the serial part when run in parallel on N processors
As N increases
Levels off at 1 / (1 − p)
Keeps growing nearly in proportion to N
Worked example
With p = 0.95, about 17× at N = 100; even with infinite N, the limit is 20×
With s = 0.05, about 95× at N = 100
Corresponding scaling
Strong scaling
Weak scaling
Outlook
Pessimistic. A small serial part sets the upper limit
Optimistic. Parallelism pays off if the problem is made larger
Examples where it applies
When you want to process a fixed-size input quickly: processing a single image, interactive responses, etc.
Simulations with finer grids, or when you want to process larger data or models in the same time
Not included in either
Communication and synchronization overhead, load imbalance, insufficient memory bandwidth
Communication and synchronization overhead, load imbalance, insufficient memory bandwidth
when: Amdahl's law
When the problem size is fixed and you want to shorten the response time. Use it to estimate the limit of parallelization and decide whether to reduce the serial part.
Gustafson's law
When the problem can grow along with the number of processors. Use it to estimate the value of solving finer and larger problems in large-scale simulations and data processing.
Reporting results
When reporting parallel performance, state clearly whether it was measured with strong or weak scaling. Under different conditions, the speedup of the same program can differ greatly.
faq: Don't the two laws contradict each other?

No. Amdahl's law fixes the problem size and Gustafson's law fixes the run time, so they answer different questions. The serial fraction is also measured differently: by the time on one processor in Amdahl's law and by the time on N processors in Gustafson's law, so you cannot plug the same number into both and compare.
If 90% can be parallelized, why is the maximum only 10×?

Because the remaining 10% does not get shorter no matter how many processors you add. Even as the time of the parallel part approaches zero, the total time cannot drop below 10% of the original, so the speedup levels off at 1 / 0.1 = 10×.
Why is the actual speedup smaller than these laws predict?

Neither law includes communication and synchronization between processors, load imbalance, or insufficient shared memory bandwidth. These effects grow as processors are added, and parallel efficiency drops.
Which law should I apply to my program?

If the input size is fixed and you want results sooner, use Amdahl's law. If you want to handle finer grids or larger data as processors are added, use Gustafson's law. The same program can fall under either law depending on how it is used.

nmos-vs-pmos.title: nMOS vs pMOS: Key Differences Explained
nmos-vs-pmos.description: nMOS vs pMOS in one table: structure, carriers, mobility, threshold voltage sign, turn-on condition, role in CMOS, logic levels and gate width.
nmos-vs-pmos.lead: An nMOS is a MOSFET in which electrons flow through the channel, and a pMOS is one in which holes do; all the voltage polarities are reversed. An nMOS turns on when the gate is raised above the source, and a pMOS turns on when the gate is lowered below the source. In silicon, electron mobility is about 2–3 times hole mobility, so for the same dimensions an nMOS can carry more current. In CMOS circuits, the nMOS pulls the output to ground and the pMOS pulls it to the supply, and the pMOS gate is made wider to match the drive strength.
rows: Structure
n⁺ source and drain in a p-type substrate or p-well
p⁺ source and drain in an n-well
Channel carriers
Electrons
Holes
Mobility (silicon inversion layer)
High. About 2–3 times that of holes
Low
Threshold voltage (enhancement mode, referenced to source)
Positive (e.g. +0.3 V)
Negative (e.g. −0.3 V)
Turn-on condition
VGS > Vth. Raise the gate above the source
VGS < Vth (negative). Lower the gate below the source by at least |Vth|
Source connection in CMOS
Ground side
Supply (VDD) side
Role in CMOS
Pull-down. Pulls the output to ground. In series in NAND, in parallel in NOR
Pull-up. Pulls the output to the supply. In parallel in NAND, in series in NOR
Value passed well as a switch
Passes 0 well. A 1 rises only to about VDD − Vth
Passes 1 well. A 0 falls only to about |Vth|
Gate width needed for equal drive
Reference (1×)
Typically about 2–3 times that of the nMOS
Strain that boosts mobility
Tensile strain (stress liners, Si:C source/drain, etc.)
Compressive strain (SiGe source/drain, etc.)
Typical degradation
PBTI (a concern with high-k/metal gates)
NBTI
when: nMOS
When pulling an output down to ground: CMOS pull-down networks, switches that pass 0, switches on the current-sinking side, etc.
pMOS
When pulling an output up to the supply: CMOS pull-up networks, switches that pass 1, switches placed on the supply side (high-side switches), etc.
Combined
CMOS uses both in pairs, and in steady state one of them is always off, so almost no static current flows. A transmission gate, made of an nMOS and a pMOS in parallel, passes both 0 and 1 well.
faq: Why is the pMOS gate made wider than the nMOS in CMOS?

Hole mobility is about 1/2–1/3 of electron mobility, so a pMOS of the same dimensions carries less current. Making the pMOS about 2–3 times as wide as the nMOS equalizes the rise and fall delays and puts the inverter's logic threshold at about half the supply voltage.
Why is the threshold voltage of a pMOS negative?

A pMOS needs a hole inversion layer at the surface of the n-type well, and that requires the gate to be at a lower voltage than the source. To avoid confusion over signs, designers often compare the absolute value |Vth|.
Why aren't logic circuits built from nMOS alone?

In nMOS-only circuits, current keeps flowing through a resistor or load device whenever the output is 1, so static power is large. In CMOS, which combines nMOS and pMOS, one of the two is always off in steady state, so almost none of this current flows.
Is the difference between nMOS and pMOS still 2–3 times in advanced processes?

The gap has narrowed considerably, because pMOS mobility is boosted by compressive strain from SiGe source/drain, and FinFETs use crystal planes for the channel along which holes flow more easily. Even so, cell designs still set dimensions with the drive-strength difference between the two in mind.

enhancement-vs-depletion-mosfet.title: Enhancement vs Depletion MOSFET: Key Differences
enhancement-vs-depletion-mosfet.description: Enhancement vs depletion MOSFETs compared: state at 0 V gate, threshold voltage sign, channel formation, turn-off, circuit symbol, safety and uses.
enhancement-vs-depletion-mosfet.lead: An enhancement-mode MOSFET has no channel when the gate voltage is 0 V; current flows only after a gate voltage creates an inversion layer (normally off). A depletion-mode MOSFET has a channel built in, so current flows even with the gate at 0 V, and it stops when a gate voltage of the opposite polarity removes the channel (normally on). In an n-channel device, the threshold voltage is positive for enhancement mode and negative for depletion mode. Enhancement-mode devices are used in almost all applications, including CMOS logic.
rows: With the gate at 0 V
No channel; off (normally off)
Channel present; on (normally on)
Threshold voltage sign (n-channel)
Positive
Negative
Threshold voltage sign (p-channel)
Negative
Positive
How the channel forms
The gate voltage induces an inversion layer at the substrate surface
A thin channel layer is formed at the surface in advance, for example by ion implantation
How to stop current (n-channel)
Lower the gate voltage below the threshold (0 V is enough)
Apply a negative gate voltage to deplete the channel
Origin of the name
The gate voltage enhances the channel
The gate voltage depletes the channel
Circuit symbol
The channel line is broken into three dashes
The channel line is a single solid line
If the drive circuit stops
Turns off, so it is safe
May turn on, so care is needed to avoid short circuits
Typical uses
Almost all applications: CMOS logic, power MOSFETs, analog circuits, etc.
Load devices in early NMOS logic, constant-current sources, power supply start-up circuits, etc.
when: Enhancement mode
Almost always. Setting the gate to 0 V reliably turns it off, so it is used for switches in logic circuits and for power switches that must turn off safely.
Depletion mode

When you want current to flow without a gate voltage: load devices in place of resistors, simple constant-current sources with the gate tied to the source, and start-up circuits that run before the power supply has come up.
Using normally-on devices

Devices that are inherently normally on, such as GaN HEMTs, are used as normally-off devices either by modifying the gate structure or with a cascode configuration in series with a low-voltage silicon MOSFET.
faq: Why do power applications require normally-off devices?

If the gate drive circuit loses power or fails, a normally-on device turns on, which can short the supply and cause a large current to flow. An enhancement-mode device is off with its gate at 0 V, so it is safe.
In what circuits have depletion-mode devices been used?

In NMOS logic before CMOS became mainstream, depletion-mode devices with the gate tied to the source were used as load devices in place of resistors. Today they are still used in simple constant-current sources and power supply start-up circuits.
How do you tell them apart in a circuit symbol?

By the line representing the channel. An enhancement-mode device is drawn with the line broken into three dashes, showing that there is no channel without a gate voltage. A depletion-mode device has a channel from the start, so it is drawn with a single solid line.
Can you tell them apart by the threshold voltage?

Yes. In an n-channel device, a positive threshold voltage means enhancement mode and a negative one means depletion mode. In a p-channel device the signs are reversed: negative means enhancement mode and positive means depletion mode.

hybrid-bonding-vs-microbump.title: Hybrid Bonding vs Microbumps: Key Differences
hybrid-bonding-vs-microbump.description: Hybrid bonding vs microbumps for chip stacking: solder, pitch, interconnect density, surface flatness, process, electrical performance and uses.
hybrid-bonding-vs-microbump.lead: Both technologies connect chips to chips, or chips to wafers, vertically through many terminals. Microbumps join the chips by melting small amounts of solder, for example on the tips of copper pillars, so spacing is needed to keep solder from squeezing out and bridging to neighbors, and the pitch is typically tens of µm. Hybrid bonding uses no solder; it directly bonds polished flat surfaces of copper electrodes and dielectric, so the pitch can be below 10 µm and the interconnect density can be raised by orders of magnitude. In return, the bonding surfaces must be flat and clean at the nanometer level.
rows: Bonding method
Copper electrodes to copper and dielectric to dielectric, bonded directly surface to surface
Solder bumps, for example on copper pillars, are bonded by heating
Solder
Not used
Used
Typical pitch
Below 10 µm. Can be narrowed to a few µm
Tens of µm. About 20 µm at the narrowest
Interconnect density (per mm²)
About 10,000 (10 µm pitch) to more than 100,000 (3 µm pitch)
Hundreds (40 µm pitch) to thousands (20 µm pitch)
Surface flatness and cleanliness
Nanometer-level flatness is required. Even a small particle creates a void that cannot bond
Solder absorbs height variations, so requirements are less strict
Between chips
No gap; no underfill needed
A gap forms, which is filled with underfill or a resin film
Main process steps
Planarize by CMP → clean and activate with plasma → align and bond → anneal (typically at a few hundred °C) to join copper to copper
Form bumps by plating → align → bond by thermocompression (TCB) or reflow → underfill
Bonding unit
Wafer-to-wafer or die-to-wafer
Mainly die level (die-to-wafer, die-to-die)
Electrical characteristics
Extremely short joints with small parasitic capacitance. Low energy needed per bit transferred
Bumps add parasitic capacitance, a disadvantage compared with hybrid bonding
Typical uses
Stacked image sensors, stacking cache SRAM on top of processors, etc.
Stacking DRAM in HBM, connecting chips on interposers, etc.
when: Hybrid bonding
When you need a very large number of short, low-power connections between chips and a pitch below 10 µm: for example, stacking pixels on logic or memory on processors.
Microbumps
When a pitch of tens of µm is sufficient and you want to stack chips or mount them on an interposer with a proven process, without strict control of planarization and cleanliness.
Trend
Microbumps are being replaced by hybrid bonding, starting with applications that demand finer pitch and higher bandwidth, but for cost and yield reasons, both are used depending on the application.
faq: Why can hybrid bonding achieve a much finer pitch?

Because it uses no solder. Microbumps need spacing so that molten solder does not bridge to the neighboring bump, but hybrid bonding joins flat surfaces in which copper electrodes are embedded in dielectric, so that constraint does not apply. The number of connections is inversely proportional to the square of the pitch, so reducing the pitch to 1/10 increases density 100 times.
Why must the bonding surfaces be so flat and clean?

Because the surfaces are bonded directly to each other, any unevenness or particle lifts the area around it and leaves a cavity (void) that cannot bond. Even a single small particle can prevent bonding over a much larger area, so CMP, cleaning and control of a clean environment are critical.
What does "hybrid" combine?

It refers to bonding dielectric to dielectric and copper electrode to copper electrode simultaneously in the same process. The dielectric surfaces bond first, and during subsequent heating the copper expands, the copper surfaces come into close contact, and they interdiffuse into a single body.
Will microbumps stop being used?

Not soon. Microbumps are a proven process with looser flatness and cleanliness requirements, and many applications need only a pitch of tens of µm. The two are chosen according to the required pitch, bandwidth, cost and yield.

copper-vs-ruthenium-cobalt-interconnect.title: Copper vs Cobalt vs Ruthenium Interconnects Compared
copper-vs-ruthenium-cobalt-interconnect.description: Cu, Co and Ru interconnects compared: bulk resistivity, resistivity rise in narrow lines, barrier needs, electromigration, processing and layers used.
copper-vs-ruthenium-cobalt-interconnect.lead: For wide interconnects, copper, with the lowest bulk resistivity, is the best material, and most interconnects are still copper today. But when line widths shrink to tens of nm or less, electrons scatter at the wire surfaces and grain boundaries, raising resistivity (the size effect), and the barrier layer copper requires takes up a large share of the cross-section. Cobalt and ruthenium have bulk resistivities several times that of copper, but their electron mean free paths are short, so their resistivity rises less as lines narrow, and their barrier layers can be thinner. That is why they are being introduced in the narrowest lines, contacts and vias.
rows: Bulk resistivity (room temperature, typical)
About 1.7 µΩ·cm
About 6 µΩ·cm
About 7 µΩ·cm
Electron mean free path (typical)
Long, about 40 nm
Short, around 10 nm or less
Short, around 10 nm or less
Resistivity rise in narrow lines
Large. Below tens of nm, surface and grain-boundary scattering increase, sometimes reaching several times the bulk value
Smaller than copper
Smaller than copper
Barrier layer
Required. A few nm of TaN/Ta or similar surrounds the sides and bottom
Uses a thin liner (TiN, etc.), which can be thinner than for copper
Diffuses little into dielectrics, so the barrier may be made very thin or omitted
Melting point (approx.)
About 1085 °C
About 1495 °C
About 2334 °C
Electromigration resistance
Needs countermeasures. Strengthened with top cap layers and liners
Higher than copper
High
Processing and fill
Damascene process. Filled by electroplating over a seed layer. Dry etching is difficult
Narrow holes and trenches are easy to fill by CVD or plating
Can be deposited by CVD or ALD. Depositing a film and then patterning it by etching is also being explored
Layers where used
Most interconnects, from intermediate to upper layers
Contact and via fill, some narrow lines in the lowest layers, caps and liners for copper interconnects
Being researched and developed for the narrowest lines and vias. Also used in liners
Material availability
Abundant and inexpensive
More expensive than copper
A platinum-group precious metal; scarce and expensive
when: Copper (Cu)
Intermediate and upper interconnect layers with relaxed line widths, where the advantage of the lowest bulk resistivity applies directly.
Cobalt (Co)

Places near the transistors, such as contacts and vias, where holes are very narrow and copper's effective resistance rises because of its barrier and seed. Also caps and liners that improve the reliability of copper interconnects.
Ruthenium (Ru)

A candidate for the narrowest lines and vias, with line widths in the teens of nm or less. Because the space freed by omitting the barrier can be used for conductor, its effective resistance may be lower than copper in narrow lines.
faq: Copper has the lowest bulk resistivity, so why are cobalt and ruthenium being considered?

In narrow lines, the effective resistance is determined less by bulk resistivity than by surface and grain-boundary scattering and by the thickness of the barrier layer. Copper's mean free path is long, about 40 nm, so its resistivity rises sharply as lines narrow, and it also needs a barrier a few nm thick. Cobalt and ruthenium show less resistivity rise as lines narrow and allow thinner barriers, so in very narrow lines their resistance may be close to or even lower than copper's.
What is the size effect?

When the width or thickness of a wire becomes comparable to or smaller than the electron mean free path, electrons scatter more readily at the wire surfaces and grain boundaries, and the resistivity rises above the bulk value. Narrow wires also have smaller grains, which further increases grain-boundary scattering.
Why do copper interconnects need a barrier metal?

Copper diffuses easily into dielectrics and silicon. In silicon it causes transistor leakage and degradation, and in dielectrics it degrades the insulation between wires. So the sides and bottom are surrounded by a barrier metal such as TaN/Ta, and the top is covered with a dielectric cap film.
Will all copper interconnects be replaced by other metals?

No. In intermediate and upper layers with relaxed line widths, copper, with the lowest bulk resistivity, remains advantageous. New materials are introduced first where copper's weaknesses stand out, such as contacts and vias near the transistors and the narrowest lines.

jitter-vs-phase-noise.title: Jitter vs Phase Noise: Key Differences Explained
jitter-vs-phase-noise.description: Jitter vs phase noise for clocks: what each measures, units, instruments, typical metrics, converting to RMS jitter by integration, and uses.
jitter-vs-phase-noise.lead: Jitter and phase noise are two views of the same fluctuation in a clock or oscillator. Jitter is in the time domain: it expresses, in seconds (ps or fs), how far each edge deviates from its ideal time. Phase noise is in the frequency domain: it expresses the noise level at a given frequency offset from the carrier, as a ratio to the carrier in dBc/Hz. Integrating phase noise over a frequency range converts it to RMS jitter, but the result depends on the integration range, so the range must always be stated.
rows: Domain
Time domain
Frequency domain
Quantity expressed
Deviation of edge times from their ideal times
Ratio of noise power per 1 Hz to carrier power at each offset frequency from the carrier (single sideband)
Units
Seconds (ps, fs), or UI (fraction of one bit period)
dBc/Hz (given together with the offset frequency)
Typical metrics
Period jitter, cycle-to-cycle jitter, TIE (time interval error). RMS and peak-to-peak values
Values or curves at each offset, e.g. −140 dBc/Hz at 1 MHz offset
Main instruments
Oscilloscopes, time interval analyzers, bit error rate testers
Phase noise analyzers, spectrum analyzers with phase noise measurement capability
Random vs deterministic components
Random jitter is handled as an RMS value and deterministic jitter as a peak-to-peak value, and total jitter is derived from the target error rate
Random components appear as a smooth curve, and periodic components as lines at specific frequencies (spurs)
Conversion between them
A jitter value alone does not reveal the frequency profile of the phase noise
Integrating over offsets f1–f2 converts it: RMS jitter = √(2∫10^(L(f)/10) df) ÷ (2π f0)
Effect of range
The value changes with the instrument bandwidth and how many cycles are observed
The converted RMS jitter changes with the integration range (e.g. 12 kHz–20 MHz)
What it tells you
A quantity that directly affects timing margin (setup, horizontal eye opening)
Which frequencies have large fluctuations. Clues to the PLL loop bandwidth and the sources of noise
Main fields of use
Timing analysis of digital circuits, high-speed serial links
RF oscillators, PLL and VCO design, clocks for high-speed ADCs
when: Jitter
When you want to know the timing margin directly: clock uncertainty in static timing analysis, evaluating eye diagrams and error rates in high-speed serial links, etc.
Phase noise
When you want to know which frequencies the noise comes from: evaluating local oscillators in radios, designing PLL loop bandwidth, comparing oscillators, etc.
Combined

Clock source specifications often give both the phase noise curve and the RMS jitter converted over a fixed integration range. For high-speed ADC clocks, the SNR limit is set by −20 log₁₀(2π f tj), so it is estimated using the jitter derived from phase noise.
faq: How do you get RMS jitter from phase noise?

Convert the phase noise L(f) from dBc/Hz to a linear value, integrate it over the chosen offset range, and double it to get the mean-square phase fluctuation (rad²). Take the square root and divide by 2π f0 (f0 is the carrier frequency) to get the RMS jitter. For example, a 100 MHz clock with 1 mrad (RMS) of phase fluctuation has about 1.6 ps of jitter.
Why must the integration range be stated?

The total phase noise depends on the offset range over which it is integrated, and so does the converted RMS jitter. Without the range, values cannot be compared correctly with those of other oscillators. Clock specifications often use a fixed range such as 12 kHz–20 MHz.
Why do jitter values for the same clock differ between documents?

The definitions may differ (period jitter, cycle-to-cycle jitter, TIE), RMS and peak-to-peak values may be mixed, or the measurement bandwidth may differ. The peak-to-peak value of random jitter grows with longer observation time, so it is given together with an error rate.
Should I look at jitter or phase noise?

Jitter suits you if you want to know the timing margin in digital circuits or high-speed serial links; phase noise suits you if you want to know the noise sources or frequency-dependent behavior when designing RF oscillators or PLLs. They are two views of the same fluctuation, so use whichever fits the purpose.

cpu-vs-gpu-vs-npu.title: CPU vs GPU vs NPU: Key Differences Explained
cpu-vs-gpu-vs-npu.description: CPU vs GPU vs NPU: design philosophy, compute units, control, memory, data types (INT8, FP16, etc.), performance metrics, power efficiency and flexibility.
cpu-vs-gpu-vs-npu.lead: A CPU is a general-purpose processor that can run anything, using a small number of complex cores to finish a single task quickly. A GPU processes large amounts of data in parallel with many compute units and is used for a wide range of parallel computing, including graphics and AI training. An NPU is dedicated circuitry specialized for the matrix multiply-accumulate operations that make up most of the computation in neural networks; by arraying many low-precision units such as INT8 and reusing data in on-chip memory, it performs inference with very high power efficiency. In return, it handles poorly any operations it does not support.
rows: Design philosophy
General-purpose, low latency. Finish a single task as fast as possible
High throughput. Handle large amounts of parallel computation together
Specialized for neural network operations (mainly inference), maximizing performance per watt
Compute unit organization
A few to a few hundred complex cores, each with SIMD units
Thousands of simple compute units; many also have matrix units
A large array of multiply-accumulate units (such as a systolic array), plus vector units for activation functions and the like
Control
Branch prediction and speculative (out-of-order) execution per instruction
Switches among many threads to hide memory latency
Most follow a data flow determined in advance by the compiler, with little per-instruction control
Strengths
Branch-heavy code, operating systems, application logic
Graphics, AI training and inference, scientific computing
AI inference centered on convolutions and matrix multiplication
Memory
Large caches and main memory such as DDR
High-bandwidth memory such as GDDR and HBM
Reuses weights and intermediate data in on-chip SRAM buffers. When built into an SoC, shares main memory with the CPU
Main data types
Almost anything, centered on FP64, FP32 and integers
Mainly FP32, FP16 and BF16. Also FP8 and others for training
Mainly low precision such as INT8, INT4 and FP16
Performance metrics
Clock frequency, core count, IPC
FLOPS (TFLOPS, etc.)
TOPS (usually a theoretical peak counted in INT8)
Power efficiency for AI inference
Low
High
Highest. Can be an order of magnitude or more higher than a CPU
Flexibility
Highest. Runs any program
High. Broadly usable for parallelizable workloads
Low. Unsupported operations fall back to the CPU or GPU
Programming
General-purpose programming languages and compilers
Kernels written in a GPU parallel programming model
Trained models are converted and run by AI compilers and inference runtimes. Rarely programmed directly
Where it is found
Every kind of computer
Discrete cards, or built into SoCs
Often built into smartphone and PC SoCs. Dedicated chips for data centers also exist
when: CPU
Branch-heavy, sequential processing and control of the whole system. Also used to run small models and operations the NPU does not support.
GPU
Large-scale parallel computation that needs a choice of precisions and flexibility: AI training, inference of large models, graphics, scientific computing, etc.
NPU

When you want inference such as photo enhancement, speech recognition and translation to run constantly on smartphones and PCs without draining the battery. Models are quantized and run in formats the NPU handles well, such as INT8.
faq: What is the difference between an NPU and a GPU?

A GPU is a general-purpose parallel processor whose many compute units can be used flexibly by programs, and it can also handle graphics and training. An NPU focuses on the multiply-accumulate operations of neural network inference and is built around low-precision compute units and on-chip memory, so it is highly power-efficient for the workloads it supports but handles other workloads poorly.
Why is an NPU so power-efficient?

A CPU activates many circuits for each instruction, such as branch prediction and instruction reordering, whereas an NPU omits most of them and arrays many small multiply-accumulate units for formats such as INT8. It also reuses weights and intermediate data in on-chip SRAM, reducing energy-hungry accesses to external memory.
Can an NPU be used for training?
NPUs in smartphones and PCs are designed mainly for inference. Training requires gradient computation and higher precision, so GPUs or training accelerators for data centers are generally used.
Is an NPU with a higher TOPS number always faster?

Not necessarily. TOPS is usually a theoretical peak counted in INT8 or similar, and sometimes assumes sparse data. Actual speed varies greatly with memory bandwidth, compute utilization, and whether the model's operations are supported by the NPU.

pn-vs-schottky-diode.title: PN Junction vs Schottky Diode: Key Differences Explained
pn-vs-schottky-diode.description: PN junction vs Schottky diode in one table: structure, carriers, forward voltage, reverse recovery, leakage, breakdown voltage, temperature and uses.
pn-vs-schottky-diode.lead: A PN junction diode rectifies with a junction between p-type and n-type semiconductors, while a Schottky diode rectifies with a junction between a metal and a semiconductor. In a PN junction, minority carriers are injected and stored under forward bias, so a reverse recovery current flows when the diode is switched to reverse bias. A Schottky diode runs on majority carriers only, so it has almost no reverse recovery, and in silicon its forward voltage of about 0.2 to 0.4 V is also lower than the roughly 0.6 to 0.7 V of a PN junction. The trade-off is a larger reverse leakage current and, in silicon, difficulty reaching high breakdown voltages.
rows: Structure
A junction of p-type and n-type semiconductors
A junction of a metal and a semiconductor (mainly n-type), called a Schottky junction
Current carriers
Injected minority carriers. Both electrons and holes are involved
Majority carriers only. Current flows by thermionic emission over the barrier
Forward voltage (silicon, typical)
About 0.6 to 0.7 V
About 0.2 to 0.4 V. Depends on the metal and the voltage rating
Reverse recovery
Yes. Reverse current flows until the stored minority carriers disappear. On the order of µs for general-purpose rectifiers and about tens of ns for fast-recovery parts
Almost none. The only current is the one that charges and discharges the junction capacitance
Reverse leakage current
Small
Large. The lower the barrier, the larger the leakage
Breakdown voltage (silicon, typical)
High voltage ratings are easy to make, up to the several-kV class
Up to about 200 V. In SiC, 600 to 1700 V class parts are in practical use
Voltage drop at high current in high-voltage parts
Conductivity modulation lowers the resistance of the lightly doped layer, keeping the voltage drop down
No conductivity modulation, so the drift-layer resistance adds directly
Temperature behavior
Forward voltage falls by about −2 mV/°C. Leakage current rises with temperature
Leakage current rises sharply with temperature, so thermal runaway must be watched. Forward voltage falls with temperature
Main uses
Rectifying mains power, high-voltage rectification, general-purpose protection and signal circuits
Low-voltage, high-current rectification in switching power supplies, freewheeling diodes, reverse-polarity protection, high-frequency detection
when: PN junction diode
For rectification under high reverse voltage, or when leakage current must stay small even at high temperature. Used in mains rectifiers and high-voltage circuits.
Schottky diode
For rectifying large currents at low voltage, or for fast switching. Used for output rectification in switching power supplies, freewheeling diodes and protection against reverse battery connection.
Combined

For high-voltage, high-speed applications, SiC Schottky diodes or fast-recovery diodes with lifetime control are chosen. There are also JBS diodes that combine PN and Schottky junctions to balance leakage current against forward voltage.
faq: Why is the forward voltage of a Schottky diode low?

The thermionic emission current over the Schottky barrier has a saturation current orders of magnitude larger than the diffusion current of a PN junction, so the same current flows at a lower voltage. The barrier height depends on the metal: a lower barrier lowers the forward voltage but increases the reverse leakage current.
Why does a Schottky diode have almost no reverse recovery?

Current is carried by majority carriers only, and minority carriers are not injected and stored as in a PN junction. When the diode is switched to reverse bias, the only current is the one that charges and discharges the junction capacitance, so switching losses and noise can be kept small.
Why are there few high-voltage silicon Schottky diodes?

A higher breakdown voltage requires a thick, lightly doped drift layer, and because a Schottky diode has no conductivity modulation, that resistance adds directly to the forward voltage drop. Leakage current also grows, so silicon parts are generally limited to about 200 V. SiC, with its high critical electric field, reaches 600 V or more with a thin drift layer.
What should I watch for when using a Schottky diode at high temperature?

The reverse leakage current rises sharply with temperature. Heat from the leakage current can raise the temperature further and lead to thermal runaway, so check the high-temperature leakage in the datasheet and allow margin in heat dissipation and reverse voltage.

zener-vs-avalanche-breakdown.title: Zener vs Avalanche Breakdown: Key Differences Explained
zener-vs-avalanche-breakdown.description: Zener vs avalanche breakdown in PN junctions: mechanism, doping, depletion width, breakdown voltage, temperature coefficient, sharpness and uses.
zener-vs-avalanche-breakdown.lead: Both are breakdown phenomena in which current rises suddenly when a large reverse voltage is applied to a PN junction, but the mechanisms differ. Zener breakdown occurs in heavily doped junctions with a very thin depletion layer, where valence-band electrons tunnel through to the conduction band. Avalanche breakdown occurs when carriers accelerated by a strong electric field create electron-hole pairs by impact ionization, and these multiply in a chain reaction. In silicon, Zener breakdown dominates at breakdown voltages below about 5 V and avalanche breakdown above about 6 to 7 V, and the two have temperature coefficients of opposite sign.
rows: Mechanism
Tunneling. Valence-band electrons pass through a thin barrier into the conduction band
Impact ionization. Carriers accelerated by the field create new electron-hole pairs, which multiply in a chain
Junction doping
Very high on both sides
Low on at least one side. The lower the doping, the higher the breakdown voltage
Depletion width
Very thin (about 10 nm or less)
Wide. Carriers need distance to accelerate
Breakdown field (silicon, typical)
A very strong field of about 10⁶ V/cm
About 3×10⁵ V/cm (depends on doping)
Breakdown voltage (silicon, typical)
About 5 V or less. Between about 5 V and about 6 to 7 V, both mechanisms occur together
About 6 to 7 V or more. High-voltage junctions of hundreds to thousands of V are also set by this breakdown
Temperature coefficient of breakdown voltage
