Negative. As temperature rises the bandgap shrinks and the breakdown voltage falls
Positive. As temperature rises, scattering by lattice vibrations increases and the breakdown voltage rises
Sharpness of breakdown
Relatively gradual
Abrupt
Noise
Relatively low
High, from avalanche multiplication
Main uses
Voltage-regulator diodes of about 5 V or less, low-voltage references and clamps
Voltage-regulator diodes of about 6 V or more, surge-suppression diodes, avalanche photodiodes, SPADs
when: Zener breakdown
When you need to hold a voltage at a low level of about 5 V or less. Used in low-voltage regulator diodes and in clamps that limit input voltage.
Avalanche breakdown

For regulated voltages of about 6 V or more, or to protect circuits from surges. Avalanche photodiodes and SPADs, which detect light by multiplying it, use this breakdown deliberately. In power devices it is designed in as the phenomenon that sets the breakdown voltage.
Combined

In regulator diodes with a breakdown voltage of about 5 to 6 V, the negative temperature coefficient of Zener breakdown and the positive coefficient of avalanche breakdown cancel out, so the voltage changes little with temperature. When a temperature-stable reference is needed, choose parts in this range or temperature-compensated types.
faq: Do all Zener diodes use Zener breakdown?

No. Voltage-regulator diodes are customarily called Zener diodes, but in silicon those of about 6 to 7 V or more mainly use avalanche breakdown. Zener breakdown by tunneling dominates only in low-voltage parts of about 5 V or less.
Why do the temperature coefficients have opposite signs?

In Zener breakdown, a rising temperature shrinks the bandgap and makes tunneling easier, so the breakdown voltage falls. In avalanche breakdown, a rising temperature increases scattering by lattice vibrations, making it harder for carriers to gain the energy needed for impact ionization, so the breakdown voltage rises.
Is a diode destroyed when it breaks down?

Neither type of breakdown damages the junction by itself, and the diode recovers if the current is limited. It fails when the heat from current and voltage during breakdown is too great. In regulator circuits, a resistor is placed in series with the diode to limit the current.
How is avalanche breakdown handled in power devices?

The breakdown voltage of power MOSFETs and diodes is mainly set by the voltage at which avalanche breakdown occurs. Making the drift layer more lightly doped and thicker raises the breakdown voltage but also increases on-resistance. A device can enter the breakdown region, for example when an inductive load is switched off, and the energy it can withstand there is specified as its avalanche ruggedness.

direct-vs-indirect-bandgap.title: Direct vs Indirect Bandgap: Key Differences Explained
direct-vs-indirect-bandgap.description: Direct vs indirect bandgap semiconductors: band structure, phonons, emission efficiency, carrier lifetime, absorption depth, materials and uses.
direct-vs-indirect-bandgap.lead: In a direct-bandgap semiconductor, the bottom of the conduction band and the top of the valence band sit at the same position in momentum (wave-vector) space, so an electron and hole can recombine and emit light directly. In an indirect-bandgap semiconductor the two positions are offset, so emitting or absorbing light requires a phonon (lattice vibration) to take part at the same time and make up the momentum. That is why direct-bandgap materials such as GaAs, InP and GaN are used in LEDs and semiconductor lasers, while the indirect-bandgap Si and Ge are poor light emitters but are widely used in photodetectors and LSIs.
rows: Band structure
The conduction-band bottom and valence-band top are at the same position in momentum space
The conduction-band bottom and valence-band top are offset in momentum space
Light emission/absorption and phonons
Transitions can occur without phonons
A phonon must take part at the same time to make up the momentum
Emission efficiency
High. Radiative recombination is likely
Extremely low. Most recombination is non-radiative and becomes heat
Minority-carrier lifetime (typical)
Short, on the order of ns
Long. In high-quality silicon it reaches µs to ms
Absorption near the band edge
Rises steeply from the absorption edge (about 10⁴ cm⁻¹ or more)
Weak near the absorption edge, growing gradually as photon energy increases
Absorption depth
Shallow. In GaAs, a thickness of about 1 to 2 µm absorbs most of sunlight
Deep. In silicon, light of about 1 µm wavelength penetrates 100 µm or more
In photodetectors
A thin absorption layer is enough, suiting high-speed detectors
Needs a thick absorption layer or a light-trapping structure
Typical materials
GaAs (about 1.42 eV), InP (about 1.34 eV), GaN (about 3.4 eV), alloys such as InGaN
Si (about 1.12 eV), Ge (about 0.66 eV), SiC, GaP
Main uses
LEDs, semiconductor lasers, high-efficiency solar cells, photodetectors for communications
LSIs, power devices, photodiodes, image sensors, solar cells
when: Direct bandgap

When converting electricity into light. Used in the emitting layers of LEDs and semiconductor lasers, and in photodetectors and high-efficiency solar cells that need strong absorption in a thin layer.
Indirect bandgap
When light emission is not needed. Besides LSIs and power devices, silicon is used for light detection in photodiodes, image sensors and solar cells.
Combined

In silicon photonics, waveguides, modulators and Ge photodetectors are built on silicon, while the light source is a direct-bandgap laser, such as an InP-based one, bonded onto the silicon or combined as a separate chip.
faq: How can indirect-bandgap silicon absorb light?

In absorption, a transition can occur if a phonon is absorbed or emitted to make up the momentum. Because the probability is low, absorption is relatively weak, but with enough thickness enough light is absorbed. This is why silicon photodiodes and image sensors detect visible light well.
How do electrons and holes recombine in an indirect-bandgap semiconductor?

Radiative recombination, which emits light, is unlikely, so most recombination goes through crystal defects or impurity levels, such as SRH recombination, and the energy is lost as heat rather than light. The long minority-carrier lifetime in silicon is also due to radiative recombination being rare.
Why is Ge used in photodetectors for communications even though it has an indirect bandgap?

Ge has an indirect bandgap, but its direct gap of about 0.8 eV is close to its indirect gap (about 0.66 eV). It therefore strongly absorbs light at communication wavelengths up to around 1.55 µm, and because it can be grown readily on silicon, it is used in silicon photonics photodetectors.
What determines the emission wavelength?

Mainly the bandgap of the emitting layer: the wavelength λ (nm) is roughly 1240 ÷ Eg (eV). GaAs, at about 1.42 eV, emits near-infrared light at about 870 nm, while GaN-based materials emit blue to ultraviolet light. Changing the alloy composition tunes the bandgap; in InGaN, adding more indium makes the wavelength longer.

n-type-vs-p-type.title: N-Type vs P-Type Semiconductor: Key Differences Explained
n-type-vs-p-type.description: N-type vs p-type semiconductors: dopants (donors vs acceptors), majority carriers, impurity levels, Fermi level, mobility, resistivity and uses in devices.
n-type-vs-p-type.lead: An n-type semiconductor is made by adding a group V impurity (donor) such as phosphorus or arsenic to silicon, so that the extra electrons become the majority carriers. A p-type semiconductor is made by adding a group III impurity (acceptor) such as boron, so that the holes left by missing electrons become the majority carriers. The Fermi level shifts toward the conduction band in n-type material and toward the valence band in p-type material. In silicon, electron mobility is about 2 to 3 times hole mobility, so at the same doping concentration n-type material has the lower resistivity.
rows: Dopants (silicon)
Group V phosphorus (P), arsenic (As), antimony (Sb)
Group III boron (B). Indium and others are also used
Name and role of the impurity
Donor. Gives up one electron
Acceptor. Accepts one electron, creating a hole in the valence band
Charge of the ionized impurity
Positive. Fixed in the lattice and immobile
Negative. Fixed in the lattice and immobile
Impurity level (silicon)
About 0.045 eV (phosphorus) or about 0.054 eV (arsenic) below the conduction-band edge
About 0.045 eV (boron) above the valence-band edge
Majority / minority carriers
Electrons / holes
Holes / electrons
Carrier density (fully ionized)
n ≈ ND, p = ni² / ND
p ≈ NA, n = ni² / NA
Fermi level
Above the intrinsic Fermi level, toward the conduction band. Moves closer to the conduction band as doping increases
Below the intrinsic Fermi level, toward the valence band. Moves closer to the valence band as doping increases
Majority-carrier mobility (lightly doped silicon, typical)
About 1400 cm²/V·s for electrons
About 450 cm²/V·s for holes
Resistivity at the same doping
Lower
About 2 to 3 times higher than n-type
Where it is used in CMOS
nMOS source/drain, the n-well in which pMOS is built
pMOS source/drain, the p-well in which nMOS is built. Silicon wafers for CMOS are mostly p-type
when: n-type
When you want electrons to carry current. Used for nMOS source/drain, the emitter and collector of npn transistors, and the n-well in which pMOS is built.
p-type
When you want holes to carry current. Used for pMOS source/drain, the base of npn transistors, and the p-well in which nMOS is built.
Combined

Placing n-type and p-type material in contact forms a PN junction, the basis of diodes, transistors, solar cells and LEDs. In manufacturing, adding a large amount of the opposite-type impurity to an existing layer to invert its type (counter-doping) is also used.
faq: Since n-type semiconductors have many electrons, are they negatively charged overall?

No, they are electrically neutral overall. When a donor gives up one electron, the donor itself remains in the lattice as a positive ion, which cancels the negative charge of the electron. The same holds for p-type: the positive charge of the holes balances the negative charge of the ionized acceptors.
Are there holes in n-type material too?

Yes. In thermal equilibrium the product of electron and hole densities equals the square of the intrinsic carrier density (n × p = ni²), so with a donor concentration of 1×10¹⁶ cm⁻³ the hole density at room temperature is about 1×10⁴ cm⁻³. They are few, but these minority carriers play an important role in the operation of PN junctions and bipolar transistors.
What happens if both donors and acceptors are added?

They cancel each other out (compensation), and the material takes the type of whichever is more abundant. The carrier density is roughly set by the difference in concentrations, but mobility falls because of scattering by both kinds of ionized impurities. This property is used to invert the type when forming source/drain regions of the opposite type inside a well.
Why is the Fermi level in a different position in n-type and p-type material?

The Fermi level is the energy at which the probability of occupation by an electron is 1/2, so it reflects the carrier distribution. It shifts toward the conduction band in n-type material, which has many conduction-band electrons, and toward the valence band in p-type material, where electrons have left the valence band and holes are plentiful. In silicon at room temperature, it moves about 60 mV closer to the band edge for every tenfold increase in doping concentration.

l1-vs-l2-vs-l3-cache.title: L1 vs L2 vs L3 Cache: Key Differences Explained
l1-vs-l2-vs-l3-cache.description: L1 vs L2 vs L3 cache in typical PC and server CPUs: size, latency, per-core vs shared, split instruction/data caches, inclusion and design goals.
l1-vs-l2-vs-l3-cache.lead: L1, L2 and L3 caches form a multi-level hierarchy ordered by distance from the CPU core: the closer a level is, the smaller and faster it is, and the farther it is, the larger and slower. In typical PC and server CPUs, representative ranges are tens of KB and a few cycles for L1, hundreds of KB to a few MB and a dozen or so cycles for L2, and a few MB to tens of MB and tens of cycles for L3. L1 and L2 are usually private to each core, while L3 is shared by several cores. An access to main-memory DRAM takes hundreds of cycles, so this hierarchy absorbs as many accesses as possible.
rows: Relationship to cores
Private to each core
Usually private to each core. Some designs share it among a few cores
Shared by multiple cores (the whole chip or a cluster of cores)
Capacity (representative range for PC and server CPUs)
About 32 to 64 KB each for instructions and data
About 256 KB to a few MB per core
A few MB to tens of MB for the whole chip
Latency (representative range)
About 3 to 5 cycles
About 10 to 20 cycles
About 30 to 70 cycles. Longer for parts farther from the core
Instructions and data
Split (I-cache and D-cache)
Shared (unified cache)
Shared (unified cache)
Design priority
Short hit time. Used every cycle within the pipeline
Absorbing L1 misses and reducing the miss penalty
Reducing main-memory accesses and sharing data among cores
Where a miss goes
L2
L3
Main memory (DRAM)
Addressing
Often virtually indexed, physically tagged (VIPT)
Physical addresses
Physical addresses
Inclusion
Topmost level. Whether it is contained in the lower levels depends on their policy
Depends on the design, such as inclusive or non-inclusive
Making it inclusive makes it easier to narrow down coherence checks. Exclusive designs that eliminate duplication and non-inclusive designs also exist
Physical placement
Inside the core, right next to the execution units
Just outside the core, placed as part of the core
Often divided into per-core slices connected by a ring or mesh network
Line size
64 bytes is common
64 bytes is common
64 bytes is common
when: L1 cache
The closest cache, used on every instruction fetch and every load and store. It pays off when frequently used data is packed into a small range to improve temporal locality.
L2 cache
Absorbs working data that does not fit in L1. Techniques such as loop blocking work well when they keep the working data to around hundreds of KB to a few MB.
L3 cache

Helps when multiple cores share data or when handling large data that does not fit in the per-core caches. Because it competes for capacity with other cores, it is affected by programs running at the same time.
faq: Why isn't the L1 cache made larger?

A larger capacity lengthens the memory-cell arrays and wiring, which increases hit time. L1 is used every cycle in the pipeline, so even one cycle of delay has a large impact on performance. L1 is therefore kept to tens of KB, and large capacity is provided by L2 and L3. With VIPT, capacity is also limited by the relationship between page size and associativity.
Why is only L1 split into instruction and data caches?

In a pipeline, instructions are fetched every cycle while other instructions read and write data. Splitting the caches lets the two accesses happen simultaneously and lets each cache be organized to suit its use. From L2 on, accesses are less frequent, so it is common to use a unified cache whose capacity can be shared flexibly.
Which is better, inclusive or exclusive?

Each has pros and cons. In an inclusive cache, the contents of the upper levels are always also in the lower level, so snoops from other cores can be answered by the lower level alone, but duplication reduces the effective capacity. An exclusive cache has no duplication and makes good use of the total capacity, but moving lines and managing coherence become more complex. The choice depends on the number of cores and the cache sizes.
Are the capacities and cycle counts in the table the same for every CPU?

No, they are representative ranges assuming PC and server CPUs. They vary with the design generation, clock frequency, number of cores and chip organization. Many embedded microcontrollers have no L2 or L3, while some CPUs enlarge L3 by stacking cache chips. Actual values are checked with performance counters or programs that measure memory latency.

simd-vs-simt.title: SIMD vs SIMT: Key Differences Explained
simd-vs-simt.description: SIMD (CPU vector instructions) vs SIMT (GPU warps): execution model, programming, parallel width, branch handling, memory access and latency hiding.
simd-vs-simt.lead: SIMD and SIMT both apply the same operation to many data elements with a single instruction, but they look different to the program. SIMD is the CPU's vector instructions: the programmer or compiler lays data out in fixed-width vector registers and uses the instructions explicitly. SIMT is the GPU's approach: you write ordinary code for a single thread, and the hardware groups threads, such as 32 of them, into a warp and runs them with the same instruction. Each thread can have its own branches, but when threads in a warp take different paths, both paths are executed one after the other, which lowers efficiency.
rows: Execution model
One instruction processes multiple elements laid out in a vector register at the same time
One instruction is executed at the same time by many threads grouped into a warp. Each thread has its own registers
How it looks to the program
Written with the vector width in mind, using intrinsics, assembly or the compiler's auto-vectorization
The work of a single thread is written as scalar code. The hardware does the grouping
Parallel width
Set by the register width. Example: 512 bits holds 16 numbers of 32 bits
The warp width (such as 32 threads). The whole chip holds tens of thousands of threads at once
Branch handling
Per-element branches cannot be written. Both sides are computed and selected with a mask from a comparison
Can be written per thread. If threads in a warp diverge, both paths run in turn while threads not on the current path sit idle (divergence)
Managing active elements
The programmer or compiler specifies them explicitly with masked or blend instructions
The hardware manages active threads automatically
Memory access
Good at reading contiguous addresses together. Scattered addresses are handled with gather/scatter instructions, but slowly
Each thread can specify any address. When adjacent threads read adjacent addresses, the accesses are combined (coalescing)
Hiding memory latency
Large caches, out-of-order execution, prefetching
Switching among many warps, running other warps while some wait
Place in Flynn's taxonomy
SIMD itself
A form of SIMD presented in the shape of threads
Typical uses
CPU vector instructions. Loops for image and audio processing, cryptography, matrix operations and so on
GPU warps. Large-scale parallel computing such as graphics, AI training and inference, and scientific computing
when: SIMD

When you want to speed up loops on a CPU that do the same calculation for each array element. It works best when data is laid out contiguously and iterations have no dependencies, and it can also be used through the compiler's auto-vectorization.
SIMT

Large-scale parallel computing that applies the same processing to thousands to millions of independent elements. You write and run per-thread programs on a GPU. Efficiency improves when the code is structured so that branches and memory addresses line up within each warp.
Combined

Inside a GPU, SIMT execution in units of warps runs on SIMD execution units. In systems that use both CPUs and GPUs, preprocessing and control are handled with the CPU's SIMD and large parallel computations with the GPU.
faq: Is SIMT a completely different mechanism from SIMD?

Inside the hardware they are similar. Each thread in a warp corresponds to one lane of a SIMD execution unit and runs with the same instruction. The difference is in presentation: in SIMT the hardware handles per-thread registers, addresses and branches, so programmers can write code without thinking about the vector width.
How can I reduce warp divergence?

Make threads in the same warp take the same side of a branch as much as possible. Methods include reordering data so that condition results line up, assigning thread indices so that conditions switch at warp boundaries, and replacing short branches with select operations.
How do I write processing with an if statement in SIMD?

Use a compare instruction to turn the per-element condition into a mask, compute both results, and then select each element according to the mask. In instruction sets with masked instructions, only the elements that meet the condition are computed and stored. Because both paths are computed, efficiency drops when the branch bodies are heavy, which is similar to divergence in SIMT.
When does the compiler's auto-vectorization fail?

When there are dependencies between iterations (a result is used in the next iteration), when pointers may refer to the same memory, when data is not laid out contiguously, or when the loop contains complex branches or function calls. Telling the compiler there are no dependencies, or changing the data layout, can sometimes make vectorization possible.

in-order-vs-out-of-order.title: In-Order vs Out-of-Order Execution: Key Differences Explained
in-order-vs-out-of-order.description: In-order vs out-of-order execution: issue order, stalls, hazard handling, register renaming and the ROB, circuit size, power, IPC and where each is used.
in-order-vs-out-of-order.lead: An in-order CPU issues and executes instructions in program order. When an earlier instruction waits, for example on a cache miss, the instructions behind it stop too. An out-of-order CPU checks dependencies, executes whichever instructions are ready first, and commits the results in program order through a reorder buffer (ROB). Because it can make progress on other instructions during waits, it achieves higher IPC, but it needs register renaming and instruction-selection logic, which increase circuit size and power.
rows: Order of issue and execution
Program order
Ready instructions are executed first, out of order
Committing results (retirement)
Program order
In program order, through the reorder buffer (ROB)
When an earlier instruction is waiting
Later instructions stop too (stall)
Independent later instructions proceed first
Handling data hazards
Forwarding and stalls. Instruction ordering is left to the compiler
Forwarding plus dynamic instruction scheduling in hardware
False dependencies (WAR, WAW)
Since order is preserved, they rarely cause problems
Removed by register renaming, which reassigns physical registers
Main additional circuitry
Little. A simple pipeline
Rename tables, physical registers, issue queues, the ROB, load/store queues
Impact of cache misses
Large. The pipeline tends to stall on every miss
Other instructions proceed within a window of hundreds of instructions, hiding part of the wait
IPC
Lower. Below out-of-order at the same issue width
High. Combined with a wide issue width, well above 1
Circuit size and power
Small. Performance per area and per watt is easy to raise
Large. Instruction-selection logic and the ROB add area and power
Where it is used
Microcontrollers, small embedded cores, some cores that prioritize power saving, GPU compute cores
High-performance cores in PCs, servers and smartphones
when: In-order execution
When you want to keep area and power small, or make execution time easy to predict. Used in microcontrollers, embedded cores, and designs that line up many small cores.
Out-of-order execution
When you want to run a single thread as fast as possible. Used in the high-performance cores of PCs, servers and smartphones.
Combined

Some chips combine out-of-order high-performance cores with power-saving cores that are in-order or reduced-size out-of-order. Heavy work goes to the high-performance cores and light work to the power-saving cores, balancing performance and power.
faq: Can out-of-order execution change a program's results?

Not within a single thread. Even when the execution order is changed, true data dependencies (RAW) are respected, and results are committed in program order through the reorder buffer. When a branch misprediction or exception occurs, the results of later instructions are discarded and the correct state is restored, so from the outside it looks as if the program ran in order.
Can an in-order CPU execute multiple instructions per cycle?

Yes. In-order superscalar processors issue adjacent independent instructions at the same time while preserving order. However, if an earlier instruction stalls, later ones cannot proceed, so IPC does not rise as much as with out-of-order execution.
What do register renaming and the ROB each do?

Register renaming removes the false dependencies (WAR and WAW) caused by reusing the same register names, by reassigning physical registers, which increases the number of instructions that can run in parallel. The ROB holds the results of instructions executed out of order and commits them in program order, enabling precise exceptions.
How can the performance of an in-order CPU be improved?

The compiler arranges instructions in an order that avoids waits, for example by placing instructions that use a load's result farther from the load. Besides reducing stalls with forwarding, data layouts that reduce cache misses and prefetching are also effective.

single-mode-vs-multimode-fiber.title: Single-Mode vs Multimode Fiber: Key Differences Explained
single-mode-vs-multimode-fiber.description: Single-mode vs multimode optical fiber: core diameter, wavelength and light source, reach, modal dispersion, loss, component cost and typical uses.
single-mode-vs-multimode-fiber.lead: Single-mode fiber has a thin core about 9 µm in diameter, and light travels in only one mode, so there is no difference in speed between modes (modal dispersion). It is used for long-distance links of tens of km or more and for high-speed communications. Multimode fiber has a thicker core of 50 µm or 62.5 µm, and many modes travel at once, so modal dispersion limits its reach to roughly tens to hundreds of m. In return, it can use inexpensive light sources such as 850 nm VCSELs, and alignment is easy, so it suits short connections inside data centers and buildings.
rows: Core diameter (typical)
About 9 µm (cladding 125 µm)
50 µm or 62.5 µm (cladding 125 µm)
Number of modes carried
Only one
Hundreds to around a thousand modes travel at once
Main wavelengths
1310 nm (O-band) and 1550 nm (C-band)
Mainly around 850 nm
Main light sources
Edge-emitting semiconductor lasers (such as DFB lasers), with light focused into the thin core
VCSELs (vertical-cavity surface-emitting lasers). Older generations also used LEDs
Modal dispersion
None. However, chromatic dispersion becomes significant with distance (nearly zero around 1310 nm)
Present. Graded-index fiber, whose core refractive index changes gradually, reduces it, but it still limits bandwidth and reach
Loss (typical)
About 0.35 dB/km at 1310 nm and about 0.2 dB/km at 1550 nm
About 2.5 to 3.5 dB/km at 850 nm
Reach (typical)
Hundreds of m to tens of km. Thousands of km or more with optical amplifiers
About hundreds of m at 10 Gbit/s, and about 100 m or less for lanes of 25 Gbit/s or more
Alignment
Tight. Sub-µm precision is required, and active alignment is often used
Relaxed. The thick core makes coupling to light sources and photodetectors easy
Cost
The fiber itself is cheap, but lasers, optical transceivers and assembly tend to be expensive
The fiber is somewhat more expensive, but light sources and assembly are cheap, so the total tends to be lower over short distances
Main uses
Long-distance and intercity communications, access lines (FTTH), connections of hundreds of m to km scale between buildings and within data centers
Short connections such as between racks in data centers, in-building LANs and storage connections
when: Single-mode fiber

Cabling for distances over a few hundred m or in anticipation of future speed increases. Long-distance communications, access lines, and connections between data-center buildings or between switches. Also when you want to carry many signals on one fiber with wavelength-division multiplexing (WDM).
Multimode fiber
When you want to build short connections of roughly 100 m or less cheaply, such as within the same room or building. Combined with optical transceivers that use 850 nm VCSELs.
Trend
As the speed per lane rises, the reach of multimode fiber gets shorter, so single-mode fiber is being used more widely even inside data centers.
faq: Why can't multimode fiber reach far?

Because the core is thick and many modes (light paths) travel at the same time. Each mode travels a slightly different distance at a slightly different speed, so a pulse that started out as one spreads out in time by the time it arrives (modal dispersion). Faster signals have shorter intervals between pulses, so their reach is shorter.
Is single-mode fiber more expensive?

The fiber itself is, if anything, cheaper for single-mode. The cost tends to be in the optical transceivers: coupling light into a thin core of about 9 µm requires a laser with stable output and alignment with sub-µm precision. Over short distances, multimode, which can use VCSELs, is often cheaper for the link as a whole.
Why is 850 nm light commonly used with multimode fiber?
VCSELs around 850 nm can be made cheaply in volume, tested at the wafer level, and coupled easily to multimode fiber. Multimode fiber is also designed to have wide bandwidth at this wavelength.
What limits the distance of single-mode fiber besides modal dispersion?

Loss and chromatic dispersion. Loss is at its minimum around 1550 nm (about 0.2 dB/km), and the chromatic dispersion of standard single-mode fiber is nearly zero around 1310 nm. Over long distances, optical amplifiers make up for loss, and dispersion is handled by compensation or signal processing.

nrz-vs-pam4.title: NRZ vs PAM4: Key Differences Explained
nrz-vs-pam4.description: NRZ vs PAM4 in one table: bits per symbol, baud rate at the same bit rate, eye opening and SNR, need for FEC, circuitry and the standards that use each.
nrz-vs-pam4.lead: NRZ is the most basic scheme, sending 1 bit per symbol with two signal levels. PAM4 sends 2 bits per symbol with four levels, so at the same bit rate the baud rate (symbols per second) is halved, avoiding the high-frequency loss of the channel. The trade-off is that three eyes are stacked vertically within the same amplitude, so each eye is about 1/3 as tall, a penalty of about 9.5 dB in SNR. For this reason, forward error correction (FEC) is almost essential in PAM4 links.
rows: Signal levels
Two (0 and 1)
Four (corresponding to 2-bit combinations such as 00, 01, 11, 10)
Bits per symbol
1 bit
2 bits
Baud rate at the same bit rate
Equal to the bit rate (e.g. 64 GBd for 64 Gbit/s)
Half the bit rate (e.g. 32 GBd for 64 Gbit/s)
Nyquist frequency
Half the baud rate. Twice that of PAM4, so channel loss is larger
Half that of NRZ. Loss is smaller on the same channel
Eye opening
One large eye
Three eyes stacked vertically, each about 1/3 the height of NRZ
Required SNR
Baseline
About 9.5 dB (20 log₁₀ 3) worse at the same amplitude
FEC
Often none, or a lightweight code is enough
Almost essential. A certain pre-FEC bit error rate is tolerated and corrected by FEC, at the cost of added latency
Transmit and receive circuits
Relatively simple. A single decision threshold
Decisions with three thresholds, and high linearity to keep the level spacing even. Many high-speed parts receive with an ADC and DSP
Bit mapping
Each level corresponds to 1 bit
Assigned with Gray coding so that an error to an adjacent level costs only 1 bit
Example standards
Up to PCI Express 5.0 (32 GT/s), Ethernet up to about 25 Gbit/s per lane
PCI Express 6.0 (64 GT/s), Ethernet at 50 Gbit/s or 100 Gbit/s and above per lane, data-center optical transceivers
when: NRZ
When the speed per lane is up to tens of Gbit/s and there is margin in channel loss. When you want simple circuits and to avoid FEC latency.
PAM4
When 50 Gbit/s or more per lane is needed and NRZ's baud rate would be too high to tolerate the channel loss. Used together with FEC and strong equalization.
How to think about it
It is a choice between raising the baud rate and increasing the bits per symbol. PAM4 turns a frequency problem into an SNR problem and makes up the shortfall with FEC.
faq: Is PAM4 faster than NRZ?

At the same baud rate, PAM4 sends 2 bits per symbol, so its bit rate is doubled. Conversely, at the same bit rate, the baud rate can be halved. Either way, it is a scheme for using channel bandwidth efficiently, and it is correspondingly more vulnerable to noise.
Why is PAM4 about 9.5 dB worse in SNR?

Because the same voltage swing is divided into three intervals, the difference between adjacent levels is about 1/3 that of NRZ. This is equivalent to reducing the signal amplitude to 1/3, a penalty of 20 log₁₀ 3 ≈ 9.5 dB.
Why does PAM4 need FEC?

Because the level spacing is narrow and noise easily causes bit errors. Even if the pre-FEC bit error rate is fairly high, an error-correcting code corrects the errors in blocks so the link as a whole meets the required error rate. PCI Express 6.0 combines a lightweight, low-latency FEC with retransmission when errors are detected.
Why did PCI Express 6.0 switch to PAM4?

Sending 64 GT/s, twice the 32 GT/s of PCI Express 5.0, with NRZ would put the Nyquist frequency at 32 GHz, making board and connector losses too large. With PAM4, twice the transfer rate is obtained while staying at 32 GBd.

fixed-vs-floating-point.title: Fixed-Point vs Floating-Point: Key Differences Explained
fixed-vs-floating-point.description: Fixed-point vs floating-point: representation, range and precision, arithmetic unit size and power, overflow handling, programming effort and typical uses.
fixed-vs-floating-point.lead: Fixed-point fixes the position of the binary point in advance and handles fractions with the same bit strings and arithmetic units as integers. Its circuits are small and use little power, so it is used in DSPs, in microcontrollers without floating-point units, and in the integer arithmetic of AI inference. Floating-point represents a number with a sign, an exponent and a mantissa, and the exponent moves the binary point, so it can handle values over an extremely wide range with nearly constant relative precision. Its arithmetic units are larger, but because it can be used without worrying about scaling, it is the standard for general-purpose computing and AI training.
rows: Representation
An integer bit string read with a predetermined scale (2 to the power −n). Written in forms such as Q15
Three fields, sign, exponent and mantissa, expressed as (−1)^sign × 1.mantissa × 2^(exponent − bias). Defined by IEEE 754
Representable range (example)
Q15 (16 bits): −1 to 1 − 2⁻¹⁵
Single precision (32 bits): roughly 10⁻³⁸ to 10³⁸, and closer to 0 with subnormal numbers
Precision
Constant step size (constant absolute error). The smaller the value, the larger the relative error
Nearly constant relative precision (about 7 digits in single precision). The larger the value, the larger the step
Arithmetic unit
Integer adders and multipliers as they are
Needs circuits for exponent comparison, mantissa alignment, normalization and rounding
Circuit size and power
Small. Much less than floating-point at the same bit width
Large. Often several times or more the area and energy of an integer unit of the same bit width
Overflow handling
In two's complement, the value wraps around to the opposite end. Prevented with saturating arithmetic or accumulators with extra bits (guard bits)
Exceeding the largest representable value gives ±infinity. Results such as 0 ÷ 0 give NaN
Scaling
The programmer estimates value ranges and designs the shifts and binary-point positions for each operation
The exponent adjusts automatically, so it rarely needs attention
Reproducibility of results
Results tend to be bit-for-bit identical
The order of additions can change results slightly (addition is not associative)
Where it is used
DSPs, small microcontrollers without floating-point units, signal processing in FPGAs and ASICs, integer arithmetic for AI inference (such as INT8)
General-purpose computing in PCs and servers, scientific computing (double precision), graphics, AI training (FP32, BF16, FP16, FP8)
when: Fixed-point

When you want to do signal processing whose value range is known in advance with small circuits and low power. Audio and communications filters, motor control, FPGA implementations, and inference of quantized AI models.
Floating-point

Calculations whose value range is wide or not known in advance. When you want to prioritize ease of development and numerical stability, as in scientific computing, physics simulation, graphics and AI training.
Combined
In AI, it is now common to train in floating-point and, for inference, quantize to scaled integers (such as INT8) and compute with integer arithmetic units similar to those used for fixed-point.
faq: Why are fixed-point circuits small?

Because the binary point is in a fixed position, integer adders and multipliers can be used as they are. Floating-point needs circuits that compare exponents and align the mantissas on every addition, then normalize and round the result, which increases area and power.
What happens when a fixed-point value overflows?

As with two's-complement integers, exceeding the maximum wraps around to the minimum side, causing large errors such as a large positive value becoming negative. DSPs prevent this with saturating arithmetic, which holds the result at the maximum or minimum, and with wide accumulators that have guard bits.
Does floating-point have no error?

No. Floating-point also uses a finite number of bits, so values that cannot be represented exactly in binary, such as 0.1, have rounding errors, and cancellation and absorption (loss of small addends) also occur. Its advantages are a wide representable range and nearly constant relative precision.
Is INT8 in AI inference fixed-point?

The idea is similar. Floating-point values are divided by a scale to make INT8 integers, integer multiply-accumulate operations are performed, and finally the scale is multiplied back in. The difference from fixed-point is that the scale is not limited to powers of 2 and can be set per layer or per channel.

sti-vs-locos.title: STI vs LOCOS Isolation: Key Differences Explained
sti-vs-locos.description: STI (shallow trench isolation) vs LOCOS: isolation method, bird's beak, surface planarity, scalability, process steps, issues and technology generations.
sti-vs-locos.lead: Both are device isolation methods that electrically separate neighboring transistors with thick oxide. LOCOS thermally oxidizes the silicon not covered by a nitride film to grow thick oxide. The process is simple, but oxide encroaches under the edge of the nitride to form a bird's beak, so the isolation width cannot be made narrow. STI etches shallow trenches into the silicon, fills them with oxide and planarizes with CMP. It has no bird's beak and gives a flat surface, so from around the 0.25 µm generation it became the standard for scaled LSIs.
rows: Isolation method
Etch shallow trenches in the silicon and fill them with oxide
Thermally oxidize the silicon not covered by nitride to grow a thick field oxide
Main process steps
Pad oxide and nitride deposition → lithography → silicon dry etch → liner oxidation → oxide fill (HDP-CVD, etc.) → CMP → nitride removal
Pad oxide and nitride deposition → lithography → nitride etch → thermal oxidation (such as wet oxidation at about 1,000 °C) → nitride removal
Isolation dimensions (typical)
Trench depth of about several hundred nm. Trench width can be as narrow as the minimum feature size
Field oxide thickness of about several hundred nm to 1 µm. The isolation width is hard to narrow
Bird's beak
None
Present. Oxide encroaches under the nitride edge, reducing the effective device width
Surface planarity
Flat after CMP. An advantage for lithography depth of focus
Part of the oxide rises above the silicon surface, leaving a step
Suitability for scaling
High. The isolation width can be narrowed, raising device density
Low. The narrower the isolation, the larger the share taken by the bird's beak, making sub-µm isolation difficult
Main issues
Trench fill defects (voids), CMP dishing, trench-corner shape (divots), stress from the filled oxide
Bird's beak, gate-oxide defects caused by nitride formed under the nitride film (Kooi effect), long high-temperature steps
Number of steps and cost
Many. Requires etch, fill and CMP tools
Few. Centered on thermal oxidation and inexpensive
Generations used (typical)
From around the 0.25 µm generation to the present. Also used to isolate fins from each other in FinFETs
Up to around the 0.35 to 0.5 µm generations of the 1990s. Still remains in some older-generation processes and in power and analog processes
when: STI
When you want to pack devices at high density, as in scaled logic and memory. When you want to narrow the isolation width to the minimum feature size and do subsequent lithography on a flat surface.
LOCOS
In older-generation processes with relaxed dimensions, when you want a simple process and low cost.
Transition
Improvements were made to shrink the LOCOS bird's beak, but they had limits, and LOCOS was replaced by STI as scaling progressed and CMP became practical.
faq: What is a bird's beak?

During LOCOS thermal oxidation, oxygen also diffuses sideways under the edge of the nitride film, and the oxide encroaches into the device area in a shape like a bird's beak. Because it makes the width available for transistors narrower than designed, it became a major obstacle to scaling.
Why does STI need CMP?

When oxide is filled into the trenches, a thick layer of oxide also builds up on the nitride outside the trenches. CMP removes it, using the nitride as the polish-stop layer, leaving oxide only in the trenches and making the surface flat.
How deep are STI trenches?

It depends on the generation, but several hundred nm is typical. Insulator of sufficient depth is placed so that leakage current does not flow to neighboring devices and parasitic transistors do not turn on.
Is LOCOS no longer used?
It has been replaced by STI in scaled logic and memory, but in older-generation processes with relaxed dimensions it is sometimes still used because it has fewer steps and is cheaper.

fan-in-vs-fan-out-wlp.title: Fan-In vs Fan-Out WLP: Key Differences Explained
fan-in-vs-fan-out-wlp.description: Fan-in vs fan-out wafer-level packaging: redistribution area, package vs die size, I/O count, manufacturing, warpage and other issues, cost and uses.
fan-in-vs-fan-out-wlp.lead: Both are packages in which the redistribution layer (RDL) and solder balls are formed while still in wafer form, and then the wafer is diced. Fan-in WLP is built directly on the original wafer, so terminals can be placed only within the die area and the package is almost the same size as the die. Fan-out WLP places known-good dies cut from the wafer at intervals and embeds them in resin to make a reconstituted wafer, then extends the redistribution beyond the edges of each die. It allows many terminals and can combine multiple dies, but adds process steps, and warpage and die position shift become issues.
rows: Redistribution area
Only within the die area
Extends onto the resin outside the die
Package vs die area
Almost the same (chip-scale)
The package is larger
I/O count (typical)
Lower. Set by die area and ball pitch, from a few to a few hundred
Higher. Terminals can also be placed outside the die, sometimes exceeding a thousand
Starting point for manufacturing
The original device wafer
A reconstituted wafer of known-good dies placed on a carrier and embedded in mold resin (panel-based methods also exist)
Substrate
None
Mostly none. The redistribution layer acts as the substrate, allowing a thin package (high-performance parts may also be mounted on a substrate)
Multiple dies
A single die only
Multiple dies and passive components can be combined in one package
Main issues
With large dies, the thermal-expansion mismatch with the printed circuit board shortens solder-joint life
Warpage from the thermal-expansion mismatch between silicon and resin, die position shift during molding (die shift), fine redistribution on resin
Cost
Low. Few process steps
Higher than fan-in. Die placement, molding and redistribution on resin add steps
Main uses
Small chips for smartphones and similar devices: power ICs, RF components, sensors, audio ICs and so on
Smartphone application processors, RF modules, integrating multiple dies, and connecting high-performance chiplets
when: Fan-in WLP
When you want to package a small die with few terminals as small and cheaply as possible. Power ICs, sensors and RF components for mobile devices.
Fan-out WLP
When there are many terminals relative to the die area, when you want a thin package, or when you want to combine multiple dies into one.
How to tell
If the terminals fit within the die area, use fan-in; if they do not fit and must be spread outward, use fan-out.
faq: What do "in" and "out" mean in fan-in and fan-out?

They refer to the area over which redistribution routes the terminals. Fan-in arranges terminals only within (in) the die area, while fan-out extends the wiring to the resin outside (out) the die and arranges terminals there.
What is a reconstituted wafer?

A wafer-like structure rebuilt for making fan-out packages by placing known-good dies at intervals on a carrier and embedding them in mold resin. Because a resin region surrounds each die, redistribution can be extended into it.
Why is warpage a problem in fan-out WLP?

Silicon, mold resin and the redistribution-layer dielectric have very different coefficients of thermal expansion. Each time the resin is cured or heated, the difference in expansion and contraction causes warpage, making exposure, handling and solder joining difficult.
Why aren't large dies made as fan-in WLP?

The package has no substrate, and the silicon is soldered directly to the printed circuit board, so the larger the die, the greater the strain on the joints from the thermal-expansion mismatch. Also, the terminals may no longer fit within the die area.

user-mode-vs-kernel-mode.title: User Mode vs Kernel Mode: Key Differences Explained
user-mode-vs-kernel-mode.description: User mode vs kernel mode: executable instructions, accessible memory, what triggers a switch, switching cost, impact of bugs and the purpose of protection.
user-mode-vs-kernel-mode.lead: A CPU has a user mode, in which applications run, and a kernel mode (privileged mode), in which the OS kernel runs. In user mode, privileged instructions such as setting up page tables, performing I/O operations and disabling interrupts cannot be executed, and only the memory of the process itself can be accessed. When something like reading or writing a file is needed, the program asks the kernel through a system call. This keeps a bug or malicious behavior in one application from affecting other processes, the OS or the hardware.
rows: Programs that run
Applications
The OS kernel and most device drivers
Executable instructions
Ordinary instructions only. Executing a privileged instruction raises an exception
All instructions, including switching page tables, enabling and disabling interrupts, and setting control registers
Accessible memory
Only the pages permitted to the user in the process's own virtual address space
Everything, including the kernel area. Can also handle physical memory and device registers
Device operations
Not directly. Asks the kernel through system calls
Reads and writes registers directly and handles interrupts
Names in architectures (examples)
x86 ring 3, Arm EL0, RISC-V U-mode
x86 ring 0, Arm EL1, RISC-V S-mode
What triggers a mode switch
Entry into kernel mode on system-call instructions (syscall, svc, ecall, etc.), device or timer interrupts, and exceptions (page faults, division by zero, illegal instructions, etc.)
A dedicated return instruction (sret, eret, etc.) restores the return address and mode at the same time, returning to user mode
Switching cost (typical)
A system-call round trip takes roughly 100 ns to 1 µs. Vulnerability mitigations can increase it
Work within the kernel uses function calls, with no mode switch. Switching processes (a context switch) is heavier still
Impact of bugs
Only that process is forcibly terminated
The whole system can stop (kernel panic, etc.)
when: User mode
Ordinary processing in applications and libraries. Computation and memory reads and writes are done quickly in user mode without going through the kernel.
Kernel mode
Processing that requires resource management and protection, such as file and network I/O, memory allocation, process switching and interrupt handling.
Performance techniques

To reduce the number of system calls, data is accumulated in user-space buffers and written out in batches, or some processing is done while staying in user mode using shared memory or dedicated mechanisms.
faq: Why are user mode and kernel mode separated?

To prevent applications from manipulating page tables or devices on their own. With the separation, even if a program has a bug, it cannot corrupt the memory of other processes or the OS or take over devices, and the problem is handled simply by terminating that program.
When does the CPU switch from user mode to kernel mode?

There are three triggers: system calls, which the program requests itself; interrupts from devices or timers; and exceptions caused by executing instructions, such as page faults or division by zero. In every case, the CPU switches modes and starts processing at a fixed kernel entry point.
Why are system calls slow?

Besides the mode switch, they require saving and restoring registers, checking arguments, and work at the kernel entry and exit. When page tables are switched as a vulnerability mitigation, they become heavier still. Even if each call is short, calling one for every small read or write becomes a large burden.
Is a mode switch the same as a context switch?

No. A mode switch on a system call simply enters kernel processing while staying in the same process. A context switch replaces the process or thread being executed, which also involves switching the address space and more, so it is a heavier operation.

can-vs-lin-vs-automotive-ethernet.title: CAN vs LIN vs Automotive Ethernet: Key Differences Explained
can-vs-lin-vs-automotive-ethernet.description: CAN vs LIN vs automotive Ethernet: speed, wiring, node topology, access method, error detection, cost and uses in body, control and camera/backbone roles.
can-vs-lin-vs-automotive-ethernet.lead: Inside a car, several networks are used side by side to match the speed and cost each job needs. LIN is an inexpensive network that uses a single signal wire at up to about 20 kbit/s and connects body components such as switches and motors. CAN uses a differential signal on two wires, lets ECUs communicate with priorities, and serves as a highly reliable network of up to 1 Mbit/s (several Mbit/s for the data phase in CAN FD) for controlling the engine, brakes and so on. Automotive Ethernet sends 100 Mbit/s or more over a single twisted pair and carries large volumes of data, such as from cameras, as well as the backbone that links ECUs.
rows: Maximum speed (typical)
About 20 kbit/s
Up to 1 Mbit/s for classic CAN (500 kbit/s is commonly used in practice). CAN FD reaches several Mbit/s in the data phase
100 Mbit/s (100BASE-T1) and 1 Gbit/s (1000BASE-T1). Faster standards also exist
Wiring
One signal wire plus ground
Differential signal on two twisted wires (CAN_H and CAN_L), with 120 Ω termination resistors at both ends
Full duplex over a single twisted pair
Node topology
One master and multiple slaves
A multi-master bus in which all nodes are peers
Star or tree topologies with point-to-point links centered on switches (a 10 Mbit/s bus-type standard also exists)
How transmission order is decided
The master transmits according to a schedule, and slaves respond to the master's requests
Arbitration by ID. The smaller the ID, the higher the priority, and the winning frame is not corrupted
Switches forward the traffic. For communication that must arrive within a fixed time, TSN manages time and bandwidth
Data per transmission
Up to 8 bytes
Up to 8 bytes for classic CAN, up to 64 bytes for CAN FD
Up to about 1,500 bytes per frame
Error detection
Checksum
CRC, acknowledgment (ACK), and disconnecting nodes based on error counts
CRC. Higher-layer protocols handle retransmission and similar functions
Cost per node
Lowest. Slaves can run without a crystal
Moderate. Many automotive microcontrollers have a built-in controller
Higher. Requires PHYs and switches, but is cheap per bit
Main uses
Body functions: power windows, mirrors, seats, switches, wipers, rain sensors and so on
Control functions: engine, transmission, brakes, steering, communication between body ECUs, fault diagnosis
Camera and radar data, infotainment, the backbone linking ECUs, software updates
when: LIN
When connecting switches, motors and sensors that need no speed and where low cost is the top priority to a nearby ECU. Used as a subnetwork of CAN.
CAN
When you want to exchange control data reliably according to priority. When many ECUs need to be connected on one bus with noise-resistant communication. When data volume grows, CAN FD is used.
Automotive Ethernet

When bandwidth of 100 Mbit/s or more is needed, such as for large volumes of camera and sensor data, software updates, and the backbone linking the central computer to zone ECUs in a zonal architecture.
faq: What happens in CAN when two nodes start transmitting at the same time?

Each node monitors the bus state while sending the ID bits, and only the node sending the higher-priority frame (the smaller ID value) continues transmitting. The losing node stops and retransmits later, so the winning frame arrives intact. This is called non-destructive arbitration.
Why is LIN cheap?

It needs only one signal wire, and the master decides communication timing, so slave circuits are simple. Because slaves align their clocks to a synchronization signal sent by the master, they can run on oscillators without a crystal.
How does automotive Ethernet differ from ordinary Ethernet in offices and elsewhere?

It performs full-duplex communication over just a single twisted pair, making the wiring lighter and cheaper. It is also built to withstand the strong noise and wide temperature range inside a vehicle, and for communication that must arrive within a fixed time, time and bandwidth are managed with TSN standards.
Will CAN and LIN disappear as automotive Ethernet spreads?

Not any time soon. Ethernet is used for the high-speed backbone and for cameras and the like, but for low-volume communication where reliability matters, such as switches, motors and control data, the inexpensive and proven CAN and LIN will continue to be used.

open-drain-vs-push-pull.title: Open-Drain vs Push-Pull Output: Key Differences Explained
open-drain-vs-push-pull.description: Open-drain vs push-pull outputs in one table: output stage, how H is driven, rise time, wired-AND, mixed-voltage interfacing, current draw and uses.
open-drain-vs-push-pull.lead: Both are output stages that drive digital signals, but they differ in how they output H. A push-pull output combines a pMOS on the supply side with an nMOS on the ground side and actively drives both H and L with transistors, so it is fast and draws almost no current while idle. An open-drain output has only the ground-side nMOS: it pulls the line down for L, but for H it releases the output and lets a pull-up resistor pull it up. The rise is slower, but several outputs can share one line (wired-AND) and the pull-up voltage can be chosen, so it is used for I2C and interrupt lines.
rows: Output stage
Two transistors: a supply-side pMOS and a ground-side nMOS (the same form as a CMOS inverter)
Only a ground-side nMOS. Its drain is brought out to the pin, with nothing on the supply side
How H is output
The pMOS turns on and connects the pin to the supply
The nMOS turns off, releasing the pin (high impedance), and an external pull-up resistor pulls it up
How L is output
The nMOS turns on and connects the pin to ground
The nMOS turns on and connects the pin to ground (the same)
Rise speed
Fast. The pMOS charges the line
Slow. Set by the RC time constant of the pull-up resistor R and the line capacitance C (e.g. about 0.47 µs with 4.7 kΩ and 100 pF)
Fall speed
Fast. The nMOS discharges the line
Fast. The nMOS discharges the line
Connecting several outputs to one line
Not possible. If H and L collide, a large current flows from the supply to ground
Possible. If any one output drives L, the line goes L (wired-AND)
Interfacing with circuits at a different voltage
The H voltage is set by its own supply voltage. A level shifter is needed for circuits at a different voltage
The H voltage is set by the pull-up voltage, so it can match the other side's voltage within the pin's voltage rating
Current consumption
Almost none while idle (leakage only). Charge and discharge current flows when switching
Current keeps flowing through the pull-up resistor while L is output (about 0.7 mA with 3.3 V and 4.7 kΩ)
Typical speed
Tens of MHz or more is possible
Limited by the pull-up resistor and capacitance. For I2C, 100 kHz, 400 kHz, 1 MHz, etc.
Typical uses
Fast signals such as SPI and UART signals, clocks, general-purpose GPIO and memory buses
I2C and SMBus, interrupt and reset lines shared by several devices, interfacing with circuits at a different voltage, driving LEDs
when: Push-pull output
When a single output drives inputs and speed or low current consumption matters. Ordinary digital signals such as GPIO, SPI and UART use this type.
Open-drain output
When several devices drive the same line (I2C, shared interrupt or reset lines), or when you want to pass a signal to a circuit at a different voltage by changing the pull-up voltage.
Switching between them
Many microcontroller GPIOs can be configured as either push-pull or open-drain. Pins used for I2C are set to open-drain, with external pull-up resistors.
faq: How do you choose the pull-up resistor value?

A smaller value gives a faster rise, but increases the current that flows while L is output and also raises the L voltage (VOL). The upper limit is set by the line capacitance and the required rise time, and the lower limit by the current the output can sink and the VOL specification. For I2C, a few kΩ (e.g. about 2.2 to 10 kΩ) is commonly used.
What happens if push-pull outputs are connected directly together?

If one outputs H and the other L, a large current flows from the supply to ground through the pMOS on the H side and the nMOS on the L side (bus contention). The line voltage is also left somewhere in between, which can cause heating or device damage, so shared lines use open-drain outputs or tri-state outputs that can release the line.
Why does I2C use open-drain?

Because several devices drive the same SDA and SCL lines. Operations such as the receiver pulling SDA L to return an ACK, a slave holding SCL L to make the master wait (clock stretching), and arbitration when several masters start sending at the same time all rely on the wired-AND property: if any one device outputs L, the line goes L.
How is open-collector different?
The idea is the same. It is called open-collector when the output transistor is a bipolar transistor and open-drain when it is a MOSFET. Both only pull L down, and H is created by a pull-up resistor.

class-a-vs-ab-vs-d-amplifier.title: Class A vs AB vs D Amplifiers: Key Differences Explained
class-a-vs-ab-vs-d-amplifier.description: Class A, AB and D amplifiers in one table: operation, conduction angle, max efficiency, distortion, heat, noise and uses, plus how Class B fits in.
class-a-vs-ab-vs-d-amplifier.lead: An amplifier's class describes how its output transistors are operated. Class A keeps current flowing through the transistor over the whole cycle, so distortion is lowest, but it consumes power even with no signal, and its efficiency is 25% or 50% even in theory. Class AB is Class B, in which two transistors share the positive and negative half-cycles, with a small idle current added to suppress crossover distortion; its efficiency approaches Class B's theoretical maximum of about 78.5%. Class D switches the transistors on and off and filters pulses such as PWM back into the original signal, achieving high efficiency of around 90% at high output.
rows: Operating principle
Current always flows through the transistor (linear region) and increases or decreases with the signal
A push-pull pair of two transistors shares the positive and negative half-cycles. A small idle current is kept flowing
The transistors switch on and off; the signal is converted into pulses such as PWM, amplified, and restored by an LC low-pass filter
Conduction angle (period during which one transistor conducts)
360° (full cycle)
More than 180° and less than 360° (Class B is 180°)
Used fully on or off, so it is not classified by conduction angle
Theoretical maximum efficiency
25% (with a series resistive load). 50% with transformer or choke coupling
Slightly below Class B's approximately 78.5% (π/4)
100% with ideal switches. In practice, around 90% at high output
Efficiency at low output
Very low. Uses the same power even with no signal
Drops with output, but much better than Class A
Easy to keep high (at very low output, switching losses take a larger share)
Distortion
Lowest. No crossover distortion
Low. Crossover distortion is suppressed by the idle current and negative feedback
Distortion arises from dead time, imperfect switching and supply variation. It can be reduced with negative feedback and similar techniques
Heat
Highest. Maximum when there is no signal
Moderate. A heat sink is often needed
Low. The heat sink can be made small or omitted
Noise and EMI
No switching noise
No switching noise
Switching at hundreds of kHz to several MHz produces EMI. Care is needed with the output filter and wiring
Circuit and components
Simple. Can be built with a single transistor
A pair of output transistors and a bias circuit
A pulse modulator, a gate driver circuit and an output filter (inductor and capacitor)
Typical uses
Small-signal amplification, preamplifiers, driver stages that drive the following stage, some high-end audio
Audio power amplifiers, headphone amplifiers, op-amp output stages
Speaker drive in smartphones and TVs, car audio, portable speakers, high-power amplifiers
when: Class A
When the output is small and low distortion is the top priority. Small-signal amplification, preamplifiers and driver stages that drive the following stage.
Class AB
When you want both low distortion and good efficiency. Audio power amplifiers, headphone amplifiers, and output stages of op-amps and buffers.
Class D
When you want long battery life, less heat or a smaller heat sink, or high output power. Speakers in smartphones and TVs, car audio.
faq: Why does Class A have two maximum efficiencies, 25% and 50%?

Because the load is connected differently. If the load resistor is connected in series with the transistor, DC current also flows through the load and wastes power, so the theoretical maximum is 25%. If the load is coupled through a transformer or choke, the DC power is not wasted in the load and the output voltage can swing up to twice the supply voltage, so the maximum is 50%.
What is crossover distortion?

In a Class B push-pull stage, when the signal passes near 0 there is a region where neither transistor is on, which distorts the output waveform. With bipolar transistors it occurs because no current flows until about 0.6 to 0.7 V is applied between base and emitter. Class AB removes this region by keeping a small idle current flowing.
Does the D in Class D stand for digital?

No. The name simply follows Class A, B and C and does not mean digital. Many Class D amplifiers work by comparing an analog input signal with a triangle wave in a comparator to convert it into PWM pulses.
Why is Class D so efficient?

Because the output transistors are used fully on or fully off. When on, the voltage across them is nearly zero, and when off, the current is nearly zero, so little power is turned into heat in the transistors. The remaining losses include conduction losses due to on-resistance, losses during switching transitions and the power needed to drive the gates.

op-amp-vs-comparator.title: Op-Amp vs Comparator: Key Differences Explained
op-amp-vs-comparator.description: Op-amps vs comparators in one table: feedback or open loop, output stage, speed, saturation recovery, phase compensation, hysteresis and substitution.
op-amp-vs-comparator.lead: Both use the same triangle symbol and greatly amplify the voltage difference between two inputs, but they are designed for different purposes. An op-amp is designed to be used with negative feedback: it includes phase compensation so that it does not oscillate, and its output moves smoothly as an analog voltage. A comparator is used open loop and is built to output which of two voltages is larger quickly as a binary H or L; it has no phase compensation, and its output is easy to connect to logic. That is why an op-amp used as a comparator is slow, and a comparator with negative feedback tends to oscillate.
rows: Main usage
Used with negative feedback; gain and frequency response are set by external resistors and capacitors
Used open loop (or with positive feedback for hysteresis) to judge which voltage is larger
Output
An analog voltage that varies continuously with the input
Binary H or L. Normally saturated at one or the other
Output stage
Push-pull. Some rail-to-rail parts swing close to the supply rails
Open-drain (open-collector), or push-pull matched to logic levels
Phase compensation
Built in. Many parts do not oscillate even at unity gain with negative feedback
None. As a result, it switches faster
Speed metrics
Gain-bandwidth product (GBW) and slew rate
Propagation delay (a few ns to a few µs depending on the part) and output rise and fall times
Recovery from saturation
Not intended to be saturated. Recovery can take time and is often not specified
Designed to repeatedly saturate and toggle, and switches quickly
Hysteresis
Normally not used
Positive feedback through external resistors, or a part with built-in hysteresis, prevents output chatter caused by noise
Inputs
Negative feedback keeps the two input voltages nearly equal (virtual short). Some parts have protection diodes between the inputs
Large differences between the two inputs are expected. Many parts tolerate large differential voltages
Substitution
Can sometimes replace a comparator if slow response is acceptable and the output levels match
Cannot replace an op-amp. Tends to oscillate with negative feedback
Typical uses
Amplification, filters, buffers, integrators, sensor signal conditioning
Threshold detection, zero-cross detection, voltage monitoring, flash ADCs, PWM generation
when: Op-amp
When amplifying a signal while keeping it analog, or building filters and buffers. Applications that use negative feedback to move the output continuously.
Comparator
When you want to judge quickly and reliably whether a voltage has crossed a threshold and pass the result to logic. Battery voltage monitoring, zero-cross detection, comparison inside ADCs, etc.
Using an op-amp instead
When slow response is acceptable and the output voltage levels suit the following circuit. Check the input differential voltage range and the behavior in saturation in the datasheet before using it.
faq: Can I use an op-amp instead of a comparator?

It can work in applications where slow response is acceptable. However, phase compensation makes it switch slowly, recovery from saturation takes time, and its output H and L voltages may not match the logic. In parts with protection diodes between the inputs, current flows when a large differential voltage is applied, so care is needed.
What happens if negative feedback is applied to a comparator?
In most cases it oscillates. A comparator has no phase compensation so that it can switch quickly, so the negative feedback loop lacks phase margin. For amplification and similar uses, use an op-amp.
Why add hysteresis to a comparator?

Because when the input changes slowly near the threshold, a little noise can make the output toggle between H and L many times. Using positive feedback to separate the thresholds for a rising input and a falling input (a Schmitt trigger) makes the output switch only once.
Why do so many comparators have open-drain outputs?

Because by changing the pull-up voltage, the output can connect directly to logic at a voltage different from the comparator's supply. It also allows uses such as tying several comparator outputs to one line that goes L when any one of them responds (wired-AND).

pll-vs-dll.title: PLL vs DLL: Key Differences Explained
pll-vs-dll.description: PLL vs DLL in one table: what is controlled, VCO vs delay line, frequency multiplication, jitter, loop stability, and uses (clock generation, deskew).
pll-vs-dll.lead: Both detect the phase error relative to a reference clock and use feedback to drive it to zero, but they adjust different things. A PLL adjusts the frequency of a voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO) and aligns the clock it generates itself with the reference, so combined with a divider it can produce frequencies many times the reference. A DLL passes the input clock itself through a delay line and only adjusts that delay to align the phase, so it cannot change the frequency, but jitter does not accumulate and the loop is stable and easy to design.
rows: Name
Phase-Locked Loop
Delay-Locked Loop
What it controls
VCO frequency (phase is the integral of frequency)
The delay of the delay line
Main building blocks
Phase-frequency detector, charge pump, loop filter, VCO, feedback divider
Phase detector, charge pump, loop filter (capacitor), voltage-controlled delay line
Output clock
A clock generated by the VCO itself
A delayed version of the input clock
Frequency multiplication
Possible. A 1/N divider in the feedback gives N times the reference (fractional schemes also exist)
Basically not possible. The output has the same frequency as the input (some schemes multiply by combining multiphase outputs)
Jitter
VCO fluctuations accumulate cycle by cycle, and only components below the loop bandwidth are corrected. Reference jitter components above the bandwidth are removed
The delay line does not accumulate jitter. Input jitter passes almost unchanged to the output
Loop stability
The VCO acts as an integrator, making the loop second order or higher, so the loop filter must be designed with phase margin in mind
The delay line has no integrating action, so the loop can be first order, stable and easy to design
Locking
Can lock over a wide frequency range, but takes longer to lock
Locks quickly, but the delay range is limited and false lock (locking one cycle off) must be watched for
Typical uses
Generating high-frequency clocks from a crystal reference, RF frequency synthesizers, SerDes clocks and clock and data recovery (CDR)
Aligning DDR DRAM output timing with the clock, clock deskew, multiphase clock generation
when: PLL
When you need a clock at a different frequency from the reference (usually many times higher). Generating CPU or SerDes clocks from a crystal reference, or generating radio frequencies.
DLL
When the same frequency is fine and you want to cancel on-chip delay to align clock phase. Aligning DDR DRAM data output timing, and clock deskew.
Combined

A common combination is to generate a clock at the required frequency with a PLL and then, in memory interfaces and similar circuits, use a DLL referenced to that clock for fine phase adjustment (for example, shifting a strobe by 1/4 cycle).
faq: Why can't a DLL change the frequency?

Because a DLL's output is the input clock delayed by a delay line. No matter how the delay is changed, the edge spacing stays the same as the input, so the frequency does not change. A PLL has a VCO that oscillates on its own and aligns its divided clock with the reference, so it can produce N times the reference frequency.
Why does jitter not accumulate in a DLL?

Because each output edge of a DLL is a delayed copy of an input edge and does not inherit errors from the previous cycle. In a PLL's VCO, each cycle starts where the previous one ended, so fluctuations add up and remain until the loop corrects them. On the other hand, a DLL passes input jitter straight through.
How is the PLL loop bandwidth chosen?

A wider bandwidth corrects VCO fluctuations quickly but lets more reference clock jitter through. A narrower bandwidth rejects reference jitter well, but leaves more VCO fluctuation and slows locking. It is chosen by considering whether the reference or the VCO has lower noise, along with loop stability (phase margin).
Why are DLLs used in DDR DRAM?

The on-chip clock path and output circuits have delays that vary with voltage and temperature. Canceling this delay with a DLL lets data be output aligned with the edges of the external clock. There is no need to change the frequency, so a DLL, which adds little jitter, is well suited.

single-ended-vs-differential-signaling.title: Single-Ended vs Differential Signaling: Key Differences Explained
single-ended-vs-differential-signaling.description: Single-ended vs differential signaling in one table: wire count, reference, noise immunity, EMI, swing and speed, routing and standards (LVDS, USB, PCIe).
single-ended-vs-differential-signaling.lead: Single-ended signaling reads the voltage on one signal line relative to ground, which is simple and needs few wires. Differential signaling sends opposite signals on two lines and reads 0 and 1 from the voltage difference between them. Noise and ground potential differences that appear equally on both lines cancel when the difference is taken, and the electromagnetic fields from the opposite currents also cancel, so signals can be sent faster and farther with a small swing. The trade-off is that each signal needs two lines, and the design must match the length and spacing of the two lines.
rows: Wires per signal
One (the return current shares ground)
Two (a positive and negative pair)
Reference for reading
Voltage relative to ground
Voltage difference between the two lines
Common-mode noise
Adds directly to the signal
Cancels when the difference is taken (depending on the receiver's CMRR)
Ground potential differences
A ground offset between transmitter and receiver becomes error directly
Little effect as long as it is within the receiver's allowed common-mode voltage range
Radiated noise (EMI)
Current loops are large, so it radiates easily
Fields from the opposite currents cancel, so it radiates little
Signal swing
Large. Close to the supply voltage (e.g. 0 to 3.3 V)
Small. A few hundred mV (about 350 mV for LVDS)
Typical speed
Tens to hundreds of Mbit/s. Memory buses with careful termination reach several Gbit/s per line
Hundreds of Mbit/s to tens of Gbit/s per pair
Routing design
Simple. For fast signals, watch the characteristic impedance and termination
Match the length and spacing of the two lines and maintain the differential impedance (often 85 to 100 Ω)
Cost and pin count
Low cost, fewer pins
Twice the pins and wiring. Transmitter and receiver circuits are also more complex
Typical examples
GPIO, I2C, SPI, UART, DDR data (DQ)
LVDS, USB, PCI Express, SATA, HDMI, Ethernet, CAN, RS-485
when: Single-ended
When speed is not very high, distances are short, and you want to keep pin count and cost down. On-board GPIO, I2C, SPI, etc.
Differential
For high-speed signals in the Gbit/s class, connecting separate equipment by cable, noisy environments, or when radiated noise must be suppressed. PCIe, USB, Ethernet, automotive CAN, etc.
Example of using both

DDR memory uses single-ended signaling for the numerous data lines (DQ) and differential signaling for the clock and strobes (DQS) that serve as timing references, balancing pin count and reliability.
faq: Why is differential signaling robust against common-mode noise?

When two lines run close together, external noise couples onto both by nearly the same amount. The receiver reads only the voltage difference between them, so noise that appears equally on both (common-mode noise) is removed by subtraction. A shift in ground potential also appears equally on both lines, so it has little effect.
Differential signaling needs two lines, so why can it go faster?

Because it is robust against noise, the swing can be reduced to a few hundred mV, and the smaller voltage to charge and discharge allows faster switching. It also radiates little and is less sensitive to ground potential differences, so serial links can reach tens of Gbit/s per pair.
What should you watch for when routing a differential pair?

First, match the lengths of the two lines. If the lengths differ, the two signals arrive at different times, the difference waveform is distorted, part of it turns into common-mode noise, and radiation increases. Also keep the spacing constant to hold the differential impedance at the specified value (often 85 to 100 Ω), and terminate at the receiver.
Does differential signaling need no ground?

It is not that no ground is needed at all. The average of the two voltages (the common-mode voltage) must stay within the range the receiver allows. To ensure this, either share a common ground, or block DC with capacitors or transformers and re-establish the common-mode voltage at the receiver. Ethernet uses transformers to isolate the equipment from each other.

buck-vs-boost-converter.title: Buck vs Boost Converter: Key Differences Explained
buck-vs-boost-converter.description: Buck vs boost converters: output range, ideal ratio (D vs 1/(1−D)), component layout, input and output current continuity, efficiency, control and uses.
buck-vs-boost-converter.lead: Both are switching DC-DC converters built from the same parts (a switch, an inductor, a diode or second switch, and a capacitor), but the parts are arranged differently. A buck converter places the switch between the input and the inductor, chops and averages the input voltage according to the fraction of on-time (duty cycle D), and ideally outputs a lower voltage of D times the input. A boost converter places the inductor on the input side, uses the switch to connect it to ground to store energy in the inductor, then releases that energy to the output, ideally outputting a higher voltage of 1/(1−D) times the input.
rows: Output voltage range
Lower than the input (0 to the input voltage)
Higher than the input (the input voltage or above)
Ideal conversion ratio (continuous conduction mode)
Vout/Vin = D
Vout/Vin = 1/(1−D)
Example (D = 0.5)
12 V to 6 V
12 V to 24 V
Component layout
Switch between the input and the inductor; inductor on the output side. Diode between ground and the node between the switch and the inductor
Inductor on the input side; switch between ground and the node after the inductor. Diode between that node and the output
Operation
When on, current flows through the inductor to the output; when off, the inductor current keeps flowing through the diode
When on, energy is stored in the inductor; when off, the inductor voltage adds to the input and the energy is released to the output
Input current
