Discontinuous (flows only while the switch is on). The input capacitor is important
Continuous (keeps flowing through the inductor)
Output current
Continuous (keeps flowing from the inductor). Output ripple is small
Discontinuous (delivered only while the switch is off). The ripple current in the output capacitor is large
Efficiency
About 80 to 95% depending on conditions
About 80 to 95% depending on conditions. Drops at high boost ratios
Control
The control loop is easy to design
In continuous conduction mode there is a right-half-plane zero, making it hard to raise the control loop bandwidth
When switching stops
The input and output are disconnected
The input voltage remains at the output through the inductor and diode. A separate switch is needed to disconnect completely
Typical uses
Generating CPU or SoC core voltages (around 1 V) from 12 V or 5 V, generating low voltages from batteries
Generating 5 V from a lithium-ion battery (about 3.0 to 4.2 V), driving series LEDs, power factor correction (PFC) in AC power supplies
when: Buck (step-down) converter
When you want to efficiently generate a voltage lower than the input at high current. CPU and SoC core supplies, and generating various voltages from 12 V or 5 V.
Boost (step-up) converter
When you need a voltage higher than the input. Generating a 5 V USB output from a battery, driving series-connected LEDs, or generating a high DC voltage in PFC.
Buck-boost
When the battery voltage crosses above and below the output voltage as it is used, use a buck-boost converter, which can do both.
faq: How are the conversion ratios D and 1/(1−D) derived?

In steady state, the voltage across the inductor averages to zero over one cycle (the volt-second balance). In a buck converter, (Vin − Vout) is applied during the on-time and −Vout during the off-time, so (Vin − Vout) × D = Vout × (1 − D), giving Vout = D × Vin. In a boost converter, Vin × D = (Vout − Vin) × (1 − D) gives Vout = Vin/(1 − D).
Why does a boost converter output a voltage higher than its input?

While the switch is on, current flows through the inductor and stores energy. When the switch turns off, the inductor tries to keep the current flowing and generates a voltage, which adds to the input voltage and flows through the diode to the output, so the output is higher than the input.
Can the boost ratio be made arbitrarily large by bringing D close to 1?

Ideally 1/(1−D) grows without limit, but in practice losses from the resistance of the inductor and switch increase, the output voltage levels off and efficiency drops. Practical boost ratios are up to a few times; for higher ratios, approaches such as transformer-based topologies are chosen.
What is synchronous rectification?

It replaces the diode with a MOSFET that is turned on when the diode would conduct. It reduces the loss from the diode's forward voltage (about 0.3 to 0.5 V even for a Schottky barrier diode), so efficiency improves more as the output voltage gets lower.

clock-gating-vs-power-gating.title: Clock Gating vs Power Gating: Key Differences Explained
clock-gating-vs-power-gating.description: Clock vs power gating: power saved (dynamic or static), what stops, wake-up time, state retention, cells needed (ICG, power switch, isolation), granularity.
clock-gating-vs-power-gating.lead: Both are low-power design techniques that reduce the power of unused circuits, but they stop different things. Clock gating stops the clock to registers, eliminating signal switching and reducing dynamic power. Power stays on, so state is retained and operation can resume immediately within one to a few cycles. Power gating cuts a block's power with a switch, eliminating almost all static power from leakage current in addition to dynamic power. The trade-off is that state is lost, so a mechanism to save it is needed, and wake-up takes longer.
rows: Power reduced
Dynamic power (switching in the clock network, flip-flops and downstream logic)
Both static power (leakage) and dynamic power
What is stopped
The clock to registers
The power supply to the block
Power supply
Stays on. Leakage current keeps flowing
Power switches disconnect the block's supply rail
State retention
Retained
Lost. Required state is saved in retention flip-flops (retention registers) or memory
Wake-up time
One to a few cycles
Long. Power is restored while limiting inrush current and the state is restored, typically on the order of µs
Required circuits
ICG (a clock-gating cell built from a latch and an AND gate) and logic to generate the enable
Power switches (headers or footers), isolation cells, retention flip-flops and a power sequencing controller
Granularity
Fine. Can be applied to groups of just a few registers
Coarse. Applied per block (power domain), such as a CPU core or an IP block
Design and verification
Logic synthesis tools can insert it automatically from enable conditions. STA performs clock-gating checks
Power intent is described in UPF or similar formats, and behavior and sequencing when power is cut must also be verified
Overhead
Small. ICG area and delay
Power switch area and voltage drop, plus energy to save and restore. Not worthwhile for short idle periods
Typical use
In almost all digital circuits, stopping the registers of inactive functions
Shutting down blocks that are unused for long periods. Deep CPU idle states, unused blocks in smartphone SoCs
when: Clock gating
Any time a circuit has an inactive period, from a few cycles to long durations. It resumes immediately and retains state, so it is used in almost all digital circuits.
Power gating

When a block is unused for a long time, or when leakage power is a large share (advanced processes or high temperatures). Used when the idle period is long enough to recover the energy spent saving and restoring.
Combined
A common staged approach is to stop the clock first and, if the idle period looks long, save state and cut power as well. It is also combined with DVFS.
faq: Why isn't an AND gate alone enough to stop the clock?

Because if the enable signal changes while the clock is 1, a short pulse (glitch) appears on the clock and flip-flops can operate erroneously. An ICG holds the enable in a latch that passes it only while the clock is 0 and then ANDs it with the clock, so no glitch occurs.
Why does power gating take long to wake up?

Because the large capacitance of the powered-down block must be recharged. Turning all the switches on at once causes a large inrush current that drops the supply voltage of other active circuits, so the switches are turned on gradually in sequence. After that, reset and state restoration are also needed.
Why are isolation cells needed?

The outputs of a powered-down block sit at a voltage that is neither 0 nor 1. If active blocks receive them directly, they can malfunction or shoot-through current can flow in their input gates. Isolation cells clamp the signals at the boundary to a fixed value (0 or 1).
Should power be cut even for short idle periods?

Not necessarily. Cutting power uses energy to save and restore state and to recharge capacitance, so unless the block can stay idle longer than the time needed to recover that energy through reduced leakage power (the break-even time), it actually costs more. Use clock gating for short idle periods.

scan-test-vs-bist.title: Scan Test vs BIST: Key Differences Explained
scan-test-vs-bist.description: Scan test vs BIST (built-in self-test): pattern generation (ATPG vs on-chip), tester dependence, logic and memory, fault coverage, added logic, test time.
scan-test-vs-bist.lead: Scan test connects the flip-flops in a chip into shift registers (scan chains), shifts test patterns in from an external tester, and shifts out the circuit's responses to compare them with expected values. The patterns are generated from the netlist by ATPG tools. BIST builds a circuit that generates patterns and a circuit that checks results into the chip, so that the chip tests itself. In production test, it is common to combine scan test for logic with memory BIST for embedded memories, and BIST can also be used for self-diagnosis after shipment.
rows: Basic idea
Flip-flops are connected into scan chains; a pattern is shifted in, the circuit is clocked once, and the result is shifted out and compared
Circuits that generate patterns and check responses are built into the chip, which tests itself and reports pass or fail
How test patterns are generated
ATPG creates deterministic patterns from the netlist that target stuck-at and transition delay faults
Logic BIST generates pseudo-random patterns with an LFSR. Memory BIST generates addresses and data using fixed procedures such as March tests
Response checking
The tester compares responses with expected values (with test compression, responses compressed on chip are compared)
Logic BIST compresses responses with a MISR into a signature that is compared with an expected value. Memory BIST checks read values directly with comparators
Dependence on the tester
Patterns and expected values are held in tester memory. Requires scan pins plus tester performance and memory capacity
Only starting the test and reading the result (via JTAG, etc.) are needed, so a simple tester suffices
Main targets
Logic circuits (combinational logic and flip-flops)
Memory BIST: embedded memories such as SRAM. Logic BIST: logic circuits
Fault coverage
Easy to make high because patterns are generated for the targeted faults

Logic BIST tends to leave faults that are hard to detect with pseudo-random patterns, which test point insertion compensates for. Memory BIST achieves high coverage with procedures tailored to memory fault models
Added circuitry
Flip-flops are replaced with scan flip-flops (with a selection multiplexer), and chain wiring is added
Requires a pattern generator, a response compactor and a control circuit. Logic BIST also requires preparing the design so that no unknown values (X) occur
Test time
Long chains take time to shift, and speed is also limited by the tester. Test compression shortens it
Many patterns can run quickly with on-chip clocks. Logic BIST needs a large number of patterns
When it is used
Mainly in production wafer test and final test. Also used for failure diagnosis of defective parts
In addition to production test, it can also be used for inspection after board mounting and for self-diagnosis after shipment, such as at power-on
when: Scan test
When you want to find structural logic faults with high coverage in production test, or to narrow down the fault location in a failed chip.
BIST

Testing embedded memories that are hard to access directly from outside. When you want to reduce tester pins or memory. When self-diagnosis after shipment is needed at power-on or before driving, as in automotive applications.
Combined
Real chips commonly use scan test (with test compression) for logic and memory BIST for memories. Logic BIST also runs on top of the scan chains.
faq: If a chip has BIST, is scan test unnecessary?

Many chips use both. Logic BIST uses pseudo-random patterns, so hard-to-detect faults tend to remain, and production test typically secures high fault coverage with scan test using ATPG-generated patterns. Memories have a regular structure, so they are tested with memory BIST.
How are logic BIST and scan test related?

Logic BIST also uses scan chains. Patterns generated by an LFSR are shifted into the chains, the circuit is clocked, the responses that come out are compressed by a MISR, and the final signature is compared with an expected value. It is built on a scan design.
Why is BIST widely used to test embedded memories?

Because memories embedded in a chip are hard to read and write directly from external pins, and their regular structure lets a small circuit generate addresses and data in fixed sequences such as March tests. It is also often combined with repair that replaces failing bits with spare rows or columns.
Why do automotive chips run BIST at power-on?

To find faults that arise after shipment and latent faults that do not show up in normal operation. BIST can run on the chip itself without a tester, so it can be used for self-diagnosis inside the vehicle.

wafer-test-vs-final-test.title: Wafer Test vs Final Test: Key Differences Explained
wafer-test-vs-final-test.description: Wafer test (probe test) vs final test: timing and target, contact method (probe card vs socket), temperature, test items, screening purpose and KGD.
wafer-test-vs-final-test.lead: Wafer test is performed on the wafer after front-end processing and before dicing: the needles of a probe card are placed on each chip's bond pads to check whether it is good or bad. Removing defective chips before assembly avoids wasting packaging and assembly costs. Final test measures packaged ICs that a handler places in sockets; it confirms that they operate to specification, including catching defects introduced during assembly, before they are shipped.
rows: Timing
After front-end processing, before dicing
After assembly (encapsulation in a package), before shipment
Target
All chips on the wafer
Packaged ICs (chips that passed wafer test, after assembly)
Contact method
A prober moves the wafer and the probe card needles are placed on the chip's bond pads
A handler places the IC in a socket, and pogo pins or similar contact the package terminals (leads or balls)
Equipment
Tester, prober, probe card
Tester, handler, load board with sockets
Temperature
Measured by changing the temperature of the chuck that holds the wafer. Besides room temperature, it is sometimes measured hot or cold
The handler heats or cools the ICs, which are often measured hot and cold within the product's guaranteed temperature range
Main test items
DC parameters (such as leakage current), functional test, scan test. For memory, measurements for repair that replaces failing bits with spares
Function, DC parameters, AC parameters such as timing, operation at actual speed. Grading by speed and other criteria
High-speed signal measurement
The electrical characteristics of the needles impose limits, and high-speed signals or high-current measurements can be difficult
Sockets are electrically more favorable, making high-speed signals easier to measure
Purpose of finding defects
Remove defective chips before assembly to save packaging and assembly costs. Find process problems early from the wafer map
Remove defects, including those introduced in assembly (such as connection defects), to guarantee quality before shipment
Handling of defects
Defective chips are recorded in electronic wafer map data and are not used in assembly (formerly they were marked with ink)
Defective parts are removed, and good parts are sorted by performance and other criteria before shipment
Relation to KGD
When several chips are mounted in one package, chips confirmed good at this stage (KGD) are required
Even if a defect is found after assembly, it is difficult to replace only the defective chip
when: Wafer test
When you want to remove defective chips before assembly to save packaging and assembly costs. For products with several chips in one package, when you want to use only chips confirmed good (KGD).
Final test
When you guarantee after assembly that the packaged part works to specification before shipping it. When you want to verify operation over the guaranteed temperature range and at actual speed.
Combined
Typical products undergo both tests in the order wafer test → assembly → final test → shipment. The two tests divide the test items between them, reducing overlap to lower test cost.
faq: Why perform wafer test when there is a final test?

Because assembling defective chips wastes package materials and assembly costs. Removing defects at the wafer stage means only good chips are assembled. Also, the distribution of defects on the wafer map helps find the responsible process step early.
How does wafer test differ from WAT (parametric test)?

WAT measures parameters such as threshold voltage and sheet resistance on TEGs (evaluation test patterns) on the wafer to confirm that the process was completed to specification. Wafer test checks whether each product chip operates correctly to judge whether it is good or bad.
What is KGD?

A chip confirmed to be good before mounting (Known Good Die). When several chips are mounted in one package, a single defective chip makes the whole package defective, so the chips must be verified thoroughly at the wafer test stage.
At what stage is burn-in performed?

Burn-in is a test that applies high temperature and voltage to weed out chips prone to early failure, and it is often performed after packaging. Where KGD is required, wafer-level burn-in, performed on the wafer, is also used.

damascene-vs-subtractive-etch-interconne.title: Damascene vs Subtractive Etch Interconnects: Key Differences
damascene-vs-subtractive-etch-interconne.description: Damascene vs subtractive etch interconnects: process order, metal (Cu vs Al), use of CMP, via formation, and renewed interest for the finest wires.
damascene-vs-subtractive-etch-interconne.lead: Subtractive etch interconnects are formed by depositing a metal film over the whole surface, removing the unwanted parts by dry etching through a resist pattern, and filling the gaps between the remaining lines with dielectric; this method was long used for aluminum wiring. The damascene process works in the opposite order: trenches are first etched into the dielectric, metal is filled in, and the excess metal is removed by CMP. Copper hardly forms volatile compounds and is difficult to dry etch, so damascene became the standard for copper wiring. For the finest wires, forming ruthenium or other metals by etching is also being studied.
rows: Process order
Deposit dielectric → etch trenches and via holes → barrier metal and seed layer → copper plating → remove excess by CMP
Deposit metal film → lithography → dry etch the metal → fill between lines with dielectric and planarize
What is etched
Dielectric
Metal film
Main metal
Copper (Cu)
Aluminum (Al-Cu alloy). Ruthenium and others are also being studied for the finest wires
Metal fill
Trenches are filled by electroplating. Filling narrow trenches without gaps (voids) is a challenge
Only a flat film made by sputtering or a similar method is needed
Dielectric fill
The dielectric is deposited flat first, so it is rarely a problem
Narrow gaps between lines must be filled with dielectric without voids (HDP-CVD and similar methods have been used)
CMP
Essential. Removes the copper and barrier metal outside the trenches, separating each line
Not used to pattern the metal. Used to planarize the dielectric
Barrier layer
Trench bottoms and sidewalls are lined with TaN/Ta or similar to prevent copper diffusion. In narrow lines it takes up a larger share of the cross section
Diffusion is less of a problem with aluminum; Ti/TiN or similar films are stacked above and below
How vias are made
In dual damascene, line trenches and vias are filled at the same time and finished with a single CMP
Vias are opened in a separate step, filled with tungsten or similar and planarized by CMP before the next wiring layer is made
Challenges for fine wires
As lines narrow, copper resistivity rises (size effect) and the barrier layer takes a larger share
Precision in etching thin metal lines, and filling between lines with dielectric, are challenges
when: Damascene process
When making copper interconnects. Multilevel interconnects in advanced LSIs that need low-resistance wiring with high resistance to electromigration.
Subtractive etch interconnect
When making aluminum interconnects. Products with few wiring layers, or relatively wide wires. It is also being studied as a method for the finest wires using ruthenium or other metals.
Trend

Today's advanced LSIs make most of their wiring with copper dual damascene. For the finest layers, forming metals whose resistance rises less and that allow thinner barrier layers by etching is being reconsidered.
faq: Why is copper difficult to dry etch?

Because the copper compounds formed by reaction with chlorine and other etch gases are hard to volatilize and remain on the surface near room temperature. They can be volatilized at high temperatures, but the resist and other materials cannot withstand that, making practical patterning difficult. That is why copper is shaped by filling trenches and using CMP.
What is dual damascene?

A method in which both the line trenches and the via holes connecting to the layer below are formed in the dielectric, filled at the same time in a single copper plating step, and finished with a single CMP. It requires fewer steps than single damascene, which makes trenches and vias separately.
Where does the name damascene come from?

It comes from damascening, a decorative inlay technique in which grooves are carved into a metal surface and filled with another metal. The name was chosen because the process of filling trenches in the dielectric with metal resembles this technique.
Will interconnects return to subtractive etching?

Not entirely. Layers with wide wires will continue to be made with copper damascene. For layers with very small line widths, rising copper resistivity and barrier layer thickness become problems, so methods that pattern ruthenium or other metals by etching are being studied.

msi-vs-mesi-vs-moesi.title: MSI vs MESI vs MOESI: Key Differences Explained
msi-vs-mesi-vs-moesi.description: MSI, MESI and MOESI cache coherence protocols in one table: number and meaning of states, benefits of Exclusive and Owned, memory write-back and complexity.
msi-vs-mesi-vs-moesi.lead: MSI, MESI and MOESI are protocols that attach a state to each line held in each cache of a multicore system so that data at the same address never becomes inconsistent. MSI is the basic form with only three states: Modified, Shared and Invalid. MESI adds Exclusive (held only by this cache, with the same contents as memory), which saves bus traffic when writing data that no other core holds. MOESI further adds the Owned state, which allows modified data to be shared with other caches without writing it back to memory.
rows: Number of states
Three (M, S, I)
Four (M, E, S, I)
Five (M, O, E, S, I)
Modified (M)
Held only by this cache; contents differ from memory
Same
Same
Shared (S)
Other caches may also hold it. Contents match memory
Same
Other caches may also hold it. Contents may differ from memory (when a line in O state exists)
Exclusive (E)
None
Held only by this cache; contents match memory
Present (same as MESI)
Owned (O)
None
None
Contents differ from memory, but other caches share it in S. Responsible for writing back to memory
When reading data no other core holds
Enters S state
Enters E state
Enters E state
When then writing to that data
To change from S to M, issues a request on the bus or similar to invalidate other copies
Changes from E to M without any communication
Changes from E to M without any communication
When another core reads an M line
Writes back to memory; both become S
Writes back to memory; both become S (the data may also be passed directly from the cache)
Passes the data without writing back; this cache becomes O and the other becomes S
Write-back to memory
Occurs each time a modified line is read by another core
Occurs each time a modified line is read by another core
Can be deferred until the O line is evicted
State bits and complexity
2 bits. Simplest
2 bits. Moderate
3 bits. Most complex
when: MSI
As the basic form for learning how coherence works. When you want to keep state transitions as simple as possible.
MESI
When there are many reads and writes to data used by only one core. Thanks to the E state, read-then-write operations avoid communication. It forms the basis of the protocols in many multicore CPUs.
MOESI
When modified data is frequently passed between cores. When you want to reduce write-backs to memory and save memory bandwidth.
faq: What is the benefit of MESI's E state?

Reading data that no other core holds puts the line in E state, and a later write can change it to M without notifying other cores. In MSI, the same case enters S state, so an invalidation request must be issued for each write. It reduces bus traffic for read-then-write operations on data used by only one thread.
What is the benefit of MOESI's O state?

When another core reads modified data (M state), MESI writes it back to memory before sharing it, but MOESI passes the data between caches without writing back, and the original cache keeps responsibility for the write-back in O state. This reduces writes to memory.
How do the E and M states differ?

In both, this cache is the only one holding the line. In E state the contents match memory, so no write-back is needed on eviction. In M state the line has been modified and differs from memory, so it must be written back on eviction.
Are these protocols used with snooping or with directory-based coherence?

Either. MSI, MESI and MOESI define how line states are assigned, which is a separate matter from how other caches are notified (snooping, which monitors a shared bus or similar, or a directory scheme, which records the owners of each line).

spinlock-vs-mutex.title: Spinlock vs Mutex: Key Differences Explained
spinlock-vs-mutex.description: Spinlock vs mutex: waiting (busy-wait vs sleep), CPU use, suitable hold time, kernel use (interrupt context), priority inversion and implementation (futex).
spinlock-vs-mutex.lead: Spinlocks and mutexes are both locks that admit only one thread at a time into a critical section, but they differ in how they wait for the lock to become free. A spinlock waits by busy-waiting, repeatedly checking the lock variable in a loop, so it keeps using the CPU while waiting but can take the lock immediately once it is free. A mutex puts the waiting thread to sleep, giving up the CPU, and has the OS wake it when the lock is released. Use a spinlock when the hold time is very short or inside an interrupt handler that cannot sleep, and a mutex when the lock is held for a long time or the holder may sleep.
rows: How it waits
Repeatedly checks the variable in a loop until the lock is free (busy-waiting)
If the lock is not free, sleeps and is woken when it is released
CPU while waiting
Keeps using it
Gives it up. Other threads can use the CPU meanwhile
Waiting overhead
No context switch; takes the lock immediately once it is free
System calls and context switches add overhead when sleeping and waking
Suitable hold time
Very short (shorter than the time a context switch takes)
Long. When the holder may sleep, such as waiting for I/O while holding the lock
Sleeping while holding
Not allowed. Waiters would keep using the CPU
Allowed
On a single core
While a thread waits, the lock holder cannot run, so spinning never frees the lock. In the kernel it is used with preemption disabled
Works without problems
Use in the kernel
Usable even where sleeping is not allowed, such as interrupt handlers (interrupt context). When sharing data with an interrupt, disable interrupts before taking it
May sleep, so usable only in process context, not in interrupt handlers
Priority inversion
If the lock holder is preempted, waiters keep spinning. The kernel prevents this by disabling preemption while the lock is held
Can be addressed with priority-inheritance mutexes
Implementation examples
Atomic instructions (test-and-set or compare-and-swap) update the variable. Test-and-test-and-set waits with ordinary reads to reduce inter-core traffic
Linux futex locks with only user-space atomic instructions when uncontended and asks the kernel to put the thread to sleep only on contention. Some implementations spin briefly before sleeping
when: Spinlock
On multicore systems when the lock is held for a very short time (shorter than the context-switch overhead). Kernel code where sleeping is not allowed, such as interrupt handlers.
Mutex
When the lock is held for a long time, or the holder may sleep for I/O, memory allocation and the like. Ordinary mutual exclusion in user-space applications.
Combined

Many mutex implementations combine the strengths of both, taking the lock with atomic instructions alone without sleeping when uncontended, and spinning briefly before sleeping when it cannot be taken.
faq: Spinlocks waste CPU time, so why are they used?

Because if the lock is held for a very short time, spinning briefly is faster than paying the context-switch overhead of sleeping and waking. Also, in situations where sleeping is not allowed, such as kernel interrupt handlers, only spinlocks can be used.
Why can't a mutex be used in an interrupt handler?

A mutex puts the waiting thread to sleep when the lock cannot be taken, but an interrupt handler does not run as a particular thread, so it cannot sleep and be woken later. When sharing data with an interrupt handler, use a spinlock combined with disabling interrupts.
What is a futex?

A Linux mechanism for implementing mutexes and similar locks quickly. When there is no contention, it just updates the lock variable with atomic instructions in user space, and only when it must wait due to contention does it make a system call to have the kernel put it to sleep. When most locks are uncontended, it saves system call overhead.
What happens if you use a spinlock on a single-core system?

Even if a thread spins in user space, the lock-holding thread cannot run on that core, so the lock is not freed until the spinning thread uses up its time slice. That is why kernels on single-core systems disable preemption or interrupts for mutual exclusion instead of using spinlocks.

fp32-vs-fp16-vs-bf16-vs-int8.title: FP32 vs FP16 vs BF16 vs INT8: Key Differences Explained
fp32-vs-fp16-vs-bf16-vs-int8.description: FP32 vs FP16 vs BF16 vs INT8: bit layout (sign, exponent, mantissa), range, precision, FP32 conversion, memory, compute efficiency, training and inference.
fp32-vs-fp16-vs-bf16-vs-int8.lead: FP32 is the 32-bit single-precision floating-point format and is used as the reference for calculations. FP16 and BF16 are both 16 bits but allocate their bits differently. FP16 spends more bits on the mantissa for precision, so its range is narrow, with a maximum of 65504. BF16 keeps the exponent at 8 bits, the same as FP32, preserving an FP32-like range at the cost of precision. INT8 is an 8-bit integer used for quantization, which approximates real numbers by applying a scale, and it greatly reduces memory and power in AI inference.
rows: Bit width
32 bits
16 bits
16 bits
8 bits
Sign, exponent and mantissa bits
No exponent or mantissa. Two's complement integer from −128 to 127
Largest representable value
About 3.4 × 10³⁸
About 3.4 × 10³⁸ (almost the same as FP32)
127 (real values are represented with a scale)
Smallest normal number
About 1.2 × 10⁻³⁸
About 6.1 × 10⁻⁵ (2⁻¹⁴)
About 1.2 × 10⁻³⁸
None (the step between representable values is set by the scale)
Precision
About 7 decimal digits (the gap between 1 and the next number is 2⁻²³ ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻⁷)
About 3 decimal digits (2⁻¹⁰ ≈ 9.8 × 10⁻⁴)
2 to 3 decimal digits (2⁻⁷ ≈ 7.8 × 10⁻³)
256 levels
Conversion from FP32
None (the reference)
The range is narrow, so large values can overflow and small values can become 0
Just take the upper 16 bits and round; the range does not overflow
Quantize by choosing a scale (and zero point). Calibration to examine the value range is needed
Memory per value
4 bytes
2 bytes
2 bytes
1 byte
Arithmetic unit efficiency
Large multipliers; fewer multiply-accumulates fit in the same area
Arithmetic units are smaller than for FP32, so many more multiply-accumulates can be placed
About the same as FP16. The shorter mantissa makes the multiplier even smaller
Smallest multipliers and lowest power. Products are often accumulated as 32-bit integers
Use in training
Master weights, optimizer states, accumulation of products
Mixed-precision training. Loss scaling keeps small gradients from becoming 0
Widely used in mixed-precision training. Loss scaling is often unnecessary
Generally not used (quantization-aware training simulates the effects of quantization)
Use in inference
Accuracy reference. When accuracy takes priority over performance
Inference on GPUs and similar hardware
Inference on GPUs and AI accelerators
Inference of quantized models, especially on edge NPUs
when: FP32
Calculations that need precision, master weights and product accumulation in training, and as a reference for checking low-precision results.
FP16 and BF16
When you want to halve memory and compute in AI training and inference. BF16 for training where range matters; FP16 when values fit in its range and precision matters.
INT8
When you want to quantize a trained model for faster, lower-power inference. Inference on edge devices with limited memory and power.
faq: Why is BF16 often preferred over FP16 for AI training?

BF16 has an 8-bit exponent, the same as FP32, so its range is almost the same as FP32. FP16 needs loss scaling to keep small gradients from becoming 0 and large values from overflowing, but BF16 often does not, and conversion from FP32 is simple. Its precision is lower, but this is rarely a problem for neural network training.
Why is the maximum value of FP16 65504?

FP16 has a 5-bit exponent (bias 15), and the all-ones exponent is reserved for infinity and NaN, so the largest exponent is 2 to the 15th power. With all 10 mantissa bits set to 1, (2 − 2⁻¹⁰) × 2¹⁵ is the largest finite value, which equals 65504.
How does INT8 represent values with fractional parts?

It approximates them in the form real value ≈ scale × (integer − zero point). For quantization symmetric around 0, the zero point is 0 and the scale is set to something like “largest absolute value ÷ 127”. Scales are kept per tensor or per channel.
Can INT8 be used for training?

Training generally uses floating-point formats, because gradient values span a wide range and small updates to the weights must also be handled. INT8 is mainly used for inference with quantized trained models, and even quantization-aware training performs the weight updates in floating point.

training-vs-inference.title: AI Training vs Inference: Key Differences Explained
training-vs-inference.description: AI training vs inference: forward/backward passes, compute, memory (gradients, optimizer state), formats, batch size, latency and throughput, hardware, energy.
training-vs-inference.lead: Training is the process of determining a model's weights by repeating, a huge number of times, the steps of running data through the forward pass to compute the loss, computing gradients by backpropagation and updating the weights with an optimizer. Inference runs only the forward pass with fixed weights to produce answers for new inputs. Training stores gradients, optimizer states and activations for backpropagation in addition to the weights, so it needs far more memory and compute than inference with the same model. Each inference computation is small, but it runs every time the model is used, and response speed matters.
rows: Purpose
Determine the model's weights from data
Produce answers for new inputs with fixed weights
Computation
Repeat forward pass → loss calculation → gradient computation by backpropagation → weight update by the optimizer
Forward pass only
Compute estimate
About 3 times the forward pass per input (backpropagation is about 2 times the forward pass). For Transformers, about 6 × parameters × tokens in total
About 2N per token for a model with N parameters
Memory required
Weights, gradients, optimizer states (two for Adam) and activations for backpropagation. All in FP32, 16 bytes per parameter plus activations
Weights and activations during computation (plus the KV cache for large language models). 2 bytes per parameter in FP16
Number formats
Mixed precision with BF16 or FP16 (master weights in FP32)
FP16 or BF16, or formats quantized to INT8, INT4, etc.
Batch size
Large batches to raise arithmetic unit utilization
Small when responses are urgent (sometimes 1). Servers batch multiple requests to improve efficiency
Performance priority
Throughput (time to finish training, arithmetic unit utilization)
Balancing latency (response time per request) and throughput, and cost per task
Hardware
Many GPUs or accelerators with large-capacity HBM and high compute performance, connected by a high-speed network
A wide range, from data center GPUs and inference accelerators to smartphone NPUs and microcontrollers
Parallelism
Data, tensor and pipeline parallelism. Gradients are gathered with all-reduce
Multiple requests are processed in parallel. Large models are split across multiple chips with tensor parallelism and similar methods
Energy
A single training run operates many chips for a long period, using a large amount of power
Small per run, but it runs every time the model is used, so the total becomes large with heavy use
when: Training
When creating a new model, or when further training (fine-tuning) an existing model on your own data.
Inference
When using a trained model in a service or product. Image recognition, text generation, speech recognition, etc.
Techniques
For inference, models are made lighter with quantization, pruning and knowledge distillation. For training, mixed precision and gradient checkpointing save memory and compute.
faq: Why does training use far more memory than inference?

Because in addition to the weights, training holds the same number of gradients and the optimizer states (two for Adam), and also stores intermediate activations from the forward pass for backpropagation. For example, for a 7-billion-parameter model, holding all of these in FP32 takes about 112 GB excluding activations, whereas inference with only FP16 weights needs about 14 GB.
What happens if you increase the batch size in inference?

Weights loaded once can be used for computations on multiple inputs, so the arithmetic units are used more effectively and overall throughput rises. On the other hand, the time spent waiting for inputs to gather and the time per pass increase, so the response to each request (latency) becomes slower, and more memory is used.
Can the same hardware be used for training and inference?

Yes. GPUs are used for both training and inference. However, inference alone does not need backpropagation or large memory, so power-efficient hardware is also used, such as inference accelerators with many low-precision arithmetic units like INT8, and smartphone NPUs.
How much computation does training require?

For Transformer models, with N parameters and D training tokens, the total number of operations is commonly approximated as about 6ND. This is because the forward pass takes about 2N per token and the backward pass takes about twice that.

conductor-vs-semiconductor-vs-insulator.title: Conductor vs Semiconductor vs Insulator: Band Gap, Resistivity and Temperature Compared
conductor-vs-semiconductor-vs-insulator.description: Conductors (metals), semiconductors and insulators compared in one table: band structure, band gap, resistivity, carrier count, response to temperature and light, typical materials and roles in devices.
conductor-vs-semiconductor-vs-insulator.lead: What separates conductors, semiconductors and insulators is how many electrons are available to carry current, and band structure explains this. In a metal the conduction band is partly filled with electrons, so there are many free electrons from the start. An insulator has a large band gap, so at room temperature almost no electrons can rise into the conduction band. A semiconductor sits in between: its band gap is moderate, around 1 eV, so temperature, light and added impurities can change how easily it conducts by a large amount.

The conduction band is partly filled with electrons (or the valence and conduction bands overlap)
The valence band is full, with a moderate band gap to the conduction band
The valence band is full, with a large band gap to the conduction band
Typical band gap
None
Often around 1 eV (Si about 1.12 eV, Ge about 0.66 eV, GaAs about 1.42 eV). Wide-bandgap semiconductors such as SiC and GaN exceed 3 eV
Large (about 9 eV for SiO2)
Typical resistivity at room temperature
Very low (about 1.7×10⁻⁶ Ω·cm for copper)
In between, and varies by orders of magnitude with impurity content (on the order of 10⁵ Ω·cm for pure silicon)
Very high (10¹⁴ Ω·cm or more for SiO2 and similar materials)
Charge carriers
Free electrons: 10²² or more per cm³ (about 8.5×10²² for copper)
Two kinds: electrons in the conduction band and holes in the valence band. Their density can be changed greatly by adding impurities
Almost none
As temperature rises
Resistance increases (more scattering from lattice vibrations)
In a pure semiconductor, resistance drops sharply (thermally generated carriers increase rapidly)
Resistance stays very high, but falls slightly at high temperature
Adding impurities

Even tiny amounts change conductivity by orders of magnitude, making it possible to form n-type and p-type regions
Insulation must be preserved; impurities and defects cause leakage current
Under light
Almost no change
Light with energy above the band gap creates carriers and increases current (photoconductivity)
Almost no change under visible light (SiO2 is transparent to visible light)
Typical materials
Copper, aluminum, gold, tungsten
Silicon, germanium, GaAs, SiC, GaN
SiO2, silicon nitride (Si3N4), alumina (Al2O3), resins
Role in semiconductor devices
Interconnects, electrodes, contacts, bonding wires
The parts that control current, such as transistors and diodes
Gate dielectrics, interlayer dielectrics between wiring layers, device isolation, passivation
when: Conductor (metal)
When you want to carry electricity with little loss: on-chip wiring and electrodes, and the wires and leads of a package.
Semiconductor
When you want to switch current on and off, amplify it, or convert between light and electricity. Semiconductors form the core of transistors, diodes, image sensors and solar cells.
Insulator
When you need to separate places where current must not flow: MOSFET gate dielectrics, interlayer dielectrics filling the space between wires, and isolation between neighboring transistors.
faq: Why is it called a "semi"-conductor?

Because its resistivity lies between that of conductors (metals) and insulators. What really matters, though, is not the value itself but the fact that doping, temperature, light and electric fields can change how easily it conducts by a large amount. That property is what makes transistors and diodes work.
Why does resistance change in opposite directions with temperature in metals and semiconductors?

In a metal the number of free electrons is nearly fixed, so as temperature rises, more scattering from lattice vibrations raises the resistance. In a pure semiconductor, the number of carriers excited across the band gap grows exponentially with temperature, outweighing the extra scattering, so the resistance falls.
Above what band gap is a material an insulator?

There is no sharp boundary. Materials with a large band gap and almost no carriers at room temperature are usually called insulators, but materials that can be made to conduct by adding impurities, such as diamond at about 5.5 eV or Ga2O3 at about 4.5–4.9 eV, are treated as semiconductors (ultra-wide-bandgap semiconductors).
Is silicon a conductor or an insulator?

It is a semiconductor. Pure silicon has a fairly high resistivity at room temperature, on the order of 10⁵ Ω·cm, but adding a tiny amount of phosphorus or boron lowers it by orders of magnitude. For example, n-type silicon with an electron density of 1×10¹⁶ cm⁻³ is about 0.5 Ω·cm.

intrinsic-vs-extrinsic-semiconductor.title: Intrinsic vs Extrinsic Semiconductor: Carriers, Fermi Level and Temperature Compared
intrinsic-vs-extrinsic-semiconductor.description: Intrinsic (undoped) vs extrinsic (doped n-type and p-type) semiconductors compared in one table: carrier origin and density, Fermi level, resistivity, temperature behavior and uses.
intrinsic-vs-extrinsic-semiconductor.lead: An intrinsic semiconductor is a pure semiconductor with almost no impurities. It contains equal numbers of electrons, lifted by heat from the valence band into the conduction band, and the holes they leave behind. An extrinsic semiconductor has donors or acceptors deliberately added, so either electrons or holes become the majority carriers. The intrinsic carrier density of silicon at room temperature is only about 1×10¹⁰ cm⁻³, so real devices add impurities to set the carrier density and conductivity type.
rows: Impurities
None added on purpose (ideally perfectly pure)
Donors (phosphorus, arsenic, etc.) or acceptors (boron, etc.) are added
Origin of carriers
Only thermal generation of electron–hole pairs
Mainly ionization of impurities, plus a small amount of thermal pair generation
Electrons vs holes
Equal (n = p = ni)
One type dominates: n ≈ ND in n-type, p ≈ NA in p-type
Carrier density (silicon at room temperature)
About 1×10¹⁰ cm⁻³
Set mostly by the impurity concentration; can be many orders of magnitude above the intrinsic density
Product of electron and hole densities
n × p = ni²
Also n × p = ni² in thermal equilibrium. Minority carrier density is ni² / impurity concentration
Fermi level
Near the middle of the band gap (intrinsic Fermi level)
Shifts toward the conduction band in n-type and toward the valence band in p-type
Resistivity (silicon at room temperature)
High (on the order of 10⁵ Ω·cm)
Low; drops by orders of magnitude depending on impurity concentration
As temperature rises
Carriers increase exponentially and resistivity falls sharply

Carrier density is nearly constant over a middle temperature range that includes room temperature. At very low temperatures impurities stop ionizing and carriers decrease (freeze-out); at high temperatures thermally generated carriers take over and it behaves like an intrinsic semiconductor
How it is used
Rarely used in devices as is; it is the high-purity crystal that doping starts from
Nearly every device: transistors, diodes, wells, sources and drains
when: Intrinsic semiconductor

As a reference for understanding material properties. Through n × p = ni², the intrinsic carrier density ni sets the minority carrier density in doped semiconductors and the leakage current of PN junctions.
Extrinsic semiconductor
When building devices. The type and concentration of impurities set the conductivity type and resistivity, and n-type and p-type regions are combined to make PN junctions and transistors.
Caution at high temperature

As temperature rises, the intrinsic carrier density increases rapidly and the properties set by doping are gradually lost. SiC and GaN, with their wide band gaps, have very small intrinsic carrier densities, so they can operate at higher temperatures than silicon.
faq: Does current flow in an intrinsic semiconductor?

Yes. Even at room temperature, heat creates electron–hole pairs, so it conducts slightly. In silicon, however, the intrinsic carrier density of about 1×10¹⁰ cm⁻³ is tiny compared with the atomic density (about 5×10²² cm⁻³), so the resistivity is high.
Why is a doped semiconductor called "extrinsic"?

Because most of its carriers come not from the semiconductor itself but from impurities added from outside, in contrast to an intrinsic semiconductor, whose carriers are generated thermally in the pure crystal.
How much doping does it take to change the carrier density?

Silicon's intrinsic carrier density is about 1×10¹⁰ cm⁻³, so once donors or acceptors are added well above that level, the carrier density is set almost entirely by the impurity concentration. For example, phosphorus at 1×10¹⁶ cm⁻³ is only about 1 atom in 5 million silicon atoms, yet it makes the electron density 1 million times the intrinsic value.
What happens when you heat an extrinsic semiconductor?

In silicon, over a middle temperature range that includes room temperature, the carrier density stays nearly constant and roughly equal to the impurity concentration. If the temperature rises further and the intrinsic carrier density approaches the impurity concentration, thermally generated carriers increase, the material behaves like an intrinsic semiconductor, and PN junctions and similar structures stop working properly.

npn-vs-pnp.title: NPN vs PNP Transistor: Structure, Current Flow, Symbols and Uses Compared
npn-vs-pnp.description: NPN vs PNP bipolar transistors compared in one table: layer order, majority carriers, biasing, current direction, the arrow in the circuit symbol, how to wire them as switches, and performance.
npn-vs-pnp.lead: An NPN transistor has a p-type base sandwiched between an n-type emitter and collector; a PNP transistor is the reverse, with an n-type base between a p-type emitter and collector. In NPN, current is carried mainly by electrons; in PNP, by holes, and every voltage and current direction is reversed. In silicon, electrons have higher mobility than holes, so for the same dimensions an NPN is faster and more easily gets a high current gain, which is why NPN is used more often.
rows: Layer order (emitter, base, collector)
n-type, p-type, n-type
p-type, n-type, p-type
Main current carriers
Electrons (injected from the emitter into the base)
Holes (injected from the emitter into the base)
Bias in the active region
Base–emitter forward-biased (base about 0.6–0.7 V above the emitter), base–collector reverse-biased
Base–emitter forward-biased (base about 0.6–0.7 V below the emitter), base–collector reverse-biased
Terminal voltages (active region)
VC > VB > VE
VE > VB > VC
Current direction
Flows in at the base and collector, out at the emitter
Flows in at the emitter, out at the base and collector
Arrow in the circuit symbol
Points out of the emitter
Points into the emitter
As a switch
Low-side switch between the load and GND. Turns on when current is driven into the base
High-side switch between the supply and the load. Turns on when current is drawn out of the base
Performance (same dimensions)
Higher electron mobility makes it faster and makes a high current gain easier
Lower hole mobility tends to make it slower than NPN, with a somewhat lower current gain
Typical uses
Amplifiers, low-side switches, open-collector outputs, high-speed circuits such as ECL
High-side switches, push-pull output stages paired with NPN, current sources that push current from the supply side
when: NPN
The first choice when in doubt. Commonly used to switch LEDs or relays on the GND side from a microcontroller pin, and in general-purpose amplifiers.
PNP
When you want to switch a load on the supply side, or build a current source that pushes current out from the supply.
Together

A matched NPN and PNP pair (complementary pair) can form a push-pull amplifier in which each handles one half-cycle, positive or negative. Class B produces crossover distortion, so it is common to use class AB with a small bias current.
faq: How do you tell NPN and PNP apart in a circuit symbol?

By the direction of the arrow on the emitter. The arrow shows the direction of forward current through the base–emitter PN junction (from p-type to n-type): it points out of the emitter in NPN and into the emitter in PNP.
Why is NPN used more often?

In silicon, electron mobility is about 2–3 times hole mobility, so with the same structure an NPN more easily achieves higher current gain and speed. Also, in GND-referenced circuits, an NPN low-side switch is easy to build.
Can I replace an NPN with a PNP?

Not as a drop-in replacement. All voltage and current directions are reversed, so the circuit must be redesigned, including supply polarity and load position. If you flip the whole circuit upside down between the supply side and the GND side, it can perform the same function.
How do you turn on a PNP transistor?

Make the base about 0.6–0.7 V lower than the emitter and draw current out of the base. In a high-side switch with the emitter tied to the supply, pulling the base toward GND through a resistor turns it on, and bringing the base to the same voltage as the emitter turns it off.

front-end-vs-back-end-process.title: Front-End vs Back-End Semiconductor Process: Steps, Equipment and Companies Compared
front-end-vs-back-end-process.description: Front-end (building circuits on the wafer) vs back-end (dicing, packaging and testing chips) semiconductor manufacturing compared in one table: main steps, unit of work, dimensions, cycle time, equipment, testing and the companies involved.
front-end-vs-back-end-process.lead: Semiconductor manufacturing is broadly divided into the front end and the back end. The front end builds transistors and wiring on a silicon wafer by repeating steps such as deposition, lithography, etching and ion implantation. The back end cuts the finished wafer into individual chips, assembles them into packages that connect to the outside world, and tests them for shipment. With advanced packaging such as chiplets, the steps that sit between the two are becoming more important.
rows: Purpose
Build transistors and wiring on the wafer to complete the circuit
Cut out the chips, assemble them into packages, connect them to the outside, and turn them into shippable products
Main steps
Cleaning, oxidation, deposition (CVD, PVD), lithography, etching, ion implantation, annealing, CMP, interconnect formation
Backgrinding, dicing, die bonding, connection by wire bonding or flip chip, resin encapsulation (molding), marking, final test
Unit of work
Wafers (300 mm or 200 mm in diameter, etc.)
Chips (dies) and packages
Feature sizes
Nanometer (nm) scale
Mainly micrometer (µm) to millimeter (mm) scale
Number of steps and cycle time
The same kinds of steps are repeated for each layer. Leading-edge logic has more than a thousand steps, and the front end alone takes 3 months or more
Fewer steps and a shorter cycle time than the front end
Main equipment
Lithography scanners, etchers, deposition tools, ion implanters, CMP tools, cleaning tools
Dicers, die bonders, wire bonders, molding equipment, testers (ATE), handlers
Environment
Cleanrooms with very high cleanliness
Cleanrooms are used, but often do not need to be as clean as for the front end
Testing
In-line inspection and measurement of film thickness and dimensions during processing
Wafer test (sometimes counted as the last part of the front end), final test after packaging, and burn-in when needed
Companies involved
IDMs and foundries
IDMs and OSATs (outsourced back-end providers). More foundries are also offering advanced packaging
when: Front end
This is what determines a chip's performance, power consumption and density. It is the center of the race to scale down, and investment in equipment such as lithography tools is large.
Back end
This protects the chip, removes heat and connects it to the board. The package type and connection method affect product size, heat dissipation and signal speed.
Middle end

Steps that apply near-front-end techniques to packaging while still at the wafer stage, such as TSVs, fine redistribution layers and bump formation, are sometimes called the middle end. They are becoming important for chiplets and stacked memory.
faq: Where is the boundary between the front end and the back end?

Generally, everything up to finishing the circuit on the wafer is front end, and everything from cutting the wafer into chips and assembling packages onward is back end. Whether the per-chip electrical test (wafer test) belongs to one or the other differs between companies and sources.
Why does the front end take longer?

Because steps such as deposition, lithography and etching are repeated dozens of times, once for each transistor and wiring layer. Leading-edge logic chips go through more than a thousand steps, and it takes 3 months or more from wafer start to the end of the front end.
Why is the back end getting so much attention?

Because scaling alone can no longer keep raising performance, so methods that boost performance by placing or stacking multiple chips densely in one package, such as chiplets and 3D integration, are spreading. As with HBM, where memory is stacked right next to the processor, back-end technology increasingly decides product performance.
What is an OSAT?

OSAT stands for Outsourced Semiconductor Assembly and Test: companies that take on back-end assembly and testing under contract. They receive finished wafers from fabless companies and foundries, then package and test them.

idm-vs-fabless-vs-foundry.title: IDM vs Fabless vs Foundry: Semiconductor Business Models Compared
idm-vs-fabless-vs-foundry.description: The three semiconductor business models, IDM (integrated device manufacturer), fabless and foundry, compared in one table: steps handled, fab ownership, investment, strengths and weaknesses, and typical companies and products. Fab-lite and OSAT are explained too.
idm-vs-fabless-vs-foundry.lead: An IDM (integrated device manufacturer) handles everything from design to manufacturing and sales in-house. A fabless company owns no fabs; it focuses on design and sales and outsources manufacturing to a foundry. A foundry manufactures chips designed by other companies. As building leading-edge fabs and developing process technology have come to require enormous investment, the split between design and manufacturing has spread.
rows: Steps handled
All of design, front end, back end and sales (some back-end work may be outsourced)
Design and sales; manufacturing is outsourced
Front-end manufacturing (wafer fabrication), plus some back-end work such as advanced packaging
Own fabs
Yes
No
Yes (manufacturing is the core business)
What it sells
Its own branded semiconductor products
Its own branded semiconductor products
Manufacturing services; as a rule, no products under its own brand
Main investment
Both fabs and R&D
Designers, EDA tools, IP, and mask and prototyping costs; no fab investment
Fabs and process technology development; leading-edge fabs require enormous investment
Strengths
Can optimize design and manufacturing together, and makes proprietary processes and supply control easier
No fab fixed costs, resources concentrated on design, and free choice of the most advanced processes
Gathers orders from many customers to keep fabs highly utilized and recover enormous investments
Weaknesses
Fab fixed costs weigh heavily when demand falls, and keeping up investment in advanced processes is a big burden
Capacity and pricing depend on foundries, and supply is hard to secure when manufacturing is congested
Exposed to swings in customer demand, and must keep up the race in leading-edge development and capital spending
Typical companies
Intel, Samsung Electronics, Texas Instruments, Kioxia
NVIDIA, Qualcomm, AMD, Broadcom, MediaTek
TSMC, UMC, GlobalFoundries, SMIC
Common product areas
Memory (DRAM, NAND), analog, power semiconductors, microcontrollers, CPUs
GPUs, smartphone SoCs, communication ICs, FPGAs
Mainly logic chips designed by customers, plus a wide range of other chips
when: IDM
Common in fields where process technology itself differentiates the product. In memory, analog and power semiconductors, refining process and design together is a competitive advantage.
Fabless
Suits products that stand out through circuit design or software. Because no fab is needed, even new companies can make chips on leading-edge processes.
Foundry
Takes on manufacturing for many customers at once. Leading-edge fabs require enormous investment, so manufacturing of leading-edge logic has concentrated at foundries that can gather many orders.
In-between models and related companies

There is also a fab-lite model, which makes some products in its own fabs and outsources leading-edge products and others to foundries. OSATs handle the back end and IP vendors license circuit design assets, supporting the division of labor.
faq: What is the difference between fabless and foundry?

A fabless company designs and sells chips without owning fabs; a foundry manufactures chips designed by other companies. In this division of labor, the fabless company hands design data to the foundry, and the wafers the foundry makes are packaged into products by OSATs and others.
Why did the split between design and manufacturing spread?

Because building leading-edge fabs and developing process technology came to require enormous investment, making it hard for one company to stay at the cutting edge of both design and manufacturing. Foundries recover their investment by gathering orders from many customers, and fabless companies can focus on design without the burden of fabs.
What is fab-lite?

A model in which a company makes some products in its own fabs while outsourcing products that need leading-edge processes and others to foundries. It is often adopted by IDMs that want to limit fab investment, and sits between IDM and fabless.
Can one company combine several models?

Yes. Samsung Electronics is an IDM that makes its own memory and other products, and also runs a foundry business that manufactures chips for other companies. Intel has also started a foundry business, and outsources some of its own products to external foundries.

dram-vs-nand-flash.title: DRAM vs NAND Flash: Volatility, Speed, Capacity and Uses Compared
dram-vs-nand-flash.description: DRAM vs NAND flash memory compared in one table: storage mechanism, volatility, read/write unit and speed, endurance, density techniques, cost and uses. Shows the difference between main memory and storage.
dram-vs-nand-flash.lead: DRAM stores data as charge on a capacitor. It reads and writes quickly, but loses its data when power is turned off. NAND flash stores data by trapping electrons in a layer surrounded by insulating film, so data survives power-off and the cost per bit can be kept low, but reading and writing are far slower than DRAM and the number of rewrites is limited. That is why PCs and smartphones use DRAM as working main memory and NAND as storage such as SSDs.
rows: Storage mechanism
One transistor and one capacitor (1T1C). Stores data as the presence or absence of charge on the capacitor
A transistor with an adjustable threshold voltage. Stores data as the amount of electrons held in a floating gate or charge-trap layer
When power is off
Data is lost (volatile)
Data is retained (non-volatile)
Refresh
Required (typically all rows within 64 ms)
Not required, but charge slowly leaks away, so data retention time is limited
Read/write unit
Random access in fine-grained units (in practice, burst transfers of tens of bytes)
Reads and writes in pages (a few KB to a dozen or so KB); erases in even larger blocks
Overwriting
Data can be overwritten directly
Cannot be overwritten; a block must be erased before writing
Access time
Tens of nanoseconds
Reads take roughly tens of microseconds; writes take longer, roughly hundreds of microseconds
Endurance (rewrite cycles)
No practical limit
Limited (roughly 50,000–100,000 cycles for SLC, a few thousand for TLC, about 1,000 for QLC)
How capacity is increased
Scaling, and three-dimensional capacitors (deep, tall capacitor structures)
3D NAND that stacks cells vertically, and multi-level cells that store several bits per cell
Cost per bit
High
Far lower than DRAM
Typical uses
Main memory in PCs and servers, LPDDR in smartphones, GDDR and HBM for GPUs
SSDs, smartphone internal storage, USB flash drives, SD cards
when: DRAM
When the CPU or GPU needs to read and write working data quickly. Used as main memory to hold running programs and their data.
NAND flash
When you want to store large amounts of data cheaply and keep it without power. Used as storage for the OS, apps, photos and videos.
Together
Computers load data stored in NAND into DRAM before processing it. Some SSDs also include DRAM to temporarily hold management information.
faq: What is the biggest difference between DRAM and NAND?

Whether data survives when power is turned off. DRAM is volatile memory that loses its data without power; NAND is non-volatile memory that keeps it. DRAM is fast and NAND is large and cheap, so they are used for different roles.
Is this the same as the difference between "memory" and "storage" in a PC?
Broadly, yes. What a PC spec sheet calls "memory" is DRAM, and the SSD listed as "storage" is made of NAND flash.
Why does NAND have limited write endurance?

Each write and erase sends electrons through a thin insulating film, which gradually wears the film so it holds charge less well. SSD controllers extend lifetime with wear leveling, which spreads writes across the whole device, and with error correction.
Do the same companies make DRAM and NAND?
Some companies make both. Samsung Electronics, SK hynix and Micron Technology manufacture both DRAM and NAND. Kioxia focuses mainly on NAND.

led-vs-laser-diode.title: LED vs Laser Diode: Light Emission, Beam Properties and Uses Compared
led-vs-laser-diode.description: LEDs (light-emitting diodes) vs semiconductor lasers (laser diodes) compared in one table: emission mechanism, optical cavity, spectral width, beam spread, current vs light output, modulation speed and uses.
led-vs-laser-diode.lead: LEDs and semiconductor lasers both pass forward current through a PN junction and emit light when electrons and holes recombine. An LED's light comes from spontaneous emission, so it has a wide range of wavelengths and spreads in many directions. A semiconductor laser has a cavity that bounces light back and forth and amplifies it by stimulated emission, producing an intense, straight beam with matched wavelength and phase. LEDs are used for lighting and displays; lasers for optical communication, optical discs and sensing.
rows: Emission mechanism
Spontaneous emission: electrons and holes recombine at random times and emit light
Stimulated emission: light generates more light of the same wavelength, phase and direction, and is amplified
Optical cavity
None
Yes. Light bounces between cleaved facets (edge-emitting) or multilayer mirrors (VCSEL)
Wavelength range (spectral width)
Wide (around tens of nm)
Narrow (can be 1 nm or less; DFB lasers emit at a single wavelength)
Beam spread
Spreads over a wide angle
Narrow; can be focused tightly or sent over long distances
Phase alignment (coherence)
Low
High
Current vs light output
Lights up as soon as current flows, with brightness roughly proportional to current
Lasing starts above the threshold current and light output rises sharply; below threshold there is only weak spontaneous emission
Modulation speed
Relatively slow
Fast; some lasers for optical communication are directly modulated by current to send signals at tens of Gb/s
Effect of temperature
Emission efficiency drops as temperature rises
Threshold current rises and wavelength shifts as temperature rises, so temperature control is sometimes used
Ease of use
Simple drive circuit and long lifetime
Often needs control to keep light output constant. Intense light is hazardous to the eyes, so laser safety standards (classes) apply
Typical uses
Lighting, display backlights, indicator lights, remote controls
Fiber-optic communication, optical discs, laser printers, LiDAR, face-recognition sensors, laser machining
when: LED
When you want to light a wide area or use it as an indicator. It is cheap, long-lived and simple to drive.
Laser diode

When you want to focus light tightly and send it far, modulate it quickly to carry information, or need light with matched wavelength. Used for optical communication, distance measurement and machining.
What they share

In both, the color (wavelength) of the light is set mainly by the band gap of the semiconductor in the emitting layer. Direct-bandgap compound semiconductors with high emission efficiency, such as GaN-based, GaAs-based and InP-based materials, are used; silicon, an indirect-bandgap material, is not suited to light emitters.
faq: How is laser light different from LED light?

Laser light has matched wavelength and phase and travels straight with little spread, while LED light covers a wide range of wavelengths and spreads in many directions. This is because an LED emits by spontaneous emission, while a laser emits by stimulated emission inside a cavity.
What is the threshold current of a laser diode?

It is the current at which lasing begins. Lasing starts when amplification of light by stimulated emission in the cavity exceeds the losses; above that current, light output rises sharply with current. Below threshold, only weak, LED-like spontaneous emission comes out.
What determines the color of an LED?

Mainly the band gap of the semiconductor in the emitting layer, following the relation wavelength λ(nm) ≈ 1240 / Eg(eV). InGaN is used for blue and green, and AlGaInP and similar materials for red. Most white LEDs convert part of the light from a blue LED to yellow and other colors with a phosphor and mix them.
Why is it hard to make LEDs or lasers from silicon?

Silicon is an indirect-bandgap semiconductor, so for an electron and hole to recombine and emit light, a phonon (lattice vibration) must also be involved, making emission efficiency very low. Silicon photonics therefore combines silicon with lasers made of compound semiconductors such as InP.

si-vs-sic-power-device.title: Si vs SiC Power Semiconductors: Properties, Voltage, Losses and Uses Compared
si-vs-sic-power-device.description: Silicon (Si) vs silicon carbide (SiC) power semiconductors compared in one table: band gap, breakdown field, thermal conductivity, device types, voltage rating, switching loss, wafers and cost, challenges and uses.
si-vs-sic-power-device.lead: SiC is a wide-bandgap semiconductor with about 3 times the band gap and about 10 times the breakdown field of silicon. For the same voltage rating, its drift layer can be thinner and more heavily doped, which greatly lowers on-resistance and makes fast devices such as MOSFETs and Schottky barrier diodes usable even at high voltages. Silicon, on the other hand, offers cheap, large-diameter wafers and mature manufacturing, so it remains the mainstay for many applications.
rows: Band gap
About 1.12 eV
About 3.26 eV (4H-SiC)
Breakdown field
About 0.3 MV/cm
About 3 MV/cm (about 10 times silicon)
Thermal conductivity
About 1.5 W/(cm·K)
High (about 3 times silicon)
Intrinsic carrier density at room temperature
About 1×10¹⁰ cm⁻³
Extremely small (on the order of 10⁻⁹ cm⁻³); properties set by doping are easier to maintain even at high temperature
Main devices at high voltage
IGBTs; power MOSFETs and superjunction MOSFETs at lower voltages
MOSFETs and Schottky barrier diodes; unipolar devices that do not use minority carriers work even at high voltage
Switching loss
IGBT tail current at turn-off adds loss and makes higher frequencies difficult
No tail current and almost no diode reverse recovery, so losses are small and it can run at high frequency
Typical voltage ratings
A wide range from tens of volts to several kV (IGBTs for high voltage)
Mainly about 650 V to 3.3 kV
High-temperature operation
Junction temperature generally up to about 150–175 °C
The material itself withstands high temperatures; in practice the limit is often set by the reliability of the package, bonding materials and gate oxide
Wafers and cost
Large-diameter wafers up to 300 mm are cheap and available, and manufacturing is mature
Mainly 150 mm, with a shift to 200 mm under way. Crystal growth is difficult, so both wafers and chips are expensive
Main challenges
Approaching the material's physical limits at high voltage and high frequency
Quality and reliability of the gate oxide interface, body diode degradation from crystal defects, and noise from fast switching
Typical uses
Power supplies for home appliances and PCs, industrial inverters, many automotive power circuits
Electric-vehicle traction inverters, on-board chargers, fast chargers, solar inverters, railways
when: Si (silicon)

When cost comes first. Used in power supplies of a few hundred volts or less and in high-current inverters whose switching frequency is not especially high. Its track record and large supply are also strengths.
SiC (silicon carbide)
When you want to cut losses at high voltage or make equipment smaller and lighter. In electric vehicles, higher inverter efficiency extends driving range on the same battery.
Choosing between them

SiC devices are expensive, so adoption is spreading first in applications where system-level benefits, such as lower losses and smaller cooling and passive components, outweigh the higher device cost. For applications up to a few hundred volts that need especially fast switching, GaN is also an option.
faq: Why is SiC better suited than silicon to high voltages?

Because its breakdown field is about 10 times that of silicon. The drift layer needed for a given voltage can be about one-tenth as thick, and its doping about 100 times higher, which greatly lowers on-resistance.
Will SiC MOSFETs replace silicon IGBTs?

Replacement is under way in applications where efficiency matters, such as electric-vehicle inverters. However, SiC devices are expensive, so silicon IGBTs remain widely used in cost-sensitive applications and high-current industrial applications.
What are the disadvantages of SiC?

Expensive wafers and chips, many crystal defects that make high yields hard to reach, and a low-quality gate oxide interface that lowers channel mobility. And while it can switch fast, measures against noise and surges from rapid voltage changes are also needed.
How do you choose between SiC and GaN?

SiC is used in vertical devices that excel at high voltage and high current, making it suited to electric-vehicle inverters and industrial uses. GaN centers on lateral HEMTs that switch very fast at voltages up to about 650 V, and is used in compact chargers and data-center power supplies.

htol-vs-thb-vs-hast-vs-tc-vs-hts.title: HTOL vs THB vs HAST vs Temperature Cycling vs HTS: Conditions, Purpose and Failure Modes Compared
htol-vs-thb-vs-hast-vs-tc-vs-hts.description: HTOL, THB, HAST, temperature cycling and high-temperature storage compared: purpose, stresses, bias, typical conditions, duration, failure mechanisms, acceleration models and standards.
htol-vs-thb-vs-hast-vs-tc-vs-hts.lead: Most semiconductor reliability tests are accelerated tests: they apply stresses such as temperature, voltage, humidity and temperature changes more strongly than in actual use to speed up failures, checking lifetime and failure rate in a short time. HTOL operates devices at high temperature under voltage and evaluates degradation of the chip itself, such as TDDB and electromigration. The temperature-humidity-bias test (THB) and HAST are moisture-resistance tests that use humidity and voltage to accelerate moisture-driven failures such as corrosion; HAST uses pressurized steam to perform a similar evaluation in less time. Temperature cycling repeats high and low temperatures to evaluate fatigue caused by differences in thermal expansion between materials, and the high-temperature storage test evaluates degradation driven by temperature alone, without voltage. Because each targets different failures, product qualification combines them.
rows: Purpose
Check chip lifetime and failure rate
Check package moisture resistance
Check moisture resistance in a short time
Check the resistance of joints and packages to thermal fatigue
Check resistance to degradation driven by temperature alone
Stresses applied
High temperature and voltage
Temperature, humidity and voltage
Temperature above 100 °C, humidity, pressure and voltage
Temperature changes (repeated high and low temperatures)
High temperature only
Bias applied?
Yes. Devices are operated with signals at or slightly above the maximum operating voltage
Yes. Applied so that power dissipation stays small, to limit self-heating
Usually yes. Unbiased HAST, without bias, also exists
Generally no
No
Typical conditions
Around 125 °C. Higher for some temperature grades
85 °C/85% RH at atmospheric pressure (the 85/85 test)
Pressurized steam at about 110 to 130 °C and 85% RH, e.g. 130 °C/85% RH
e.g. −55 to 125 °C or −65 to 150 °C, holding for a set time at each extreme
e.g. 150 °C. Higher for some products
Typical duration
About 1,000 hours, with interim measurements at e.g. 168 and 500 hours
About 1,000 hours
About 96 hours at 130 °C/85% RH
Hundreds to thousands of cycles
About 1,000 hours. Sometimes shortened at higher temperature
Main mechanisms accelerated
Degradation and latent defects of the chip itself, such as TDDB, BTI and electromigration
Electrochemical reactions driven by moisture ingress (corrosion, ion migration)
Same as THB, accelerated more strongly by faster moisture ingress
Fatigue from repeated strain due to differences in thermal expansion coefficients
Degradation driven by temperature alone (intermetallic growth, thermal degradation of materials, loss of stored charge)
Typical defects found
Electrical parameters out of spec (e.g. threshold voltage shift), functional failures
Corrosion of aluminum pads and interconnects, increased leakage current, shorts between conductors
Same as THB: corrosion, increased leakage current, shorts
Cracks in solder joints and wire bonds, mold compound delamination, die and passivation cracks
Increased resistance or lifting of wire bonds (Kirkendall voids), data retention failures in nonvolatile memory
Acceleration model
Arrhenius model (temperature) and a voltage acceleration model
Peck's model (a power of relative humidity times an Arrhenius temperature term)
Peck's model (same as THB)
Coffin-Manson relationship (a power of the temperature swing)
Arrhenius model
Sample condition
Packaged parts mounted on boards and operated under voltage
Packaged parts. In qualification, often run after preconditioning that applies moisture soak and reflow heat
Packaged parts. Like THB, often run after preconditioning
Individual components (often after preconditioning); board-level tests with parts mounted also exist
Packaged parts placed in a hot chamber. No electrical connection is needed
Role (example standards)
Qualification test for lifetime and failure rate. JEDEC (JESD22 series), AEC-Q100 and others
Qualification test for moisture resistance. JEDEC (JESD22 series), AEC-Q100 and others
Sometimes used in place of THB. JEDEC (JESD22 series), AEC-Q100 and others
Qualification test for packages and joints. JEDEC (JESD22 series), AEC-Q100 and others
Qualification test for temperature-only degradation. JEDEC (JESD22 series), AEC-Q100 and others
Cautions
Control temperature so self-heating does not push the junction temperature too high
If the chip heats up, relative humidity at its surface drops and humidity-driven failures become less likely
The high temperature can cause failures that never occur in actual use, such as changes in mold compound properties
A different test from thermal shock (faster temperature changes) and power cycling (self-heating)
Without voltage, it cannot evaluate degradation driven by electric field or current, such as TDDB and electromigration
when: HTOL

When you want to confirm, for a new product or a process change, that the chip design and process meet the target lifetime and failure rate. Results are converted to use conditions with the Arrhenius model and similar models, but they change greatly with the assumed activation energy, so treat them as estimates.
Temperature-humidity-bias (THB)

When you want to confirm the moisture resistance of plastic-encapsulated packages at a temperature closer to real environments. It takes about 1,000 hours, but avoids failures peculiar to high temperatures such as those of HAST.
HAST
