When you want to finish moisture-resistance evaluation in a short period. For example, a test of about 96 hours at 130 °C/85% RH is used in place of 1,000 hours of THB at 85 °C/85% RH. Which one to use is decided by the applicable standard or agreement with the customer.
Temperature cycling

When strain from differences in thermal expansion is a concern, at solder joints, wire bonds or the interface between mold compound and die. It is important for applications with large temperature changes, such as automotive, and for products whose large dies or packages experience large strain.
High-temperature storage (HTS)
When you want to check degradation driven by temperature alone, such as intermetallic growth at wire-bond joints or data retention in nonvolatile memory, separately from the effects of voltage.
Combining them in qualification

Because different stresses act on different kinds of failure, product qualification combines these tests, generally running them in parallel on separate samples for each test. Before humidity tests (THB, HAST) and temperature cycling, preconditioning is often applied, soaking the parts in moisture and then applying the same heat as reflow, so they are evaluated in the state they would be in after mounting. For every test, electrical characteristics are measured during and after the test to judge pass or fail.
faq: What is the difference between THB and HAST?

Both apply voltage at about 85% relative humidity and evaluate corrosion and increased leakage current caused by moisture. THB takes about 1,000 hours at 85 °C and atmospheric pressure, while HAST speeds up moisture ingress with pressurized steam at about 110 to 130 °C, performing an equivalent evaluation in about 96 hours at 130 °C/85% RH, for example. HAST is faster, but because of its high temperature it can cause failures that never occur in actual use.
What is the difference between HTOL and burn-in?

Burn-in is a screen that applies short high-temperature, high-voltage stress to all or most of the products to be shipped, removing units prone to early failure. HTOL is a qualification test that operates sampled units for about 1,000 hours to confirm that the product design and manufacturing process meet the target lifetime and failure rate; tested units are not shipped.
What is the difference between the high-temperature storage test and HTOL?

The high-temperature storage test simply holds products at high temperature, for example 150 °C, without voltage, evaluating degradation driven by temperature alone, such as wire-bond joint degradation and data retention in nonvolatile memory. HTOL operates devices under voltage at around 125 °C, so it also accelerates degradation driven by electric field or current, such as TDDB and electromigration.

secure-boot-vs-measured-boot.title: Secure Boot vs Measured Boot: Signature Checks, TPM Measurements and Attestation Compared
secure-boot-vs-measured-boot.description: Secure boot vs measured boot compared in one table: what each checks, whether it blocks or records, root of trust, behavior on tampering, what it needs, how the results are used, limits and how they are combined.
secure-boot-vs-measured-boot.lead: Both mechanisms check the next piece of software at each boot stage, from power-on until the OS is running. Secure boot verifies the digital signature of the next stage and stops the boot if it is not properly signed. Measured boot computes a hash of the next stage and records it cumulatively in the TPM's PCRs (Platform Configuration Registers), without stopping anything. Secure boot prevents; measured boot records so the state can be checked and proven later. They are not alternatives and are often used together.
rows: What it checks
The digital signature of the next software: whether the vendor's signature over the image hash verifies with a trusted key
The hash (measurement) of the next software: the value of what was actually loaded is recorded as is
When something is wrong
Stops the boot on the spot if verification fails (enforcement)
Lets the boot continue and only leaves a record (recording)
Root of trust
Immutable ROM boot code and the public key used for verification (often stored as its hash in eFuses to save space)
A small trusted piece of code that runs first and starts measuring, plus the TPM that holds the record
If software has been tampered with
The signature does not match, so it never runs; a modified bootloader or kernel cannot start
It boots anyway, but the PCR values differ from the expected ones, so checking the record reveals it later
What it needs
A verification public key on the device and a signing private key kept securely by the vendor; combined with anti-rollback so old versions cannot be reinstalled
TPM PCRs (which can only be extended, folding in a new measurement through a hash) and a record of each stage's measurements (the event log)
How the result is used
Prevents unauthorized software from starting on that device. To show others what booted, it is combined with measured boot or similar
Remote attestation (PCR values signed with a TPM key and presented to a server) and sealing (releasing secrets such as a disk-encryption key only when the PCRs hold the expected values)
Limits
It only tells whether code is signed by a trusted key, so it cannot tell an old but validly signed vulnerable version or a configuration change apart; it protects only the boot path
It cannot stop malicious code from running, and the record means something only when someone checks it; expected PCR values change with every software update and must be managed
Typical use
Smartphones, PCs and many embedded devices; shipped products also lock debug ports such as JTAG
PCs with a TPM, for disk encryption and device-health checks before network access; TPM-less microcontrollers use schemes such as DICE that derive keys from measurements for the same purpose
when: Secure boot
When unauthorized software must never run on the device at all. It works on its own, even on devices that cannot reach a verifying server.
Measured boot

When you need to prove to a server what booted, or to release a disk-encryption key only when the boot state is correct. An old but validly signed version can also be spotted by comparing the record with expected values.
Together
Secure boot blocks unauthorized boots, and measured boot records the boot state so it can be proven. Both can run on the same device at the same time.
faq: What is the main difference between secure boot and measured boot?

Whether the boot stops when a check fails. Secure boot refuses to start software whose signature is not valid. Measured boot lets the boot continue and records the hash of each piece of software in the TPM in a tamper-evident way, so it can be checked later or proven to a remote server.
Does measured boot need a TPM?

It usually records into TPM PCRs. A TPM can be a discrete chip or firmware running inside the CPU or SoC (fTPM). Microcontrollers without a TPM can achieve a similar goal with schemes such as DICE that derive keys from measurements.
If I have secure boot, do I still need measured boot?

They do different jobs, so using both makes sense. Secure boot only checks whether code is signed by a trusted key, so it cannot distinguish an old but validly signed vulnerable version or a configuration change, and it cannot show anyone else what booted. Measured boot keeps the values of what actually started, which enables remote attestation and sealing.

write-allocate-vs-no-write-allocate.title: Write-Allocate vs No-Write-Allocate: Write-Miss Behavior, Traffic and Pairing Compared
write-allocate-vs-no-write-allocate.description: Write-allocate vs no-write-allocate cache policies compared in one table: what happens on a write miss, line fill, pairing with write-back or write-through, traffic, write-only data, later reads, implementation techniques and where each is used.
write-allocate-vs-no-write-allocate.lead: Write-allocate and no-write-allocate are policies that decide whether a line is brought into the cache when a write misses. With write-allocate, the cache first reads the line from the level below and then performs the write in the cache. With no-write-allocate, the line is not fetched and the write is sent straight to the level below. This is a separate choice from write-back vs write-through, which decide when a write that hits reaches the level below, but write-allocate is usually paired with write-back and no-write-allocate with write-through.
rows: On a write miss
Reads the whole line from the level below, places it in the cache, then writes into it
Leaves the cache untouched and sends the write directly to the level below
Line fill (read)
Required. On multicore systems it is a read for ownership (RFO) that invalidates other cores' copies before the write, so a store miss looks like a read on the memory bus
Not needed; only the written data is sent to the level below
Usual pairing
Write-back: later writes to the fetched line hit and are absorbed without memory traffic, which pays back the cost of the initial read
Write-through: every write goes to the level below anyway, so fetching the line would not reduce write traffic
Traffic to the level below
Lower when the same line is written many times or the written data is read back
Each missing write goes out every time, but no extra reads are generated
Large write-only data (clearing memory, writing output)
Each line is read only to be overwritten and later written back, roughly doubling traffic, and useful data is evicted from the cache
No reads and no cache pollution, so it suits this kind of data
Reading right after writing
The line is in the cache, so the read hits
The line is not in the cache, so the read misses and fetches it
Implementation techniques

For write-only data, non-temporal (streaming) stores bypass the cache and send combined writes straight to main memory; some ISAs also have an instruction that zeroes a whole line without reading its old contents
A write buffer hides write latency, and it often merges several writes to the same line into one transfer
Where it is used
Common in write-back caches; most CPU L1 to L3 caches are write-back
Common in write-through caches, such as a small L1 backed by a write-back L2, or simple embedded processors
when: Write-allocate
When written data will soon be read or written again, such as a loop updating array elements: writes with temporal locality.
No-write-allocate
When writing a large amount of data that will not be read back for a while. It avoids useless reads and keeps the cache free for useful data.
In software
Even with a write-allocate cache, non-temporal stores avoid the line reads for large write-only buffers. The written data does not stay in the cache, though, so reading it back immediately is slower.
faq: What is the difference between write-allocate and no-write-allocate?
On a write miss, write-allocate loads the line into the cache and then writes it in the cache. No-write-allocate does not load the line and writes directly to the level below.
Does write-through always use no-write-allocate?

Not always. How a write hit is propagated (write-back or write-through) and whether a line is fetched on a miss are separate choices. In practice, though, write-through is usually paired with no-write-allocate and write-back with write-allocate. In a write-through cache, a store that hits updates the cached copy and is also written to the level below; a store that misses is normally sent straight down without fetching the line.
Why is write-allocate slow for write-only data?

Because each line that will only be overwritten is first read from main memory. The read plus the later write-back roughly doubles the traffic and also evicts other data that would be reused. Non-temporal stores avoid this read.

epitaxy-vs-cvd.title: Epitaxy vs CVD: Crystal Quality, Substrate, Temperature and Uses Compared
epitaxy-vs-cvd.description: Epitaxial growth vs ordinary CVD deposition compared in one table: resulting crystal, substrate requirements, pre-growth surface preparation, temperature, typical films, doping control, uses, quality concerns and equipment. Also explains why most epitaxy is itself done by CVD.
epitaxy-vs-cvd.lead: Epitaxial growth grows a single-crystal film on a single-crystal substrate with the same crystal orientation as the substrate. Most silicon epitaxy is done by CVD (chemical vapor deposition), so the two are not opposites: epitaxy can be seen as CVD that continues the substrate's crystal and grows single crystal (there are also non-CVD methods such as MBE). This table compares epitaxial growth of single crystal with ordinary CVD that deposits non-single-crystal films such as polysilicon, amorphous silicon, oxide and nitride.
rows: Resulting crystal
Single crystal that continues the arrangement and orientation of the underlying crystal
Polycrystalline (polysilicon) or amorphous; silicon oxide and nitride films are amorphous too
Substrate requirement
Needs a clean single-crystal surface to copy. In heteroepitaxy of a different material, mismatch in lattice constant and thermal expansion becomes an issue
Need not be single crystal: films deposit on oxide, metal, patterned topography or any surface the gas can reach
Surface preparation before growth

Strict. Native oxide about 1 nm thick or carbon left on the surface seeds defects such as stacking faults. For silicon, an HF clean is usually followed by a hydrogen bake at about 1,100 °C that removes the oxide
No crystal has to connect to the underlying layer, so oxide removal is generally not as strict as for epitaxy
Temperature tendency
For silicon it depends on the precursor: about 1,100–1,150 °C with trichlorosilane, about 1,000–1,100 °C with dichlorosilane, and roughly 600–900 °C with silane. SiC uses about 1,500–1,650 °C
Wide range by method: LPCVD about 600–800 °C, plasma CVD about 300–400 °C. Silicon from silane is amorphous below about 580 °C and polycrystalline above it
Typical films
Silicon epitaxial layers, SiGe, SiC, and compound-semiconductor layers such as GaN and GaAs
Polysilicon, amorphous silicon, silicon oxide (from TEOS and others), silicon nitride, tungsten
Doping control
In-situ doping with phosphine or diborane during growth lets each layer have its own concentration and gives abrupt depth profiles. Autodoping from heavily doped substrates must be controlled
Polysilicon can be made conductive by in-situ doping; for insulating films, doping is not the main purpose
Main uses

Lightly doped drift layers in power devices, epitaxial wafers for CMOS (such as p/p+), substrates for CMOS image sensors, raised transistor source/drain, SiGe HBT bases, multilayer structures in LEDs and lasers
Interlayer dielectrics, STI fill, spacers, hard masks, polysilicon gates and resistors, tungsten plugs
What quality means
Crystal defects such as stacking faults and dislocations, epi thickness and resistivity (doping). In heteroepitaxy, exceeding the critical thickness introduces misfit dislocations
Thickness uniformity, step coverage, film density and impurities such as hydrogen, film stress
Equipment
For silicon on 300 mm wafers, lamp-heated single-wafer reactors are mainstream. Compound semiconductors widely use MOCVD, and MBE is also used, for example in research
LPCVD that processes many wafers at once in a vertical furnace, plasma CVD, HDP-CVD for gap fill and others
when: Epitaxial growth
When you need a layer that does the device's electrical work, with few defects and doping chosen independently of the substrate, such as a power-device drift layer or SiGe source/drain.
CVD (ordinary deposition)
When you need insulators, electrodes, masks or fill films that do not have to be single crystal, while covering topography.
Same gas, different result

The same silicon precursor gives single crystal on clean single-crystal silicon but polysilicon or similar on oxide. Selective epitaxy strengthens this difference with chlorine-containing precursors or HCl so that single crystal grows only where silicon is exposed.
faq: Is epitaxial growth a type of CVD?

Most silicon epitaxy is done by CVD, so it can be seen as a way of using CVD to grow single crystal. Strictly, though, epitaxy names the result, growing single crystal that continues the underlying crystal, and the method is not limited to CVD. MOCVD, widely used for compound semiconductors, is epitaxy by CVD, while MBE (molecular beam epitaxy) supplies source materials as molecular beams in ultra-high vacuum and is not CVD.
Why is a hydrogen bake done before epitaxy?

Because native oxide (about 1 nm) or contamination such as carbon left on the surface prevents proper single-crystal growth and causes defects such as stacking faults. Heating in hydrogen to about 1,100 °C makes the oxide evaporate as SiO and exposes a clean crystal surface. Advanced processes that must limit the thermal budget combine it with wet cleaning or plasma treatment and run it at lower temperatures.
What is the difference between an epitaxial silicon layer and polysilicon?

An epitaxial layer is single crystal connected to the substrate, with few crystal defects, so it can serve as a layer that does the device's electrical work, such as a drift layer or source/drain. Polysilicon is a collection of small grains that can be deposited anywhere, including on oxide, and is used for gate electrodes, resistors and similar parts.

tpm-vs-hsm-vs-secure-element.title: TPM vs HSM vs Secure Element: Location, Purpose, Key Protection and Certification Compared
tpm-vs-hsm-vs-secure-element.description: TPM vs HSM vs secure element compared in one table: where each lives, main purpose, typical users, key protection, crypto performance, tamper resistance and certification (FIPS 140-3, Common Criteria), attestation, cost and typical uses.
tpm-vs-hsm-vs-secure-element.lead: All three are dedicated hardware that generates and stores cryptographic keys and performs signing or decryption inside, without letting private keys out. They differ in what they protect and where they sit. A TPM sits in each PC or server, records and proves that machine's boot state, and protects keys bound to that machine. An HSM is a dedicated appliance that holds an organization's most important keys in one place; it sits at the heart of certificate authorities, payment systems and cloud key management services and handles large volumes of signing and decryption. A secure element is a small tamper-resistant chip in smart cards and phones that protects payment and identity credentials inside devices people carry around.
rows: Location and form
A discrete chip on the motherboard of a PC or server; it can also be firmware inside the CPU or SoC (fTPM)
A PCIe card or a network-attached appliance; also offered as a cloud service
A small chip in smart cards, SIM cards, or on the board of a smartphone or IoT device; it can also be integrated into an SoC
Main purpose
Record and prove the boot state of that machine, and protect keys bound to it
Protect an organization's important keys in one place and serve signing and decryption requests from many systems
Protect payment, identity and mobile-subscriber credentials inside devices people carry
Typical devices and users
PCs and servers
Certificate authorities, banks and payment providers, key management services (KMS) in data centers and clouds
Smart cards such as credit cards and employee badges, SIMs, smartphones, IoT devices
How keys are protected
Keys are generated inside the TPM and the private part never leaves in plaintext; sealing can bind a key to PCR values so it is released only when the boot state is correct
Keys are generated and stored inside the device; applications ask it to "sign with this key" and receive only the result; user roles and an audit trail are managed
Keys and credentials are stored on the chip, and applications (applets) on the chip perform authentication and signing
Crypto performance
Low; bulk data is encrypted by the CPU using a key released by the TPM
High; built to process many signing and key operations continuously
Low; suited to authenticating or signing short pieces of data
Tamper resistance and certification
A discrete chip is tamper-resistant; an fTPM relies on the main processor's protection. Depending on the product, certified under Common Criteria or FIPS 140
Erases its keys when it detects an attempt to open it; many products are certified against standards such as FIPS 140-3
Smart-card-grade tamper resistance, with countermeasures against side-channel and fault injection attacks also evaluated; many are evaluated under Common Criteria (ISO/IEC 15408)
Attestation
A core function: PCR values are signed with a key that cannot leave the TPM (a quote) for remote attestation
Not a core function; some products can prove that a key was generated inside and cannot be exported
Used to show that a key was generated on the chip and that the chip is genuine
Cost and size
Inexpensive; one component of a PC, and an fTPM needs no extra part
The most expensive and largest; services that must not stop use several units for redundancy
The smallest; fits into cards and small devices, and is cheap per unit because it is mass-produced
Typical uses
Sealing disk-encryption keys, measured boot, device-health checks before network access
CA signing keys, payment keys, top-level KMS keys, code-signing keys for software
Contactless payment, SIM and eSIM subscriber authentication, e-passports and ID cards, IoT device authentication
when: TPM
On PCs and servers, when you want to protect keys tied to the boot state (disk encryption, for example) or prove to a server that the machine booted the right software.
HSM

When an organization's most important keys, such as CA signing keys or payment keys, must be guarded in one place while many systems use them. Also used when regulations or audits require keys to be handled in a certified device.
Secure element
In cards, phones and IoT devices that may fall into an attacker's hands, when payment or identity credentials and per-device keys must be protected against physical attacks.
Together
Systems commonly use them side by side: a server proves its boot state with a TPM, the service's critical keys live in an HSM, and the user's smartphone keeps payment keys in a secure element.
faq: What is the difference between a TPM and an HSM?

A TPM sits in a single machine, records and proves its boot state and protects keys bound to it, and is relatively slow. An HSM is a dedicated appliance that holds an organization's important keys and handles signing and decryption requests from many systems with high performance. Both follow the idea of processing keys inside without letting them out; they differ in scale and role.
Are a secure element and a TEE the same thing?

No. A secure element is a separate tamper-resistant chip with its own processor and memory. A TEE (trusted execution environment), such as Arm TrustZone, creates an isolated execution environment inside the main processor and shares cores and caches with the normal OS. Smartphones often use both, for example matching fingerprints in the TEE while keeping the most valuable keys in a secure element.
Is an fTPM as secure as a discrete TPM chip?

The interface is the same, but the protection differs. An fTPM runs in an isolated environment inside the main processor, so no extra chip is needed, but it can be affected by vulnerabilities in the processor's firmware and by side-channel attacks. A discrete chip can be purpose-built to resist physical attacks. Which to choose depends on the attacks you need to withstand.
What is the difference between FIPS 140-3 and Common Criteria?

FIPS 140-3 is a standard used in the US and Canadian programs that sets security requirements for cryptographic modules, grouped into four security levels of increasing strictness. Common Criteria (ISO/IEC 15408) is an international standard in which a product is evaluated against security targets defined for it, with the depth of evaluation expressed by evaluation assurance levels (EAL) and similar measures. HSMs are commonly validated under FIPS 140-3 and smart cards and secure elements under Common Criteria, though some products have both.

trustzone-vs-sgx-vs-sev-tdx.title: TrustZone vs SGX vs SEV/TDX: Isolation Unit, Trusted Computing Base and Memory Encryption Compared
trustzone-vs-sgx-vs-sev-tdx.description: Arm TrustZone, Intel SGX enclaves and AMD SEV / Intel TDX confidential VMs compared in one table: isolation unit, who they protect against, trusted computing base (TCB), memory encryption, attestation, typical use, porting effort, known attack classes and availability.
trustzone-vs-sgx-vs-sev-tdx.lead: All three are CPU hardware mechanisms, trusted execution environments (TEEs), that keep sensitive processing safe even if the normal OS or the hypervisor is compromised. They differ in the unit they carve out. TrustZone splits the processor into a secure world and a normal world and is used mainly in smartphones and embedded devices. SGX carves out only part of an application as an enclave, keeping the trusted computing base as small as possible. SEV and TDX encrypt the memory of an entire virtual machine (VM) so that even the cloud provider cannot read it, an approach known as confidential computing.
rows: Isolation unit
The whole processor is split into a secure world and a normal world; a small trusted OS and trusted applications run in the secure world
A part of an application that handles secrets (the enclave)
An entire virtual machine
Protects against
The OS and applications in the normal world; even if that kernel is compromised, secure-world memory cannot be read
The OS, the hypervisor, other applications, and attackers who physically read main memory
The hypervisor, the cloud provider's administrators, other VMs, and attackers who physically read main memory
Trusted computing base (TCB)
The CPU hardware, the secure monitor that switches worlds, and the trusted OS and applications in the secure world
The CPU hardware and firmware plus the enclave's own code; the OS is not included
The CPU hardware and firmware (such as AMD's secure processor or Intel's TDX module) plus everything inside the VM, including the guest OS; the hypervisor is not included
Memory encryption
Not part of the basic mechanism; a bus signal marks accesses as secure or not, and the accesses themselves are blocked
Enclave pages are kept encrypted in main memory outside the CPU; some implementations also detect tampering
The entire VM memory is encrypted with a per-VM key managed only inside the CPU; SEV-SNP and TDX add integrity protection that stops the hypervisor from rewriting or remapping memory
Attestation
No common architectural scheme; built by combining the SoC's secure boot and key mechanisms
The enclave's launch measurement is signed with a key inside the CPU; users check the report before handing over secret data
The CPU measures the VM's initial state and issues a report signed with a key inside the CPU; users check it before releasing the key that decrypts their data
Typical use
Biometric matching, payment credentials, DRM key storage and verification during secure boot on smartphones and embedded devices
Protecting only part of a server workload, such as key management or processing of sensitive data
Confidential VMs in the cloud, running existing applications while protecting them even from the provider
Porting effort
Code must be written as secure-world applications with a narrow interface to the normal world
Large: the application is split into parts inside and outside the enclave, and system calls, file and network I/O are left to code outside
Small: with a supported guest OS, existing operating systems and applications run almost unchanged
Known attack classes

Because cores, caches and power are shared, research has demonstrated cache side-channel attacks and fault injection through voltage or clock glitches; flaws in the trusted OS and applications are also targeted
Research has reported secrets leaking through side-channel attacks using cache timing, page-fault patterns and speculative execution

Research has reported attacks in which a malicious hypervisor manipulates the VM interface, such as memory mappings and interrupts, as well as side-channel attacks; integrity protection was added to counter such attacks
Availability
Widely used in Arm application processors, with a lightweight version in Armv8-M microcontrollers; Armv9-A also defines Arm CCA (Realms) for VM-level isolation
As of the early 2020s, Intel no longer offers SGX on client CPUs and provides it mainly on server CPUs
SEV is a feature of AMD server CPUs and TDX of Intel server CPUs; as of the mid-2020s, major clouds offer them as confidential VMs
when: TrustZone
On smartphones and embedded devices, when you want a secure area inside a single SoC without adding another chip. Biometrics, payments and secure boot checks run separated from the normal OS.
SGX (enclave)

On a server, when only a small, especially sensitive part of the work, such as key handling, must be isolated even from the OS and hypervisor. It gives the smallest trusted computing base but requires restructuring the application.
SEV/TDX (VM-based confidential computing)

In the cloud, when existing applications should run almost unchanged while being protected even from the provider's hypervisor and administrators. Remote attestation confirms the VM is the right one before data keys are released.
faq: Which is more secure, an enclave or a confidential VM?

They protect against similar parties but trust different amounts of code. An enclave removes even the OS from the trusted computing base, trusting only the CPU and the enclave's own code, so the TCB is the smallest. A confidential VM trusts the whole VM including the guest OS, so the TCB is larger, but existing software runs almost unchanged. The choice depends on how much code you need to protect and how much rework you can afford.
Does TrustZone encrypt memory?

The basic TrustZone mechanism is access control, not encryption. Every read or write the CPU puts on the bus carries a signal saying whether it is secure, and circuits in front of memory and peripherals reject normal-world accesses to secure regions. Some SoCs add encryption of external DRAM as a separate feature.
Does memory encryption also stop side-channel attacks?

No. Memory encryption prevents data in main memory from being read or modified, but cache usage, timing and page-fault patterns may still be observable from outside. Countermeasures are combined: code whose branches and memory accesses do not depend on secrets, microcode updates, and not sharing a core with untrusted parties.
Can SGX still be used?

As of the early 2020s, Intel no longer offers SGX on client CPUs and provides it mainly on server CPUs, so protecting applications on PCs can no longer assume SGX. On servers, VM-level schemes such as TDX are available alongside enclaves.

ids-vs-ips-vs-waf-vs-firewall.title: Firewall vs IDS vs IPS vs WAF: What They Inspect, Block or Alert, and What They Protect
ids-vs-ips-vs-waf-vs-firewall.description: Firewall vs IDS (intrusion detection system) vs IPS (intrusion prevention system) vs WAF compared in one table: layers inspected, inline or passive placement, action on detection, detection method, what they protect, impact of false positives, placement and limitations.
ids-vs-ips-vs-waf-vs-firewall.lead: All four defend against attacks that travel over the network, but they differ in what they inspect and what they do when they find something. A firewall lets through only the traffic its rules allow, based on IP addresses, port numbers and similar fields. An IDS (intrusion detection system) inspects traffic down to its contents, finds what looks like an attack and alerts administrators, but does not stop the traffic. An IPS (intrusion prevention system) sits in the traffic path and blocks the attacks it finds on the spot. A WAF (web application firewall) inspects the contents of HTTP requests and blocks attacks on web applications such as SQL injection. None of them covers everything on its own, so they are used together.
rows: What it mainly inspects
Source and destination IP addresses, port numbers and connection state (network and transport layers); some products also identify applications
Packet headers through contents (network layer up to the application layer)
Like an IDS, packet headers through contents
The contents of HTTP and HTTPS requests and responses (application layer)
Placement relative to the traffic path
In the path (inline)
Usually outside the path, receiving a copy of the traffic from a switch mirror port or similar
In the path (inline)
In the path, in front of the web server, as a reverse proxy or a cloud service
Action on detection
Blocks traffic its rules do not allow
Raises an alert and logs it; the traffic itself is not stopped
Blocks the traffic or drops the connection
Blocks requests judged to be attacks; a detect-and-log-only mode is also common
Detection method
Allow and deny rules (addresses, ports, connection state)
Matching against known attack patterns (signatures) and anomaly detection that looks for deviations from normal traffic
Like an IDS, signatures and anomaly detection
Rules for attack patterns such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting, and rules defining which input is allowed
What it mainly protects
The network's entry and exit points, keeping disallowed traffic out
Monitoring of networks and servers, noticing signs of attack or intrusion
Servers and endpoints on the network, against known attacks
Web applications, against attacks that exploit application vulnerabilities
Impact of false positives
A rule mistake stops legitimate traffic
Many false alarms bury real alerts and burden operators, but business traffic is not stopped
A false positive directly blocks legitimate traffic, so careful tuning is needed
Legitimate input, such as text containing symbols, judged as an attack makes users' operations fail
Example placement
At the boundary between the internal network and the internet, between network segments, and on each server or endpoint
On the network segment to be monitored (network-based) or on a server (host-based)
At the internet boundary, for example just inside the firewall
In front of a public web server
Limitations
Cannot stop attacks that pass through allowed ports, such as those exploiting web application flaws; has no function to encrypt traffic
Only detects and cannot stop; cannot inspect TLS-encrypted traffic unless placed where it can be decrypted
Unknown attacks without signatures depend on anomaly detection and are easily missed; cannot see encrypted contents; its capacity can become a traffic bottleneck
Does not protect non-web traffic; does not fix the application's vulnerabilities themselves
when: Firewall
The basic measure placed first on any network: allow only the traffic that is needed and block the rest.
IDS
When you want to notice signs of attack or intrusion without risking stopping traffic. It also keeps records for investigations.
IPS

When known attacks should be stopped automatically without waiting for a human decision. It is common to tune it first in detection-only mode before enabling blocking, so false positives do not stop business traffic.
WAF
When you publish a web application. It can serve as a stopgap while vulnerability fixes are pending, but it does not replace fixing the application.
faq: What is the main difference between an IDS and an IPS?

Whether it stops the attacks it finds. An IDS usually inspects a copy of the traffic and only raises alerts, leaving the traffic untouched. An IPS sits in the traffic path and blocks traffic judged to be an attack on the spot. With an IPS, false positives therefore block legitimate traffic, and care is needed so that a failure of the device does not stop all traffic. Many products can switch between the two modes.
If I have a firewall, do I still need a WAF?

They do different jobs, so if you publish a web application it makes sense to use both. Once a firewall allows traffic to port 443 of a web server, it does not distinguish whether the contents are legitimate requests or attacks. A WAF inspects the contents of HTTP requests and finds and blocks attack patterns such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting.
Can an IDS or IPS inspect encrypted traffic?

Not as is. To inspect the contents of TLS-encrypted traffic, it must sit behind a device that terminates TLS (such as a reverse proxy or a WAF), or the device itself must decrypt the traffic to inspect it. Without decryption, anomalies have to be found from destinations, volumes and timing patterns of the traffic.
What is a next-generation firewall (NGFW)?

A name for firewalls that combine, in one device, the traditional address-and-port rules with functions such as identifying applications from traffic contents and IPS features. The functions included vary by product, so check which layers it inspects and what it can block.

antivirus-vs-edr-vs-xdr.title: Antivirus vs EDR vs XDR: Prevention or Detection, Telemetry, Response and Scope
antivirus-vs-edr-vs-xdr.description: Antivirus (EPP) vs EDR (endpoint detection and response) vs XDR compared in one table: main purpose, scope, detection method, what they record, response after detection, strength against unknown attacks, operational load and limitations.
antivirus-vs-edr-vs-xdr.lead: All three protect endpoints from attacks, but they differ in purpose and scope. Antivirus software (an EPP, endpoint protection platform) aims to stop malware before it runs, using known malware patterns and suspicious characteristics. EDR assumes that intrusions cannot be completely prevented: it keeps recording processes, files and network activity on the endpoint, finds suspicious behavior, and helps investigate and respond, for example by isolating the endpoint. XDR correlates records not only from endpoints but also from the network, email, cloud services and identity authentication, to find the course of an attack across the whole organization. Most organizations combine a mechanism that stops attacks with one that finds and responds to what slips through.
rows: Main purpose
Find and stop malware before it runs (prevention)
Find suspicious activity after an intrusion, investigate it and respond (detection and response)
Find and respond to attacks that span endpoints, network, email, cloud and more, all together
Scope
Files on the endpoint and programs about to run
Activity on the endpoint: process launches, file and registry changes, network connections, logons
Records from endpoints plus the network, email, cloud services and identity authentication
Main detection method
Matching against known malware patterns (signatures); many products also judge how suspicious a file is from its characteristics
Detection by behavior rules and knowledge of attack techniques (such as ATT&CK); searching by IoCs
Detection that correlates events from several sources, combining signs that are weak on their own
What is recorded
Mainly detection results; endpoint activity is rarely kept for long
Endpoint activity is recorded continuously so it can be investigated retrospectively
Records from several sources are collected and stored in one place
Response after detection
Deleting or quarantining files
Killing processes, isolating the endpoint from the network and investigating the impact, remotely from the console
Isolating endpoints plus cross-domain actions such as disabling accounts or deleting emails
Strength against unknown attacks
Tends to miss new malware not in its patterns and attacks that abuse legitimate OS features
Fileless attacks and abuse of legitimate tools are easier to find from their behavior
Easier to find attack flows invisible from the endpoint alone, such as entry by email followed by lateral spread
Operational load
Relatively small; stopping automatically is the norm
Needs people to triage and investigate alerts; often combined with a SOC or an external monitoring service
Wide scope; needs integration settings and a team to judge alerts
Limitations
Hard to tell what something that slipped through did inside the endpoint
Cannot see outside the endpoint (network devices, cloud, unmanaged endpoints)
The range that can be integrated differs by product; collecting records does not replace the people and procedures that judge them
when: Antivirus (EPP)
The basic measure to install on every endpoint. It stops much known malware without waiting for a human decision.
EDR
When you assume intrusions can get through and want to find them early and limit the damage. It is also used in incident response investigations to trace back what happened on an endpoint.
XDR

When endpoints, email, cloud and so on are monitored on separate consoles and you want to follow the course of an attack in one place. Its role overlaps with a SIEM, so decide how it divides the work with the systems you already have.
faq: If I install EDR, do I still need antivirus?

Their roles differ, so in most cases both are used. Antivirus is strong at automatically stopping known malware before it runs; EDR is strong at finding, investigating and responding to the activity of attacks that slipped through. Many products provide both functions together.
Why does EDR need human response?

Because EDR alerts include legitimate administration work and business tools judged as suspicious. Deciding whether it is really an attack, investigating the scope and choosing actions such as isolation require operation by staff, a SOC or an external monitoring service. If no one looks at the alerts, the records alone cannot limit the damage.
What is the difference between XDR and a SIEM?

Both collect and correlate records from several sources, but a SIEM is usually described as a platform that collects, analyzes and stores logs broadly from many kinds of devices, while XDR focuses on deeply integrating a defined set of sources, such as endpoints and email, and handling everything from detection to response in one system. The boundary differs by product, so check what is collected and how much response can be automated.

zero-trust-vs-perimeter-security.title: Perimeter Security vs Zero Trust: Trust Assumptions, Authentication Frequency and Remote Access Compared
zero-trust-vs-perimeter-security.description: Perimeter security vs zero trust compared in one table: trust assumptions, where controls sit, how often authentication and authorization happen, remote access (VPN vs ZTNA), lateral movement after a breach, visibility and logging, fit with the cloud and migration difficulty.
zero-trust-vs-perimeter-security.lead: Perimeter security trusts the inside of the corporate network and places firewalls and VPN appliances at the boundary with the internet to keep attacks out. Zero trust grants no trust based on network location; for each combination of user, device and resource, it checks every access and then allows only what is needed. The US NIST defines zero trust architecture in SP 800-207 (2020). Zero trust spread as cloud services and access from outside the office grew and the things to protect moved beyond the perimeter.
rows: Trust assumption
The inside of the corporate network is trusted and the outside is not
Network location confers no trust; access from inside is checked every time, just like access from outside
Where controls sit
At the boundary with the internet (firewalls, VPN appliances, proxies and so on)

On each access path between users or devices and resources (applications and data), with a point that decides whether to allow access (policy decision point) and a point that enforces the decision (policy enforcement point)
Timing of authentication and authorization
Once, when entering the corporate network (for example, when connecting to the VPN)
Per resource and per session, based on user authentication (such as multi-factor authentication), device state, location and time, and re-evaluated when conditions change
Remote access
A VPN connects users to the corporate network and treats them as if they were in the office
ZTNA (zero trust network access) and similar approaches connect users only to the applications they are allowed to use, never to the whole network
Lateral movement after a breach
Once inside, traffic between internal machines faces few restrictions, so an attacker can spread easily
Access is divided finely and only the necessary rights are granted (least privilege), so spreading is harder
Treatment of devices
Devices connected to the internal network tend to be trusted
Whether a device is managed and whether its OS updates and anti-malware are in order are used as inputs to every access decision
Visibility and logging
Traffic crossing the boundary is logged, but traffic between internal machines is hard to see
Every access request and decision is logged and used for continuous monitoring and for improving the policy
Fit with the cloud
As use of cloud services and access from home grow, the things to protect move outside the boundary; routing all traffic through the VPN into the office tends to congest links and appliances
Decisions follow the same policy regardless of location, which suits cloud services and remote work
Migration difficulty
Easy to understand, and most organizations already have it
Requires identity management, device management, an inventory of assets and a designed access policy, and is adopted step by step; installing a single product does not achieve it
when: Perimeter security

Environments where users and the systems to protect are mainly on the internal network and narrowing the entry points is enough. Even after moving to zero trust, the boundary firewall remains as one layer of defense in depth.
Zero trust

Environments centered on cloud services and remote work, where the line between inside and outside is blurred. It also suits cases where you assume a breach will happen and want to limit how far the damage can spread.
Gradual migration
Most organizations migrate step by step while still using perimeter mechanisms: enforcing multi-factor authentication, managing devices, and moving important applications to ZTNA one by one.
faq: Does zero trust make VPNs unnecessary?

VPNs used to reach internal applications from outside are often replaced by ZTNA, because a VPN gives access to the whole network once connected, while ZTNA connects users only to allowed applications and checks each access. Some VPNs, such as those linking branch offices, remain in use for other purposes.
Is zero trust a product name?

No, it is a security design approach, not a product. NIST SP 800-207 (2020) describes zero trust and its architecture as an approach that grants no trust based solely on network location or asset ownership and performs authentication and authorization for each access to a resource. Implementing it combines identity management, multi-factor authentication, device management, ZTNA, logging and monitoring.
Does zero trust make firewalls unnecessary?

No. Zero trust means not trusting something merely because it is inside the boundary; it does not mean removing boundary defenses. Firewalls continue to be used as a layer that cuts unwanted traffic at the entrance and as a means of dividing the network into fine segments.

rsa-vs-ecc-vs-pqc.title: RSA vs Elliptic-Curve vs Post-Quantum Cryptography: Key Sizes, Speed, Quantum Resistance and Migration Compared
rsa-vs-ecc-vs-pqc.description: RSA vs elliptic-curve cryptography vs post-quantum cryptography (ML-KEM and ML-DSA) compared in one table: underlying hard problem, key sizes, ciphertext and signature sizes, speed, quantum resistance, standardization, typical uses today, migration and implementation cautions.
rsa-vs-ecc-vs-pqc.lead: All three are public-key cryptography, used to share keys (key exchange or key encapsulation) and for digital signatures. RSA rests on the difficulty of factoring large numbers, and elliptic-curve cryptography on the difficulty of the discrete logarithm problem on elliptic curves; for the same security, elliptic-curve cryptography needs much shorter keys than RSA. Both, however, would be broken by Shor's algorithm once a large fault-tolerant quantum computer exists. Post-quantum cryptography rests on problems such as lattice problems that are believed to be hard even for quantum computers; in August 2024 the US NIST published standards including the key encapsulation mechanism ML-KEM (FIPS 203) and the signature scheme ML-DSA (FIPS 204). Their main drawback is large keys and signatures.
rows: Underlying hard problem
Factoring large numbers
The discrete logarithm problem on elliptic curves

For ML-KEM and ML-DSA, lattice problems (such as Module-LWE, recovering a secret from linear equations with small errors added); there is also SLH-DSA (FIPS 205), a signature scheme based only on hash functions
Key size (guideline)
In the NIST SP 800-57 table, the guideline for 128-bit security is a 3072-bit n (384 bytes); 2048 bits corresponds to 112-bit security
In the same table, the guideline for 128-bit security is 256 bits; in X25519 key exchange the public value sent is 32 bytes
An ML-KEM-768 public key (encapsulation key) is 1,184 bytes, far larger than the 32 bytes of X25519
Ciphertext and signature size
Both ciphertexts and signatures are as long as n (384 bytes for 3072 bits)
An ECDSA (P-256) signature is two 256-bit values, r and s, for 64 bytes (slightly more depending on the encoding)
An ML-KEM-768 ciphertext is 1,088 bytes and an ML-DSA-65 signature is 3,309 bytes
Speed
Because the public exponent can be small (such as 65537), encryption and signature verification are fast; decryption, signing and key generation are heavy
Key generation and signing are much faster than RSA at the same security; signature verification is often slower than RSA
ML-KEM computation is light and is considered no slower than elliptic-curve key exchange; the size of the data sent tends to be the bigger issue than computation
Quantum resistance
None: Shor's algorithm breaks it on a large fault-tolerant quantum computer
None: Shor's algorithm also solves the discrete logarithm problem, so it is broken like RSA
Believed to be hard to solve efficiently even with quantum computers (this has not been proven)
Standardization
Invented in 1977; in practice used with randomized padding such as OAEP for encryption and PSS for signatures
Curves such as P-256, and X25519 and Ed25519 based on Curve25519, are widely used
Published by NIST in August 2024 as FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA) and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA)
Typical uses today
As of the mid-2020s, mainly certificates and software signing; TLS 1.3 removed key exchange that sends key material encrypted with RSA
As of the mid-2020s, the mainstay of TLS key exchange (ECDHE); also ECDSA and EdDSA signatures, and resource-constrained devices such as smart cards and embedded systems
As of 2025, hybrid key exchange combined with X25519 (such as X25519MLKEM768) has started to be used in TLS 1.3; migration of signatures is following after key exchange
Migration
A target of the migration to post-quantum cryptography; replacing signatures, such as in certificates and code signing, is the challenge
A target of the migration; during the transition it serves as one half of hybrid key exchange with ML-KEM, providing security against classical computers
For now, migration proceeds step by step with hybrid schemes that combine it with conventional cryptography; designs that make algorithms easy to swap later (crypto agility) are emphasized
Implementation cautions
Never use textbook RSA without padding; key generation needs good-quality randomness
Reusing or biasing the per-signature random value (nonce) lets attackers recover the private key; received points must also be checked to lie on the correct curve
Large keys and signatures require checking the impact on packet sizes and memory-constrained devices; watch for bugs in new implementations and for side-channel attacks
when: RSA
When compatibility with existing certificates and systems is required. Fast verification suits uses with many verifiers, but a plan for migrating to post-quantum cryptography is needed.
Elliptic-curve cryptography
When new systems today need key exchange and signatures with short keys and small data. It also suits smart cards and embedded devices. Plan a move to hybrid schemes to prepare for quantum computers.
Post-quantum cryptography (ML-KEM, ML-DSA)

When protecting data that must stay secret for a long time. To prepare for "harvest now, decrypt later", where ciphertext recorded today is decrypted in the future, adopt it first for key exchange in a hybrid scheme.
faq: Why does elliptic-curve cryptography need shorter keys than RSA?

Because the best known attacks differ in cost. Factoring has methods much faster than brute force, so RSA keys must be quite long. For the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problem, even the best known attacks take work on the order of half the key length in bits, so the key only needs to be about twice the security level. In the NIST SP 800-57 table, the guideline for 128-bit security is 3072 bits for RSA versus 256 bits for elliptic-curve cryptography.
Why migrate now when quantum computers do not exist yet?

Because ciphertext intercepted and stored today could be decrypted by future quantum computers (harvest now, decrypt later). On top of that, replacing cryptography takes many years across software, devices and certificate infrastructure. That is why migration is starting with key exchange, which carries data that must stay secret for a long time.
Will quantum computers also break symmetric ciphers such as AES?

They are not targets of Shor's algorithm. Under the simple guideline that Grover's algorithm gives a quadratic speedup in key search, the security level in bits is halved, which can be handled by choosing AES-256 where long-term security is needed. What must be replaced is mainly public-key cryptography such as RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography.
What is a hybrid scheme?

A scheme that uses conventional cryptography and post-quantum cryptography at the same time and combines the results. In key exchange, the shared secrets from X25519 and ML-KEM both go into key derivation, so the resulting key stays protected as long as either one is secure. Post-quantum schemes are new, and implementation errors or new attacks cannot yet be fully ruled out, so the hybrid approach serves as insurance during the transition.
